- Published
At least one person has been killed in an overnight attack on St Petersburg that successfully targeted two of the city's oil facilities.
The region's Governor Alexander Beglov said fires were being extinguished at the St Petersburg Oil Terminal and the Ruchyi oil depot following the attack, which also injured at least five.
A logistics centre belonging to Ozon - known as Russia's Amazon - and a data centre belonging to Facebook equivalent VKontakte were also hit.
Kyiv has not yet commented on the strikes. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Saturday morning that Russia had targeted his country's energy sector 76 times since Donald Trump declared an "energy ceasefire" last week.
Ukraine had paused its strikes on Russian oil facilities - which it says are to limit the main revenue stream for Moscow's war effort - for three days after the announcement, while accusing Russia of continuing.
It then resumed strikes earlier this week, drawing the ire of Trump, who called for a truce to facilitate a deal he struck with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin to supply diesel.
Ukraine has struck St Petersburg before, though regions closer to Ukraine are threatened more often. The city's oil terminal was last hit in July.
Russia's defence ministry said it had shot down more than 1,000 Ukrainian drones over Russian territory overnight into Sunday.
St Petersburg's governor said 12 apartment buildings and two homes were damaged in the attacks on the city, while Pulkovo Airport was temporarily closed.
He also said mobile internet service disruption was possible.
Social network VK confirmed a drone had targeted its regional data centre, but stressed its services were available "as usual" after users reported outages in the early hours of the morning.
Ozon also confirmed its local logistics centre had been targeted by a drone, sparking a fire.
It said staff were evacuated and no one was injured, and that it was not accepting shipments from sellers at the location "as it is currently serving other operational purposes".
As well as numerous oil facilities across Russia, Ukraine has also mounted strikes aimed at disrupting the Russian economy more broadly. Earlier this month, it launched a series of attacks on Yandex, Russia's largest search engine, that led to service disruptions.
Relations between Washington and Kyiv have frayed since the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel in the hope of bringing down US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war, ahead of the midterm elections.
Zelensky suggested the deal was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort.
Trump's decision to temporarily suspend a raft of sanctions against Russia has brought fresh criticism, including from some US Republicans.
Both Russia and Ukraine have been striking one another's energy infrastructure with increasing intensity ahead of the winter, as Moscow's full-scale invasion drags on in its fifth year.
Russia says it hits targets used by Ukraine's military, though the UN noted on Friday that the first two weeks of October had been the deadliest for Ukrainian civilians in years.
Russian strikes on energy facilities have left hundreds of thousands without power, raising concerns about civilians enduring another freezing winter.
Zelensky said on Saturday that tens of thousands of people were still without power. Russia launched nearly 2,700 drones, 1,700 aerial bombs and 66 missiles in the past week, most of which were aimed at energy facilities, he said.

ba080683b709.text: In red states and blue, unconventional candidates are downplaying — or even disowning — party labels to tap into voters' deep disdain for Washington. Why it matters: They might not all win, but the sheer number of political outsiders connecting with voters tells us something about the electorate: It's angry and willing to take risks. The candidates — whether they come from the pulpit or the NFL sidelines — are making the same bet: Voters are tired of career politicians. Zoom in: Consider three unorthodox Democrats leading in Senate contests in three red states: a Presbyterian seminarian in Texas (state Rep. James Talarico), a megachurch pastor in Kansas (Adam Hamilton), and an Alaska Native in that state (former Rep. Mary Peltola, who once skipped a week of House votes to go fishing when Chinook salmon were running). Deep-blue Minnesota's Senate race features Michele Tafoya — a former NFL sideline reporter who's endorsed by President Trump but calls herself an independent Republican. She's mounting a serious challenge to Democrat Peggy Flanagan , the lieutenant governor. In House races, on the Democratic side there's a smokejumper in Montana (Sam Forstag), a 29-year-old barista in Colorado (Melat Kiros) and a Tejano singer in Texas (Bobby Pulido). Four independent Senate candidates are courting Democratic voters without running with a (D) next to their names — and sometimes without a Democrat officially in the race. In Nebraska, Dan Osborn, a union steamfitter and former factory mechanic, is mounting a serious independent challenge to Sen. Pete Ricketts, a former two-term governor whose family owns the Chicago Cubs. In Montana, Seth Bodnar , a former Army Green Beret and University of Montana president, is running as an independent for an open Senate seat. Democrats tried to persuade their nominee to drop out, but she stayed in the race. In South Dakota, Brian Bengs, a onetime park ranger, is challenging Republican Sen. Mike Rounds as an independent. Four years ago, Bengs ran against Sen. John Thune as a Democrat. In Idaho, former Army tank commander and tech executive Todd Achilles is running as an independent against Republican Sen. Jim Risch. (Achilles previously served in the Idaho House as a Democrat. The official Democratic Senate nominee dropped out of the race in July.) For many Republicans , quasi-Democrats running as independents amount to foul play — an attempt to deceive voters by discarding an unpopular brand. Between the lines: Even candidates with more conventional backgrounds are shading their biographies to meet the populist moment. In the Maine Senate race, Democrat Troy Jackson — who spent two decades in the state House and Senate before being term-limited out in 2024 — introduces himself as a fifth-generation Maine logger. Zoom out: The populist path to Washington is at least as old as President Andrew Jackson, who first took office in 1829. It's as fresh as President Trump. In recent years, there have been unorthodox candidates on both sides. Some succeeded; others didn't. Al Franken, famous for being a writer and actor on "Saturday Night Live," won a U.S. Senate seat in Minnesota in 2008 and served more than eight years before resigning. Herschel Walker, a celebrated college and NFL running back, couldn't find the end zone in his 2022 Senate race in Georgia. Say what you want about the 45th and 47th president: The New York developer with a penchant for gold leaf has connected with disaffected working-class voters. Democrats have struggled to match Trump's appeal to non-college-educated voters, but Trump has made their task easier this cycle with an unpopular war and tariffs that voters blame for high prices. The bottom line: A version of the insurgent-vs.-establishment battle played out in Democratic primaries earlier this year, when seven House incumbents went down — tying a 21st-century high . That included Kiros, the 29-year-old Colorado barista and democratic socialist who defeated a 15-term incumbent in the primary and is on a glide path to victory next month.

134b104b418b.text: Data: U.S. Census ; Map: Erin Davis/Axios California and Louisiana have something surprising in common: Both have among the nation's highest poverty rates when the cost of living is factored in, according to Census Bureau data. Why it matters: Southern states dominate America's traditional poverty rankings. But that familiar geographic divide starts to disappear when more of a family's financial realities are taken into account. Axios analyzed 2023-2025 state poverty estimates from the Census Bureau to see what happens when housing, taxes, medical expenses and government benefits enter the picture. What we found: Under the Census' traditional-style official measure, Louisiana had a 19.6% poverty rate and California was at 10.7%. New Hampshire was the lowest at 5.4%. The South is home to 10 of the 11 states where the traditional poverty rate significantly outpaced the national average. California's poverty rate jumped by nearly two-thirds to 17.8% under the broader Supplemental Poverty Measure , or SPM. Louisiana remained near the top at 19%. Maine posted the nation's lowest SPM rate at 6.4%, followed by Nebraska at 7.5% and Minnesota at 7.9%. How it works: The traditional measure compares pretax cash income with a family-size threshold that doesn't change by geography. The SPM adds benefits such as SNAP and housing assistance, factors in taxes and tax credits, subtracts work and medical expenses, and adjusts for geographic differences in housing costs. Zoom out: The official poverty rate fell for a third straight year to 10.2%, while child poverty reached a record-low 13.4%. Yet the SPM remained statistically unchanged at 13.1% — nearly three percentage points above the official rate . Real median household income hit a record $87,460 in 2025. Yes, but: The SPM doesn't replace the official poverty rate. Census designed it as another lens — one that captures resources and unavoidable expenses the traditional measure misses. The state figures also aren't single-year 2025 estimates. Census recommends three-year averages because state samples in the Current Population Survey are smaller. The bottom line: Income alone doesn't tell you whether a family can make ends meet.

4758de419fcc.text:
Pope Leo XIV thanks wellwishers in first event after cancer surgery
Pope Leo XIV held his first public engagement since his lung cancer surgery on Sunday, as he recited the Angelus prayer from the window of Vatican's Apostolic Palace.
The surgery had taken place just a few days before, after Pope Leo had been diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer.
After the prayer, he thanked the people who have prayed for him in recent days and said he appreciated the support. He added he will now gradually return to his commitments as he recovers.

7978fd2bc8f0.text: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky spoke Sunday with President Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner about the crisis between the countries and U.S. efforts to resume peace talks with Russia. Why it matters: It was the first call between Zelensky and senior U.S. officials since tensions spiked between their countries after Trump cut a diesel deal with Russia 10 days ago. Driving the news: The call took place amid assertions by Zelensky that the Trump administration was behind restrictions imposed on the Starlink and Starshield satellite systems used by the Ukrainian military. "Who made this decision? I don't know. I think that this is really both [White House and SpaceX] decision. If President Trump will decide tomorrow, or better today, if he will personally decide to lift this decision, it will immediately work as it was before," Zelensky said on NBC's "Meet the Press" Sunday. He added, "The message came from [the U.S.] government. I don't know from whom. It's the opinion of our generals, of our government, and of course also my opinion, that it was a message from the American government to limit the speed. And technically, SpaceX did it." Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday that the U.S. government was not involved in the Starlink restrictions and said it has been restored. Ukrainian officials dispute that.

a7c7535e8169.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/jackson-doesnt-regret-telling-collins-to-shut-up-after-protester-interrupted-maine-senate-debate Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Jackson doesn't regret telling Collins to 'shut up' after protester interrupted Maine Senate debate Politics Oct 18, 2026 2:01 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Maine Democrat Troy Jackson says he does not regret telling Sen. Susan Collins that she should "shut up" after the Republican suggested a protester who interrupted their recent debate was one of his campaign's backers. READ MORE: What happened in the first Maine Senate debate between Collins and Jackson "She said that it was a Troy supporter. She accused me of setting that up. I had no idea who it was," said Jackson, a former president of the state Senate who is trying to deny Collins, the longest-serving Republican woman in Senate history, a sixth-term. He spoke in an interview with CNN's "State of the Union" that aired Sunday. During their final debate Thursday night in the closely contested race, as the Nov. 3 election nears a protester opposing data centers began yelling as Collins spoke. While moderators asked for that person to be removed, the senator said the demonstrator was "obviously one of Troy's supporters." Jackson responded: "Oh, shut up. I don't even know that kid." Watch the moment from the debate in the video player above. The Sunrise Movement group posted on its Instagram page that the outburst came from one of its members. In a caption of an Instagram post, the group's page said: "We're proud of this Sunrise volunteer who took action yesterday." The New York Times said the protester, Henry Elgie, a 19-year-old student at Bowdoin College in Maine, told the newspaper in an interview Saturday that he had "zero coordination" with Jackson's campaign. "I do not know Troy Jackson personally or at all," he was quoted as saying. The Sunrise Movement is a left-wing political advocacy organization that champions the Green New Deal, aimed at transitioning the U.S. economy to 100% renewable energy. The group, which has local arms around the country, regularly organizes protests, sit-ins and climate strikes. Jackson told CNN that he shook hands with Collins after each of their debates. "But what I'm not going to be is talked down to by Sen. Collins," he said. He added: "I'm fighting for Mainers and I just think that was another situation where she was talking down to me and I'm not going to apologize for that." WATCH: Collins, Jackson face off in testy Maine U.S. Senate debate Collins told Fox News' Sean Hannity on Friday that she was "struck by how reflective the response, 'Oh, shut up,' was." Collins said "the fact that it seemed like such an automatic, quick reply was very telling." She cited what she said was "the reputation" that Jackson had in the Legislature "particularly when he's dealing with women with whom he disagrees. So in some ways it didn't surprise me." Some state lawmakers who worked with Jackson have criticized him as having a temper, including once throwing a plastic water bottle on the ground in frustration while disagreeing with a female lawmaker. Asked by reporters during the campaign about the confrontations, Jackson said, "I wear my heart on my sleeve." He took responsibility for his outburst and apologized to those he had confrontations with at the time. Jackson was asked on CNN about some Republicans who are saying there were stories that he was aggressive in his tone to women from his time in the Legislature and that his remark Thursday night was another example of that. Jackson said some Republicans have been spending millions "attacking me and my family, making untrue claims. … So it doesn't surprise me." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Donate now By — Associated Press Associated Press

2ab5965496b3.text: President Trump's top aides offered sharply different explanations this weekend of his Russian diesel deal amid a barrage of bipartisan criticism calling the move a gift to Russia. Why it matters: Oil, gas and petroleum products help finance Russia's war on Ukraine, and Trump's moves are bringing rifts within the GOP just ahead of midterm elections. Catch up quick: Late Friday, Trump waived new sanctions against Russia and tariffs on top buyers of Russian energy that would have taken effect under the bipartisan Graham Act he signed last month. That came just days after the administration waived certain sanctions as part of a deal aimed at enabling higher exports of Russian diesel after high prices have become a political millstone for Republicans. Driving the news: Energy Secretary Chris Wright argued Sunday on CNN's "State of the Union" that Russia could only benefit from the diesel deal if it scales back its war on Ukraine enough to increase exports. "This is a carrot to try to end a war. It's not an economic lifeline for Russia," he said. Yet Secretary of State Marco Rubio offered a different explanation Saturday, saying Russia would have sold the diesel regardless of Trump's intervention. "That diesel was going to be sold one way or the other," Rubio told reporters at Joint Base Andrews, per a State Department transcript. The diesel deal "is an incentive to Russia, that if they can reduce the conflict with Ukraine, they can get an energy ceasefire or reduce the conflict such that they have diesel to export, we'll allow it to flow to world markets," Wright told ABC's "This Week." Context: Ukranian drone strikes against Russian refineries have dramatically hindered Russia's diesel exports. Ukraine resumed those strikes after Russia continued to hit Ukrainian energy infrastructure, despite Trump's claim that the two sides had agreed to an energy ceasefire. The combination of the Iran war — which has throttled supply and damaged Middle East refineries — and Russia's export decline have pushed up diesel costs. Zoom out: The Sunday shows and Rubio's remarks provided the Trump team's most detailed comments on Friday night's executive order , which declines to use new powers under the law named after the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.). The move avoids putting fresh pressure on China and India, both major buyers of Russian oil. Rubio said Trump wants time to "analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the U.S. economy." Wright pointed to ongoing negotiations with China on trade and the war in Ukraine, stressing to CNN that Trump retains the power to impose the penalties later. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, on NBC's "Meet the Press," defended the recent decisions by pointing to sanctions the administration imposed on Russian oil and gas giants Rosneft and Lukoil in 2025. "No one has been tougher on Russian sanctions than President Trump," he said. The other side: A number of Republicans have criticized the White House. Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) called the sanctions waiver "beyond irresponsible," while Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) said the late Lindsey Graham "would be appalled." Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) called the waiver a "mistake," and Rep. French Hill (R-Ark.) said the U.S. should be increasing pressure on Russia and requested a classified briefing on the decision. What we're watching: As the midterms hit their final frenzied weeks, Republicans have shown an increasing willingness to put distance between themselves and Trump.

e5e7d8c7c805.text: President Trump endorsed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday, just nine days before Israel's Oct. 27 elections. Why it matters: Trump's decision to weigh in nine days ahead of the election could give Netanyahu a boost at a critical moment in the Israeli leader's fight for political survival, with most polls showing his coalition falling short of the 61 seats needed to form a government. What he is saying: In a Sunday post on Truth Social , Trump called Netanyahu "a Great Warrior Prime Minister" and a "great partner" in the war against Iran. "If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work [in Iran] ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," Trump wrote. Trump called Netanyahu "the kind of Partner that the United States of America is demanding of Israel" and gave him his "Complete and Total Endorsement." Behind the scenes: Trump began planning his endorsement earlier this week. "I was always going to do that. I just didn't want to do it too soon," Trump told Axios in a short phone interview on Sunday. Trump said he endorsed Netanyahu because they have a "good relationship" and would "continue to do well" together if Netanyahu is reelected. "It is important that Israel has a person they can count on," Trump said. Asked if he could work with another Israeli leader, Trump said: "Maybe I will, maybe I won't. Who wants to take the chance?" The other side: Netanyahu thanked Trump for his endorsement in an X post. "Together we will complete the mission," Netanyahu wrote . Netanyahu's main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, told Israel's Channel 12 that he respects the U.S. president and appreciates what he has done for Israel. "But the elections are a domestic Israeli issue. The only ones who will decide are the citizens of Israel, and I will stand firm on this," Eisenkot said. The big picture: Trump had repeatedly declined to endorse Netanyahu in recent months amid growing tensions between the two leaders over Iran and Gaza. ⁠Some of Netanyahu's rivals urged Trump to remain neutral, Axios previously reported . Some of Trump's closest advisers believed his Middle East agenda would fare better if Netanyahu lost and a different government formed. Trump himself has been very frustrated with Netanyahu, including in recent weeks. In private conversations, Trump blamed Netanyahu for Israel's failures to prevent the Oct. 7 Hamas attacks. Trump called the prime minister "his own worst enemy" and questioned whether Netanyahu was damaging Israel's international reputation, according to two people who have discussed the matter directly with the president. However, Trump decided to stick with Netanyahu. Driving the news: Netanyahu and Trump discussed two weeks ago the possibility of launching a major new operation against Iran before the Israeli and U.S. elections, Axios reported . Trump initially seemed to be leaning toward accepting Netanyahu's proposal and resuming attacks, but he grew more hesitant and decided to wait until after the elections. In his endorsement, Trump seemed to suggest he would let Netanyahu strike Iran after the midterm elections, saying "we will soon finish the job." This is a breaking news story. a35b4cb33faf.text: By — Cara Anna, Associated Press Cara Anna, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/photographer-attacked-by-settlers-in-the-west-bank-feels-insulted-by-netanyahu Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Photographer attacked by settlers in the West Bank feels insulted by Netanyahu World Oct 18, 2026 1:13 PM EDT JERUSALEM (AP) — The photographer with The Washington Post who was attacked by Jewish settlers in the occupied West Bank so badly that several vertebrae were broken said Sunday she was increasingly angry that Israel's military seems to protect settlers more than the Palestinians they threaten. The attack on Heidi Levine and Palestinians during the sensitive olive harvest — followed a day later by an attack on European diplomats in a Christian village — again highlights the rampant settler violence that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has blamed on a small number of troublemakers. WATCH: Israeli settlers attack Palestinians during olive harvest Levine, from her hospital bed, has told The Associated Press she was "shocked and insulted" that Netanyahu referred to the attack on her and others as alleged, adding that the prime minister "had all the evidence on the table." But she described the sharp condemnation of settler violence expressed to her in a call from Israel's president, and in a letter signed by several of the country's top former security and intelligence officials. All expressed shame over the attack. Netanyahu, two weeks out from close elections that could end his time in power, is again confronted with an issue that has drawn growing international condemnation. Much of the world considers the settlements in the West Bank illegal, and yet construction and expansion continue. Hundreds of Palestinians have been attacked and a few have been killed this olive harvest alone, which started in late September, rights groups have said. Olive trees, a central part of history and heritage for Palestinians, have been destroyed. Levine blamed "Jewish terrorists" for Thursday's attack and added: "I've been covering this region for over 40 years, and I have never seen this country in such a state as it is today." Levine praises a call from Israel's president Levine was recovering Sunday from injuries that included what appeared to be stab wounds in her buttocks, which required stitches. There was nothing new from police on the case, she said. U.S. Ambassador Mike Huckabee, whose recent comments have condemned settler attacks on U.S. citizens but not on Palestinians overall, called the attack on Levine a "despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards" and said they should spend years in prison. Separately, Israeli President Isaac Herzog called Levine, and Yair Golan, a former general and leader of the opposition Democrats party, visited. Netanyahu's main rival in the elections, Gadi Eisenkot, said on X that "a handful of criminals is burning up the last shreds of legitimacy left to the state of Israel." READ MORE: Trump endorses embattled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection Herzog was "actually very sweet," Levine said Sunday. "Down to earth, calling them thugs, inviting me for a personal hug. He's ashamed for what happened: 'These people are a stain on Israeli society.'" She said she has not heard from Netanyahu. She did receive, however, a letter signed by over a dozen former Israeli security, intelligence and other officials, including former Defense Minister Moshe Yaalon, former Mossad director Tamir Pardo and former Shin Bet director Ami Ayalon. "We are deeply ashamed that Jewish terrorists in the West Bank continue to inflict suffering on innocent Palestinians, assault those who come to their defense, and target those who document and expose their despicable conduct," said the letter, shared with the AP. "Their brutality brings disgrace upon Israel and the Jewish people. Such acts undermine Israel's security, its regional and international standing, and the moral fabric of our society. They represent a betrayal of everything we have devoted our lives to defending." The letter noted that "alas, with encouragement from the highest echelons of government," only a fundamental change in policy can end the "disgraceful phenomenon." Levine says she plans to return to work Levin told the AP that "I never wanted the story to be about me but about the people I've tried to document" over decades. She said she has sought to show how the violence is "increasing, becoming more and more dangerous." She has said the attackers — armed with bottles and slingshots — "were kicking me for like 10 minutes and I was trying to hold on to my cameras and my bag." Her helmet and protective vest, which was marked "PRESS," likely saved her from more serious injuries. READ MORE: Masked settlers attack European diplomats in the occupied West Bank But she and others have openly wondered who will protect Palestinians. Rights groups have said few settlers are ever punished for the attacks that have surged in recent years. "It's about time you do something, Mr. Prime Minister," Levine said. As for herself, she plans to return to work. "I've invested decades of blood, sweat and tears into this," she said. "They cracked my bones, they haven't cracked my spirit." Associated Press writer Sam Mednick in Tel Aviv, Israel, contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Price, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-says-he-will-close-historic-d-c-golf-course-for-15-months-of-renovations Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump says he will close historic D.C. golf course for 15 months of renovations Politics Updated on Oct 18, 2026 1:02 PM EDT — Published on Oct 18, 2026 12:46 PM EDT WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (AP) — President Donald Trump on Sunday announced plans to close a historic public golf course in the nation's capital for 15 months and redevelop it despite an ongoing court challenge to his long-sought renovation. Trump posted on social media about his intent to shutter the East Potomac Golf Course, not far from the White House, starting Nov. 15 to make it "one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World." A judge last week, however, ordered a halt to his redevelopment plans until at least Oct. 26 after scolding the government for starting a large-scale tree removal at the course over a holiday weekend while providing little notice to the court or the plaintiffs trying to stop the makeover. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Trump did not acknowledge the legal fight in his post, which included an artist's rendering for the course redesign. "When completed, it will be open to the Public while, at the same time, designed to the Highest Level of Golf and able to hold World Class Tournaments such as the U.S. Open, the PGA Championship, the Ryder Cup, and the Presidents Cup," Trump wrote. Democracy Forward, which is representing the plaintiffs challenging his renovation plans, responded by saying that the course is part of a national park and recreation facility that is meant for everyone to enjoy. "Our litigation is intended to protect this community jewel for the people and communities it serves and we will continue to work with our plaintiffs to defend it from unlawful and harmful intrusion," Skye Perryman, the president and CEO of the group, said in a statement Sunday. Capital makeover extends well beyond the fairways Trump, a golf aficionado who plays often, had already announced plans to makeover the links as part of his broader push to renovate and refurbish places around Washington, including the White House and the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. Many of his projects, including plans for a huge ballroom at the White House, the installation of his own name on the Kennedy Center and construction of a massive arch, have been challenged in courts. The 106-year-old park and course has been the subject of many emergency hearings as the president has sought to renovate it. While it has been open to Washingtonians of all income levels, opponents of Trump's plans to turn it into a high-end course have argued it will alter the character of the space and make it less affordable to people. Trump in his post echoed arguments he has made to justify his plans to remake the Kennedy Center, arguing it is in such dangerous condition that it needs to close. READ MORE: Federal judge orders Trump administration to halt work for a day on historic D.C. golf course "The current Course is old, broken, dilapidated, and of no further use or effect. It is in very poor condition, with falling, dangerous, and disease infested trees and, importantly, a collapsing and hazardous seawall," Trump wrote. Debris from the demolition of the White House East Wing to make way for his ballroom project has also been dumped on the grounds. The National Park Service has said the debris tested positive for lead, chromium and other toxic metals. Trump also sought to justify the National Park Service's removal of hundreds of trees that the judge paused, writing in his announcement that when the gold course was originally built, "it was famous for no trees, with views of Washington, D.C., for all to see, but now, it is completely overgrown, dysfunctional, and unsafe." Legal case returns to court and the administration seeks to remove the judge Trump's post outlining a clear plan for construction complicates a federal court hearing scheduled for Monday in a lawsuit filed by the DC Preservation League and two golfers opposing the construction. U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes has ordered key members of the Republican administration to testify on the recent tree-cutting and whether those actions are tied to the president's plans for the historical public links. The administration on Friday asked for Reyes to be replaced on the case, questioning her impartiality and citing what it called "egregious" behavior from the bench in response to an emergency hearing Oct. 12. Her frustration boiled over in a three-hour hearing when she lambasted the government's attorney for the lack of notification she and the plaintiffs received before the trees were chopped down. At the upcoming hearing, the judge is expected to address the request that she step aside. Meanwhile, over the weekend the plaintiffs asked that she grant them a more long-standing preliminary injunction in the case and/or a stay. Associated Press writer Gary Fields in Washington contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 13108447493d.text: By — Colleen Barry, Associated Press Colleen Barry, Associated Press By — Trisha Thompson, Associated Press Trisha Thompson, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/pope-leo-tells-faithful-in-st-peters-square-he-will-gradually-resume-duties-after-cancer-surgery Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Pope Leo tells faithful in St. Peter's Square he will gradually resume duties after cancer surgery World Updated on Oct 18, 2026 1:46 PM EDT — Published on Oct 18, 2026 12:34 PM EDT VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV thanked thousands of faithful in St. Peter's Square on Sunday for their prayers while he was hospitalized for an operation to remove a malignant tumor, and said he plans to gradually return to his usual duties. READ MORE: Pope returns to Vatican days after surgery; surgeon says he should be fit for Latin America tour The crowd erupted in cheers when the pontiff showed himself in the window overlooking the square, where a week ago on the same occasion of the traditional Angelus blessing he revealed that a nodule had been located on his lung, and that it would be surgically removed. "Now that this delicate phase is behind me, I will gradually resume my activities, always with God's help and your prayers," Leo said, his voice sounding strong four days after the lower lobe of his right lung was removed. The pontiff said the experience of the last week "has made me feel especially close to those facing illness and infirmity." He told the faithful that he had "truly felt your support," and expressed "particular gratitude to the doctors, nurses and all the staff at Gemelli hospital" where he was treated. The pope paused for a moment and waved to the crowd before retreating into his apartment in the Apostolic Palace. A delegation from Africa in Rome for a congress danced and ululated after the pope's blessing. "He was always in our prayers when he was sick, and we are happy to see him today," said Alain Kalembu of the Democratic Republic of Congo. "This is an expression of our joy." The 71-year-old pontiff had the lower lobe of his right lung removed on Tuesday in the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. He told a reporter in English that he was doing "much better" as he drove away from Rome's Gemelli hospital to return to the Vatican, after a shorter hospital stay than had initially been anticipated. WATCH: What we know about Pope Leo's lung cancer and prognosis "I don't believe it, because he was just operated on the other day," Cosimo Mastrocinque, a retired factory worker visiting the Vatican from the southern region of Puglia, said. "It is a miracle that he recovered already." American tourists were especially eager to pray alongside the first pope born in the United States. Marla Marsala of Michigan was supposed to attend a Mass with the pope last week that was canceled due to his hospitalization. "I am just happy that we are praying with him today instead of for him, like we were before," Marsala said. "It was a tough week for all of the people who love him, which are many. He seems like a very strong soul. So I think he will pull through and fight it, and succeed and keep doing the wonderful work he is doing." Claire Holland from Jacksonville, Florida, said she felt "very blessed" to be present for the pope's return to his flock. "I'm so happy that he has recovered so quickly. I think there have been millions and millions of prayers. And he is a strong, determined man, and I am so happy that he is feeling well enough to do this," Holland said. Leo's next major engagement is an ambitious Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, including a dozen flights and two helicopter rides to high altitudes. His surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, told Vatican News on Saturday that "there are no clinical reasons why it should not take place." "The Holy Father has put his heart and soul into his recovery," Margaritora told Vatican News, adding that he expected the pope to recover fully from surgery "in another 10 days or so." Histological testing of the tumor and related lymph nodes was underway. The results, along with details of the tumor's molecular and genetic makeup, will help doctors determine whether the pope needs additional treatment. Options include chemotherapy, a combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy, or targeted oral therapy based on the tumor's genetic characteristics. Price, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-endorses-embattled-israeli-prime-minister-benjamin-netanyahu-for-reelection Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump endorses embattled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection Politics Oct 18, 2026 12:18 PM EDT WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (AP) — President Donald Trump on Sunday endorsed embattled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu late in his reelection campaign, a coveted boost because of Trump's popularity but one that the American had withheld for months as the vote neared and the leaders' strategies in the Middle East diverged. Trump said in a post on social media that Netanyahu "has been a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran." Israelis are set to vote Oct. 27, in the first national elections since Hamas attacked Israel on Oct. 7, 2023. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The absence of an endorsement was a setback for the Likud politician, who had billed his tight ties to the Republican president as a selling point for staying in power. "Thank you, President Trump, for the tremendous support and work together," Netanyahu said in a statement in Hebrew posted on X. "Together we will complete the mission!" His Likud Party attached to the statement a 35-second video showing clips of the two leaders together and Trump praising Netanyahu. It was not immediately clear what impact the endorsement would have on what is expected to be a tight race. Trump is still popular in Israel, but many Israelis, including leading commentators, have expressed disappointment over the inconclusive outcome of the Iran war and Trump's ceasefire proposal, which fell short of many of the countries' key goals when they jointly launched the war in February. READ MORE: Scars from Oct. 7 fuel deep divisions over Netanyahu ahead of Israeli election In his post, Trump again threatened to "soon finish the job" against Iran "unless they change their ways, rapidly," but added he might not want to if Netanyahu loses the election. "If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," Trump said. He said Netanyahu had been "Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself." Trump endorsed Netanyahu in past elections and in November he sent a letter to Israeli President Isaac Herzog asking him to pardon Netanyahu on corruption charges. But Trump's comments about Netanyahu in recent months had been much more subdued, and he repeatedly demurred when asking if he would back the prime minister. The president, when asked in a Time magazine interview published this month about backing the Israeli leader, said, "I'm not involved in politics anymore," despite his campaigning for and endorsing U.S. politicians. READ MORE: America's politically divided Jewish community braces for Israel's elections Trump, especially in his second term, has sought to give his stamp of approval to candidates in foreign elections and claimed credit when they have been successful. He endorsed Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán in his unsuccessful bid for a fifth term, as well as Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Polish President Karol Nawrocki, and several Latin American leaders. Trump and Netanyahu have been close allies and seemed more aligned than ever in the wake of the joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran's nuclear facilities in 2025. But over the course of the nearly eight-month war with Iran this year, they have had disagreements. Trump criticized Israel's decision to attack a key Iranian gas field in the first weeks of the war. In June, he called Netanyahu "crazy." Trump also said that he was "a little bit perturbed" as Israel's fighting with Hezbollah militants in Lebanon was holding back peace talks with Iran. Beyond Iran, Netanyahu in August rejected Trump's latest plan to advance a stalled ceasefire in Gaza, pushing back on the U.S. administration's call for Israel to withdraw from territory it controls in Gaza until Hamas has been disarmed. Associated Press writer Josef Federman in Jerusalem contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. cc57e81bea52.text: Former President Barack Obama issued a forceful denunciation of the Trump administration's legal pursuit of Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar over suspicions she fraudulently obtained U.S. citizenship decades ago, an allegation the Minnesota lawmaker has called "disgusting lies." Why it matters: Obama — who faced false claims for years from Donald Trump that he wasn't an American citizen — is selective about when he weighs in on political issues or the president. His decision to speak out reflects his view that the DOJ raid on Omar's home last week was a betrayal of American values. What he's saying: " The fact that any president, or any administration, is willing to engage in such transparent efforts to intimidate someone should outrage all Americans, regardless of how they feel about Congresswoman Omar's political views," Obama wrote on X . "Because if this becomes the new normal, there's no reason to believe it will stop with her — or that future presidents, in either party, won't do the same." Driving the news: Federal agents raided Omar's Washington home Monday, seizing her phone as part of an investigation into whether she or her late father provided false information on immigration paperwork 26 years ago. The Wall Street Journal reported the administration aims to build "a case to strip her of her U.S. citizenship and ultimately deport her." Omar arrived in the U.S. from Somalia in 1995 as a child. She became a citizen through her father's naturalization in 2000 when records indicate she was 17. But investigators are seeking evidence that she was a year older and therefore not automatically eligible for citizenship. Flashback: The first Trump administration reviewed similar allegations in 2019, including questions about her birth date and her father's immigration, but found insufficient evidence to pursue a full investigation, the Washington Post reported . The allegation gained attention through a viral claim on social media, according to the Post . The other side: Omar has denounced the investigation as a witch hunt meant to intimidate one of Trump's fiercest critics in Congress. Democrats have called it an abuse of power — especially just weeks before an election. U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro also said her office was investigating Omar's financial disclosures, despite a congressional watchdog's recommendation last month to dismiss allegations of misconduct related to the filings. Zoom in: Obama's more than 400-word statement was a full-throated denunciation of the Trump administration. "Think about that. The full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president. And it's not the first time this has happened," he wrote. He added, "In those cases, the prosecutions either stalled or were dismissed for having no basis in law, and the same is likely to happen in this case. But not before Congresswoman Omar's life has been turned upside down, her legal bills have piled up, and she's been forced to spend time fighting unsubstantiated charges instead of serving the people of Minnesota."

Vance, who said during the town hall there's "of course" a chance he doesn't run for president, faced an especially pointed question about "a failure of leadership" posted by the widow of one of six U.S. soldiers killed by an Iranian drone strike in Kuwait, which occurred the day after Trump started the war with Iran. "This literally is the first time I've heard of this," Vance said in response. As he went on, he said, "This job is an amazing honor, but you live in a bit of a bubble and sometimes information doesn't filter up." Questions about Iran war strategy and costs After telling the vice president about his late wife, Master Sgt. Nicole Amor, who was killed on March 1, Joey Amor asked about mistakes and fundamental failures that led up to the deaths of those soldiers and how leaders would be held accountable. Vance seemed taken aback by Amor's questions, saying, "This literally is the first time I've heard of this," and said he wanted to talk with Amor to learn more after. But as Vance went on, he acknowledged mistakes were made and said, "there were issues with where troops were located that we realized was a huge mistake that we could do better on, and we have changed that." A Michigan man who said he voted for Trump and Vance in 2024 but now plans to vote for Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed pressed Vance about the high gasoline prices resulting from the war. In response, Vance said he recognized that gas prices were too high, and said, "I think it's important to be honest about why they're so elevated." WATCH: Vance speaks at a Republican rally in Florida He said it was because of "what's happening in the Middle East" and said the administration was taking steps to try to lower prices. "We've never had a situation like this where you have effectively, the largest state sponsor of terrorism that's trying to choke off world energy supply," Vance said, without acknowledging that situation occurred because of the war Trump launched. He also blamed former President Joe Biden, saying that during his tenure, America's refining capacity was diminished. But when Vance was pressed on the Trump administration owning the current situation, the vice president suggested that looking backward for blame was not the way. "Fundamentally, we are where we are, and you have to, in my view, I'd like to know what is Abdul El-Sayed's solution for the problem that we have right now," Vance said. "It's easy to criticize something that happened seven months ago." Immigration enforcement tactics and the rhetoric around immigrants A nun who spoke to Vance about their shared Catholic faith questioned the administration's hardline immigration enforcement tactics, including children who are separated from their parents when the adults are swept up in sweeps, and how that squared with their values. "We're trying to strike the right balance," Vance said. When moderator Tony Dokoupil asked Vance if the administration is not striking that balance, Vance replied, "I think that is constantly a work in progress." He admitted that, "Sometimes you have some people who made mistakes. Sometimes you have some people who really screw up." WATCH: Vance says Americans should not be scared of AI as calls for limits grow When Dokoupil asked for specific examples, Vance said there are a number of cases the administration has investigated that resulted in further training or discipline for immigration enforcement officers, but said they don't advertise it publicly in order to let investigations play out. Another voter, who said she became an immigrant five years ago and voted for Vance after becoming a U.S. citizen, asked him pointedly about his recent remarks referring to H1-B visa holders as, "foreign indentured servants," and accused him of "scapegoating immigrants for the issues you're supposed to be solving." "To the extent that my rhetoric has been imperfect here, that's on me," Vance said, before explaining that he was trying to criticize the companies that bring in the workers, not the immigrant workers themselves. Selling access to the White House is 'disgusting and despicable' Dokoupil pressed Vance on whether Trump and others in his administration were profiting off the presidency, including the nearly $1.2 billion the president took in from his crypto businesses last year, according to a federal filing. When asked if he'd seen anything in the White House that made him squeamish, Vance said, "I've never seen anything like that from the president." He said, though, that there is evidence of corruption in Washington, but he doesn't see evidence of it from the president or the administration. Vance said he's read articles about allegations, but said he goes to investigate claims himself and finds that they are not true. 28dde7e2fbc3.text: By — Rob Gillies, Associated Press Rob Gillies, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/major-fire-breaks-out-in-alberta-after-deadly-incident-at-canadian-military-base Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Carney says 4 service members killed and dozens injured in fire at Alberta military base World Updated on Oct 18, 2026 1:50 PM EDT — Published on Oct 18, 2026 11:16 AM EDT EDMONTON, Alberta (AP) — Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Sunday that four service members were killed and dozens more seriously injured in a fire at a military base in Alberta, describing it as one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada's military on domestic soil. Fire crews scrambled late Saturday as fierce winds whipped flames beyond Canadian Forces Base Wainwright and into the surrounding rural area. The Canadian military said Sunday there were no indications that the incident was the result of terrorism, but the cause remained under investigation. Speaking in a televised address, Carney said the families of those killed had been notified and that the situation was still evolving. Carney said the service members killed and injured were participating in military training when the fire broke out Saturday. Flags would fly at half-staff on federal buildings across the country in honor of those affected by the tragedy, he said. READ MORE: How Alberta separatism went from fringe cause to referendum Carney said those affected included reservists and soldiers from Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry, one of Canada's most storied military regiments. The personnel had come from bases across the country to train at Wainwright. It was not immediately clear exactly how many people had been injured. Carney said the wounded were being treated in Wainwright, Edmonton, Red Deer and Calgary. Cathy Keane, a mayoral candidate in Ontario, said her eldest son was among the military personnel critically injured. "As a mother, right now I need to be with my son and family," she wrote on Facebook, saying she was traveling to Alberta. A doctor at a hospital in the city of Edmonton, 180 kilometers (112 miles) northwest, told Canada's national broadcaster that patients were taken to hospitals across the city as healthcare facilities around the base became "completely overwhelmed" by the number of people needing care. "This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton," Dr. Warren Thirsk, an emergency department physician at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told CBC News. "It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It's a disaster. It's a one in every 15- to 25-year disaster." Hospitals declare emergency Acute Care Alberta said several hospitals across the province had activated a "Code Orange," an emergency designation used when multiple severely injured patients require coordinated medical care. The agency said emergency medical resources were stretched so thin that extremely few ambulances were available in the Edmonton area. It urged people to avoid the University of Alberta Hospital emergency department if possible. Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh said the town's small hospital was not designed to handle a mass-casualty incident but praised the response of local medical personnel. He said helicopters and planes had been transporting patients to other facilities for treatment. A search for the wreckage of Amelia Earhart's plane on a remote island in the Pacific Ocean has resumed after severe weather caused researchers to stop for several days.
A team has travelled to Nikumaroro Island, part of Kiribati, hoping to solve the mystery of the famed aviator's disappearance by investigating the so-called Taraia Object, spotted in the atoll's lagoon in aerial imagery.
The American pioneer vanished while attempting to circumnavigate the globe in 1937, spawning decades of speculation about her fate.
Rough seas and strong winds forced the team to remain on their research vessel for three days, until the weather cleared on Sunday.
"We are finally getting off the ship and able to land on Nikumaroro," Sirisha Bandla, a technology specialist who is part of the expedition, said in a video update from the deck of the Marin Mainiku.
The researchers arrived at the uninhabited atoll last week and began an underwater survey of the area of interest.
But the weather - powered by strong El NiÃ±o conditions in the Pacific - has so far prevented them from beginning a second of three phases, in which underwater objects will be probed to determine their depth and sediment will be dredged.
"We're working to get everything done today if we can," Bandla said. "The crew's really excited."
Earhart had already successfully flown from California across South America, Africa and Asia in her twin-engine Lockheed Electra when she arrived in Lae, Papua New Guinea on 2 July 1937.
From there, she and her navigator Fred Noonan had planned to travel towards Hawaii and then finally back to California.
But her plane vanished without a trace while trying to reach Howland Island, a remote, uninhabited coral island near Nikumaroro, to refuel.
One theory is that Earhart unintentionally navigated to Nikumaroro, where she ditched her plane and died a castaway.
Images of the so-called Taraia Object - which Purdue University says is visible in photography dating back to 1938 - show what could be the remnants of a small aircraft sitting in shallow waters, though other explorers remain sceptical.
Interest in the expedition prompted New Zealand's Air Force Museum to publish, external previously unseen reconnaissance images of Nikumaroro on Friday.
While the Taraia Object is not obviously visible in any of the black-and-white slides, taken in 1938 from a seaplane, they do show the beached wreck of the SS Norwich City, a British merchant vessel that ran aground on the island during a storm in 1929, killing 11.
Purdue, which with the US-based Archaeological Legacy Institute (ALI) is spearheading the expedition, said the incident demonstrated the risks surrounding the island.
To get into the atoll's lagoon, a boat has to navigate through a narrow gap created in the reef by the British in 1963 - the last time the island was inhabited.
But the university said wind gusts of up to 27 knots (31mph) present around the island until Sunday meant the transport boat could be knocked into the reef by crashing waves.
However, it said the Norwich City wreck may lend credence to the researchers' theory.
Purdue said a 15-year-old in Florida reported hearing Earhart's voice repeating "New York City" over her father's shortwave radio shortly after the aviator vanished. Proponents of the castaway theory argue this may have been a misunderstanding of Earhart giving her location as near the Norwich City.
As a result of the three-day hold, the research team has extended the expedition time to complete its fieldwork and has yet to indicate whether they had found any promising evidence of Earhart's plane.
ALI director Rick Pettigrew said the team was aware of the global interest in the expedition and would share its results "as soon as we are able". Purdue suggested before the poor weather hit that it could identify the Taraia Object in a matter of days.
While researchers have previously found evidence of a human presence on the island around the time of Earhart's disappearance, some skeptics believe the Taraia Object was just a tree that had fallen from the atoll into the lagoon.
Previous attempts to find her Electra have also come up short.
In 2024, a group of researchers said they may have found it lying around 4,877m (16,000ft) below the surface near Howland Island through sonar imaging - but this was later confirmed to be a rock formation.
Similarly, an expedition in 2019 to investigate a photograph of what might have been landing gear protruding from the water near Nikumaroro also failed to find anything.

French President Emmanuel Macron has called for "calm and order" after a major day of protests turned into rioting and looting on Saturday, and as some disorder continued in Paris on Sunday.
In a national address from the ÃlysÃ©e Palace, he warned those who had taken part not to "escalate", adding: "We all feel anger and shame."
Some 550,000 demonstrators took to the streets for largely peaceful protests against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.
Macron said a distinction must be drawn between the "legitimate demands" of protesters and "those who destroyed, smashed and looted".
Police have arrested about 2,400 people, according to France's interior ministry.
The French president said "nothing justifies" the "unbridled" violence seen and said those involved would face justice.
Groups of rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, also came out in Paris, Marseille and other towns and cities, with some setting fire to cars and buildings.
On Sunday, looting and clashes with police continued on a smaller scale in parts of the capital and Lyon.
Tear gas and stun grenades were fired at hundreds of people in Paris, according to the AFP news agency, and bottles and rocks were again hurled at police.
Sunday saw cities across the country confront the impact of what developed into one of the worst bouts of disorder in modern French history.
In Limoges, the ornate 19th Century city hall was gutted by a fire started by rioters on Saturday, its clock tower and roof collapsing and the flames took hold.
Speaking near the ruined building, AnnÃ¨yse said: "This is very upsetting. Harming heritage buildings just because you are angry at the government is selfish, I think. It's hurting everybody."
"It's awful and unbelievable," said another man who gave his name as Gerrard. "We are very sad and I think it will be a long time to put it back as it was before."
Shopkeepers were seen early on Sunday morning picking up large shards of glass in Paris as rubbish trucks cleared up debris on some of the larger streets.
Widespread looting took place across the cities of Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas.
Macron said local prefects and mayors would draft measures to protect shops and civic buildings.
The president also said there would be "full transparency" over the police response to the demonstrations.
Tear gas and water cannon were turned on crowds over the weekend and riot police were seen hitting people with batons in several places.
France's interior ministry said about 1,000 police officers were injured on Saturday, seven of them seriously.
Student protests which began last month escalated significant on Saturday after they were joined by trade union members and other anti-government groups.
The response from political figures has pointed to France's deep political divisions as the country prepares for an election in April which could see the hard-right pitted against the hard-left.
France's Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez said that while demonstrating was a fundamental right, there were "outrages" committed by "several thousand far-left individuals" who were determined to target public buildings and confront the police.
Later, they were joined by "delinquents who looted and ransacked numerous businesses in several cities in France", he said.
Jean-Luc MÃ©lenchon - leader of the hard-left La France Insoumise party - heavily criticised NuÃ±ez and police chiefs on social media.
He said they had "shown complete incompetence" with their handling of the demonstrations and called them "specialists in organised chaos".
Meanwhile, the leader of the hard-right National Rally party, Marine Le Pen, condemned the "exploitation" of anger "by political forces that encourage violence".

c2f5d48c95b8.text: Three national polls show President Trump's approval rating hitting new lows as Democrats lead Republicans by 8 to 10 points ahead of the midterms." Why it matters: Republicans need Trump's loyalists to turn out, but embracing an unpopular president risks alienating independents they need to win competitive races . Driving the news: New polls from the Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos , NBC News and Fox News put Trump's approval at 33%, 34% and 36%, respectively — record or second-term lows in each survey. Democrats lead Republicans by eight points in the Post poll, nine points in Fox's and 10 points in NBC's among registered voters. Once a strength, the economy is now Trump's main vulnerability. Just 21% approve of his handling of the cost of living in the Post poll, 27% in NBC's and 22% approve of his handling of inflation in Fox's. Even Republicans are souring: Fox and NBC both find Trump's approval among Republicans at 76%, while the Post puts it at 79%. Zoom in: Republicans face a growing divide within their party. Fox reports 95% approval of Trump among self-described MAGA Republicans, versus 47% among non-MAGA Republicans. The Post finds 75% of MAGA Republicans say they're certain to vote or have already voted, compared with 57% of non-MAGA Republicans. The Post poll also says 37% of Republicans and Republican-leaning independents want GOP leaders to take the party in a different direction from Trump, an all-time high. The big picture: A Reuters review published earlier this month found that Republican candidates in 41 of 62 competitive congressional races either broke with Trump on policy or downplayed their ties to him. At least a dozen of those candidates removed Trump's name, image or endorsement from their campaign websites, according to Reuters. Even some Trump voters see the problem: A Politico poll found 26% of people who voted for Trump in 2024 believe Republican candidates would be better off breaking with him. What they're saying: " Distancing yourself in general, that isn't anything new," Principles First executive director and Republican political strategist Brittany Martinez told Axios. "But Republicans, many Republicans, all over the country … intentionally, strategically" moving away from him "speaks volumes." She noted some Republicans have criticized his policies without directly blaming him, pointing to an ad from Rep. Maria Salazar (R-Fla.) that warned Trump he should be careful about what his advisers were telling him about immigration policy. Kentucky Senate nominee Andy Barr , Florida gubernatorial nominee Byron Donalds and Georgia gubernatorial nominee Rick Jackson are are among the candidates who removed references to Trump from their websites. What they're saying: White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in a statement that "President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress." Donalds' campaign comms director Gates McGavick said the congressman is "proud to have President Trump's endorsement." A White House official told Axios there's no distance between Trump and candidates. Several candidates still sport their Trump ties front and center. Between the lines: Republicans still appear with him, even if they don't always agree with his policies. Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxton has privately lamented the impact of the Iran war and gas prices on his campaign. But he also appeared onstage with Trump at a campaign rally. Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa), who is also locked in a tight Senate race, called for an end to the war in Iran, citing high fuel prices for Iowans. Days later, she appeared in the Oval Office alongside Trump and fellow lawmakers. The bottom line: Republican candidates are trying to hold onto Trump's devoted base without letting his growing unpopularity define their campaigns.

84198dad12ea.text: By — Matthew Lee, Associated Press Matthew Lee, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/rubio-heads-to-central-asia-as-some-wonder-if-hes-keeping-the-most-pressing-matters-at-a-distance Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Rubio heads to Central Asia as some wonder if he's keeping the most pressing matters at a distance Politics Oct 18, 2026 3:49 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — For the 31st time as secretary of state, Marco Rubio has left on a trip abroad, flying to Uzbekistan and later India amid rumblings that America's top diplomat is ignoring pressing matters in favor of politically safer visits and meetings. This tour is intended to promote U.S. economic and security ties with Central and South Asia. But it has only tangential links to the Trump administration's current main foreign policy dilemmas in the Middle East and with the Russia-Ukraine war. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Rubio has been unapologetic about his role as both President Donald Trump's chief diplomat and national security adviser and has brushed aside suggestions that he is eschewing the most difficult issues in favor of taking on lower-hanging diplomatic fruit with less risk of failure and political damage. "It's an important relationship," Rubio told reporters Saturday before departing Washington, noting that he selected a time when the Central Asian leaders would be able to meet. "One of the things that suffers is the strategic visits — you're always visiting someplace where there's a crisis or there's a problem, or you're going because there's a conference, but there's countries you'd like to get to because we want to build our relationships with them." READ MORE: Rubio says U.S. pressure on NATO allies to boost defense spending is 'not hostile' The State Department pushed back on any criticism of Rubio's schedule. It says Rubio's "responsibility is not to generate a public profile around every challenge; it is to help the president develop and execute a strategy that advances American interests. Some of the most consequential diplomatic work takes place outside the public spotlight." In both roles, Rubio must also "look at these challenges as part of a larger strategic picture," the department said in a lengthy emailed reply to queries from The Associated Press. "The Iran, Gaza, and the Russia-Ukraine conflicts each demand serious attention, but they cannot be approached in isolation from the president's broader national security objectives. The right question is not whether the secretary is visible enough on a particular issue." Rubio is involved in many things at once Rubio is involved in behind-the-scenes discussions on Iran, Lebanon, Gaza, Russia-Ukraine and China, although he has not been the public face of any of them. The Republican president's special envoys such as Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner and Tom Barrack have taken the lead on those matters. The State Department says there is nothing unusual about this and maintains that Rubio "hasn't shied away from any issue." "He's directly involved and serves as a trusted and capable adviser to the president on what matters most," the department said. "While he has multiple jobs, he isn't the White House press secretary and his job isn't to be in the press 24/7." Rubio has concentrated on Latin America, particularly Venezuela and Cuba, bolstering ties with a new generation of Trump-friendly conservative leaders and shoring up relations with NATO allies nervous about the administration's intentions toward Europe, especially in the Arctic. Delegating onerous and particularly time-consuming challenges is not new for secretaries of state. When Hillary Clinton was in office during Democratic President Barack Obama's first term, she appointed former Sen. George Mitchell, D-Maine, to handle the Israeli-Palestinian file and veteran diplomat Richard Holbrooke to steer the Afghanistan-Pakistan portfolio. WATCH: Rubio urges Europe to defend Western values and strengthen U.S. alliance in Greece Both Clinton and Rubio had made runs for their parties' respective presidential nominations before becoming secretary of state, and both had and have clear political ambitions for their post-diplomatic careers. Rubio, however, bristles at any discussion of his political intentions. He has refused to discuss speculation about the subject or on the more delicate topic of a rivalry with Vice President JD Vance over who might succeed Trump at the helm of the "Make America Great Again" movement. Rubio's most recent foreign travels have avoided the world's main hot spots, although they have focused on areas in which the administration has shown particular interest. Rubio's aides are quick to point out that the secretary plays a key role in interagency discussions on all national security matters and has been a major behind-the-scenes actor in most, if not all, discussions on the administration's diplomatic strategy. Since the beginning of this month and before his current travels to Uzbekistan and India, Rubio went to Iceland, Greece and Portugal. Before that, he visited Colombia, Ecuador and Peru. Rubio's schedule "is driven by the president's foreign policy and national security priorities, not by a desire to focus on some regions at the expense of others," the State Department said. "Every trip, meeting, and diplomatic engagement has to serve a purpose within that broader strategy. Sometimes that means addressing an immediate crisis; other times, it means building relationships, advancing economic and security partnerships, or addressing emerging challenges before they become more difficult to manage."
