FREDERICKSBURG, Va. â In a matter of weeks, when the midterm results are tallied and the next campaign begins, Democrats with presidential dreams know the question will be coming.
Do Israelâs actions in Gaza constitute genocide?
The question flew at Democrats all year. Progressives generally said âyes.â Pro-Israel Democrats said âno.â Many rejected the idea that they had to use that word or were otherwise endorsing every action taken by the Jewish state.
As potential Democratic 2028 contenders fan out across the country this month, campaigning with battleground Democrats and building their win/loss scorecards, just two have said âyesâ to the question: Reps. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y.
Khanna has been particularly direct, using interviews and public appearances not only to insist that Israel committed genocide, but also that Democrats who wonât say so are too weak to lead the party.
âIsrael has committed a genocide in Gaza, and we should have the courage to say so,â Khanna said at the Democratic National Committeeâs summer meeting in Texas â a historically red state where this yearâs top statewide Democratic nominees, Senate candidate James Talarico and gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa, have not gone as far.
The question hasnât dominated the last few weeks of campaigning, with primaries long over and stark differences on Israel between most Democrats and Republicans. Last week, when Ocasio-Cortez made three campaign stops for Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, neither Democrat â and no audience members â brought up the topic of Gaza.
But the question still looms over the partyâs first wide-open primaries in eight years. Theyâll be the first since small armies of activists pressed Democrats to take more progressive positions on immigration, the environment, and criminal justice reform. In retrospect, many Democrats now think that the candidates in 2020 were too willing to bow to pressure with cameras rolling. There is no sign that anyone but Khanna or Ocasio-Cortez is moving towards a new Gaza answer that activists might prefer.
âI think we have to acknowledge the seriousness of the issue, the seriousness of whatâs happening in Gaza, the seriousness of whatâs happening in the West Bank,â Maryland Gov. Wes Moore told Semafor earlier this month at a campaign stop, when asked why he thought the word âgenocideâ was so important to many Democrats. Moore has accused Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of committing war crimes, but hasnât called the violence in Gaza a genocide.
âI think itâll be up to the voters to decide whether or not they feel that people are meeting the moment,â Moore continued.
Know More
When the Gaza questions do pick up again, most Democrats are likely to punt to the International Criminal Court â already a popular way to dodge them. The ICC has issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu for war crimes and crimes against humanity, but hasnât accused Israel of committing genocide.Â
âThe question of genocide is a question of whether a government has the specific intent to destroy a national or ethnic group,â Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., said in his first debate against challenger Mike Collins this month. âAnd that is a question for the International Criminal Court.â
That answer is unlikely to satisfy many Democratic primary voters, according to a poll of six early primary states conducted by YouGov on behalf of the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project.
In South Carolina, where Democrats opted to hold their first primary, 57% of likely primary voters said that Israel was âcommitting genocide against Palestinians.â In the other five early-voting states, the number was much higher: 78% in New Hampshire and Nevada, 76% in New Mexico, and 72% in Virginia. And in Michigan, where El-Sayed has said he will play an active role in the primaries if he wins his Senate race, eight in 10 likely primary voters agreed with the âgenocideâ term.
These are more lopsided numbers than other pollsters have found, but according to an Associated Press survey this summer, half of all Democrats now agree that âgenocideâ was the appropriate word to describe what they saw happen in Gaza.
âItâs certainly been a question that keeps coming up in debates,â said the IMEU Policy Projectâs spokesman, Hamid Bendaas. âAnd Iâd expect there will be a key 2028 moment where the candidates are asked to raise their hands with a yes or no.â
Some Democrats have tried to cancel the test before they can take it. In March, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear told Politico that âgenocideâ was âbecoming one of those new litmus tests that we said we would never do as a party again.â He wouldnât answer the question, but assumed heâd be asked again.
Democrats uncomfortable with the term have watched how even using it does not stop questions about their commitment to cutting off arms to Israel â the policy fight they expect, with a little less dread, next year.
In August, two months after he defeated Rep. Dan Goldman in New Yorkâs Democratic primary, Brad Lander joined a protest of a Hindu nationalist politician in Manhattan and was filmed being heckled as a âzionistâ â even though he said that the war âmeets the definition of genocide.â Last month, after Drop Site and New York magazine reported that consultants were urging Maine Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson not to say âgenocideâ so much, supporters began asking him about the war again, worried that heâd gone wobbly.

Bangladeshi authorities say they were not informed of the recent execution of two Bangladeshi nationals in the holy city of Mecca until after it had taken place, local media reports.
A Bangladeshi man and woman were executed last Wednesday after being convicted of committing an "indecent act" inside a mosque, according to the Saudi interior ministry. The ministry did not specify the nature of the offending act.
Bangladesh says it has reached out to the Saudi Arabian government to ask for more details about the case.
The two Muslim countries share a close relationship due to their religious affinity and strong economic ties.
More than three million Bangladeshis work and live in Saudi Arabia, mostly in low-paying jobs, and news of the double execution has raised public concern in Bangladesh.
According to the Saudi interior ministry, the two Bangladeshi nationals were convicted and sentenced to death under "tazir", which in Islamic law refers to punishments left to the discretion of the judge.
The ministry statement said they were handed the sentences because of the severity of the offence, and the fact that they violated the "sanctity" of the mosque.
Bangladesh has reached out to the Saudi government about the offences involved and legal proceedings in the case, said state minister for foreign affairs Shama Obaed Islam.
The government would consider next steps, such as the repatriation of the bodies, after getting information from Saudi authorities, Islam said.
She added that the government was committed to safeguarding the welfare and interests of Bangladeshis abroad.
The two executed Bangladeshis were included in a list of prisoners that Saudi Arabia had shared with Bangladesh, upon a request from the Bangladesh Consulate General in Jeddah - but that list did not indicate that the pair had been sentenced to death, the Daily Star reported.
This is not the first time that foreign nationals have been executed by Saudi authorities.
According to Amnesty International, the country has executed around 100 people this year, many of whom are foreigners convicted of drug offences.
In 2011, eight Bangladeshi men were publicly executed in the Saudi Arabian capital of Riyadh after they were found guilty of killing an Egyptian.
Earlier this month, Saudi Arabia overturned a death sentence handed to a Sri Lankan man over a comment he had made on Facebook, which had led to him being convicted of blasphemy. That decision came after the case sparked public outcry in Sri Lanka and spurred diplomatic efforts to seek clemency for the man.

Please check your inbox to confirm. The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, which is leading the bold sampling effort, launched the spacecraft before dawn from the country's main spaceport on Tanegashima Island. While NASA has successfully landed nine spacecraft on Mars over the past 50 years and China scored a 2021 touchdown, no one has ever ventured onto Phobos or its sidekick Deimos. And no one has managed to fetch samples from Mars, let alone its moons. If successful, bits of dust, soil and rocks from Phobos will arrive on Earth in 2031. "There's a lot of adrenaline and a lot of excitement and a lot of wow," said NASA astrophysicist Tom Statler, who's involved with the project. Japan has an edge going in, with two asteroid sample returns already under its cosmic belt. This photo provided by NASA/JPL-Caltech/University of Arizona, taken with NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, shows Phobos, one of Mars' moons, on March 23, 2008. Image courtesy of NASA/JPL-Caltech/University of Arizona via AP Phobos is a lumpy, potato-shaped rock just 14 miles (22 kilometers) or so across. Examining pieces of it can explain how Mars' moons — and possibly moons elsewhere — came to be. Dubbed MMX for Martian Moons Exploration, the $578 million mission features a hefty 5-ton spacecraft that should reach Mars by late next summer. It will sync up with Phobos' tight orbit around the red planet, before ejecting the French-German rover that's named Idefix after the white terrier in the Asterix comics. No bigger than a microwave oven, Idefix will plop onto Phobos by itself, bouncing for several minutes before coming to a halt in the moon's extraordinarily low gravity. The four-wheeled rover is designed to right itself if it lands upside down. All bets are off, though, if it sinks into soft soil or gets wedged between rocks, said the French Space Agency's Julien Baroukh. Once the rover's solar panels are deployed, the vehicle can no longer right itself, he added, which is why it will move at a glacial 1 millimeter per second (0.04 inches per second). Idefix will serve as a "scout for safety," according to Baroukh, as it prowls around Phobos for 100 days. Japanese flight controllers want to avoid powdery soil and rough terrain when the mothership — a four-legged stationary lander — descends to the surface to gather samples in late 2028 or 2029. The lander will spend just two hours on Phobos, drilling and vacuuming up at least one-third of an ounce (10 grams) of material, before launching back into space. It will study Deimos during a series of flybys before leaving the Martian neighborhood in 2030 and hustling back to Earth for a 2031 sample delivery in the Australian desert. It's a treacherous undertaking, with wreckage littering the path. The moons' names aren't exactly comforting: Phobos is Greek for fear and Deimos means dread. They're the twin sons of the god of war Ares — Mars in Roman mythology. Russia stumbled in all three of its Phobos attempts as well as many other Mars endeavors. In its only other Mars mission, Japan failed to get a spacecraft into orbit around the red planet. Even NASA has had its share of flops in a bid to answer the burning question: Did life ever exist on Mars? By studying Mars' moons, scientists hope to learn whether Phobos and Deimos formed in the aftermath of an ancient collision between Mars and a battering space rock. It's also possible that the moons might be stray asteroids that became ensnared in Mars' gravity. Either way, scientists anticipate finding traces of Mars on Phobos, making the samples an irresistible two-for-one that should help demystify planetary and moon formation, and perhaps even the recipe for life. The findings will help shape future Mars missions, including those by astronauts, said NASA's acting planetary science director Lindsay Hays. "It is a once-in-a-lifetime chance. We are part of the first sample return mission from the Martian system," said the Germany Space Agency's rover chief Markus Grebenstein. Japan isn't the only one looking to claim the scientific riches packed into the Martian system's rocks and dirt. China plans to launch a sample return mission to Mars in 2028, while NASA is still debating how to retrieve the more than 30 sample tubes collected by the Perseverance Mars rover, the new champion for off-Earth driving. Japan and China could be neck-and-neck in getting samples back from the Martian system. Both are targeting 2031. Japan is investing $350 million in this mission. NASA is contributing $87 million, the French Space Agency about $68 million, the German Space Agency about $56 million and the European Space Agency some $17 million. Ukrainians have died because Kyiv is still not receiving reliable US warnings of incoming Russian attacks, according to a key adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov told the BBC that lives had been lost because there had not been time to warn citizens about ballistic missile strikes, saying: "It's dangerous... I think it's really very bad... People [have] already died."
The adviser also said restrictions to Ukraine's use of the Starlink internet network were ongoing.
The White House said there had been no changes to intelligence sharing with Ukraine.
Ukraine first reported an interruption to US intelligence sharing last week, as a row with the Trump administrations over its controversial deal to import Russian oil sent relations to new lows.
Despite the denials from Washington, many in Kyiv suspect the issues are not a coincidence.
On Monday morning, Zelensky wrote on social media: "Overnight two ballistic missile attacks were reported on the capital, one without warning, the second with only minimal time to take shelter."
Hours earlier, an interview the president did with NBC was published, in which he said intelligence sharing had been restored after a three-day pause.
"We are very thankful for this," he said. "Only [the] United States has this unique intelligence to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles."
But Beskrestnov told the BBC that American intelligence continued to be incomplete and inconsistent, and that the US had failed to provide a clear explanation for the issue.
"This looks very strange," he said. "Sometimes we receive this information before the attack, another time we [do] not."
He continued: "And for example, last night we received it, but... one minute before the attack."
However, he said other collaboration with US continues, adding: "Intelligence data keeps flowing, and the issue is solely with the air raid alert component."
Beskrestnov also said the US had given no clarity about who was responsible for the ongoing restrictions to the Starlink internet network and its military service Starshield, which Kyiv uses to provide connectivity for drones, helicopters and military communications.
Last week, Starshield restricted the speed at which mobile units could move while staying connected to the network to 100mph (160km/h).
This has limited Ukraine's ability to shoot down incoming drones or to launch mid-range drone attacks into Russian-occupied areas.
Starlink owner Elon Musk said last week that the US government ultimately controls access to Starshield, which was designed for the Pentagon, suggesting it may therefore be behind the restrictions. Trump has denied involvement.
Beskrestnov said he thought both issues occurring at the same time was "probably" a deliberate move to put pressure on Ukraine.
He told BBC News: "It's probably the United States trying to say [to] us, 'let's have the conversation, negotiation with Russia, you should find the compromise'."
Beskrestnov also said Ukraine had its own radar data to provide some limited warning of incoming attacks, but was urgently looking into using alternative communication systems.
He added: "Now we understand that something begins to happen with Starlink, and we're not sure what will be the next step.
"We understand that we should be prepared for some problems in future. And now we're thinking about an alternative for Starlink, not only for air defence, for communication between our forces, between our staff, for civilians also, because we don't know what we should expect in future regarding Starlink."
On Monday, when asked about intelligence sharing, Trump said: "We've given a lot to Ukraine. They've given us nothing."
Earlier, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had said there had not been a "pause" to intelligence sharing.
"I don't know where [Zelensky is] getting these things or why he's saying these things to the press," he told reporters on Monday.
Rubio said he could not comment on the incident, adding: "I know a few nights ago there was a software problem involving their early warning system."
The BBC has contacted Starlink for a response.
A White House official said there were no changes to intelligence sharing operations between the US and Ukraine.
The official spoke on background to discuss intelligence matters. Trump is focused on ending the war, the official said, and added that the US has provided more aid to Ukraine than any other country.
Russian attacks continued late on Monday, with Ukrainian officials saying at least six people were killed - including a toddler in her pram and an 11-year-old girl - in a drone strike near a park cafÃ© in the north-eastern Kharkiv region.
Zelensky described the attack in which another 14 people were injured as "absolute atrocity".

CODY, Wyo.—On a warm October evening at a bar in downtown Cody, Wyomingites gathered to ponder the future of what some hope will be the Cowboy State’s next booming industry: data centers.
This summer, outgoing Gov. Mark Gordon signed an executive order titled “Data Centers the Wyoming Way” that he said would “guide responsible development in Wyoming,” while keeping the state an attractive landing spot for the enormous server warehouses that power the AI industry.
Data centers’ potential impacts on Wyoming’s precious water supply, already-rising electricity prices and prized public lands have rankled many corners of the state. Gordon acknowledged those concerns in a statement accompanying the release of the order, which is not binding.
Environmental groups in Wyoming agree that there need to be more guardrails on data center development, but they are not fully aligned on how to achieve that goal.
Wyoming’s chapter of The Sierra Club believes a moratorium on data centers could be useful in certain circumstances, but the group has not taken a position on the utility of halting development across the state. The Wyoming Outdoor Council sees a tangible opportunity to advance new data center policies with the incoming crop of legislators and a new director of the Department of Environmental Quality. But a moratorium, in their view, would not guarantee those guardrails and is therefore a risky way to spend environmental groups’ limited political capital.
“By its very nature, a moratorium is temporary, and a call for a moratorium on data centers would really be a stopgap,” Jocelyn Wulf, the Wyoming Outdoor Council’s data center campaign manager, told a few dozen Cody residents this month at the data center town hall the organization hosted.
Representatives from both organizations told Inside Climate News they believe the incoming crop of legislators has an appetite for changing how Wyoming manages data center construction.
Not everyone in Cody sounded convinced that data centers would be a net positive for Wyoming.
“What’s the benefit?” asked Anne Trosper, a lifelong Wyomingite who has worked in the oil and gas, and conservation industries. “Where does Wyoming get money out of this thing?”
Data centers pay property taxes and electricity sales taxes in Wyoming, in addition to hosting construction jobs in the building phase of the facilities, and employing a small number of permanent workers once they are up and running.
But data centers could provide tax revenue to Wyoming in another familiar if indirect way.
With data centers demanding enormous amounts of power—Google’s Project Tembo, formerly known as Project Jade, could use up 10 gigawatts of electricity, more than five times Wyoming’s statewide electricity consumption—many companies are choosing to meet that demand in Wyoming with fossil fuels.
Much of Wyoming’s tax base comes from royalties paid by the coal, oil and gas industries, and the state has championed the Trump administration’s support for fossil fuels.
To fuel the industry’s growth, some Wyoming counties are zoning parcels of land as industrial parks, exempting data center companies from obtaining permits under Wyoming’s Industrial Siting Act. The Wyoming Outdoor Council describes this arrangement as a “loophole” companies use to build quicker and skirt some public oversight.
“That means no comprehensive review process by state agencies,” Wulf told the Cody gathering, so communities wouldn’t receive the impact assistance payments associated with some projects that go through that process. “This is not to say that they are still not subject to state and federal laws, but we are losing out on that review process as a whole [because] local governments must then review these projects to the best of their abilities. Despite their best intentions, local governments do have more limited capacity for thorough review.”

Cheyenne, Wyoming’s capital, has spent years courting data center development with mixed success. While the new construction has created many temporary and some permanent jobs, the scale, size and impacts of the new projects have not been without controversy.
In 2025, WyoFile reported that Microsoft applied for an air permit to run 128 backup diesel generators for a data center complex south of the city.
This July, the Cheyenne Board of Public Utilities found that a contractor working on a data center project for Meta, the parent company of Facebook, accidentally introduced a rare bacteria into the city’s wastewater treatment system. That incident occurred after Cheyenne city council members voted against a proposed 12-month moratorium on data center development this May.
“Guardrails are the direction that we should be going in,” Emma Jones, an associate organizer at the Wyoming chapter of the Sierra Club, told Inside Climate News. “A lot of community members want to see groups advocating for moratoriums because [data center development] is moving too fast.”
But calling for a moratorium would be unwise without a plan for what to accomplish during the pause, she said. As a result, the Wyoming chapter of the Sierra Club hasn’t publicly supported or opposed a moratorium. “We don’t want to just push for a moratorium for the sake of having a moratorium,” she said.
Some at the Cody meeting agreed with the Wyoming Outdoor Council that the new lawmakers could be open to taking a firmer approach to regulating AI growth. “It’s just a huge responsibility,” Trosper said.
When asked whether a moratorium would be helpful given the compressed nature of Wyoming’s upcoming legislative session, which starts in January and lasts only a few weeks, Trosper said she was unsure.
“I’m undecided at this point,” she said.

f52a1283fb60.text: By — Barbara Ortutay, Associated Press Barbara Ortutay, Associated Press By — Philip Marcelo, Associated Press Philip Marcelo, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/ex-openai-worker-accused-of-bugging-conference-room-planned-to-fly-to-saudi-arabia-prosecutors-say Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Ex-OpenAI worker accused of bugging conference room planned to fly to Saudi Arabia, prosecutors say World Oct 19, 2026 4:35 PM EDT SAN FRANCISCO (AP) — A former OpenAI engineer charged with secretly installing a recording device in a conference room to glean company details had been "mere days" away from absconding to Saudi Arabia before his arrest, federal prosecutors said in new court filings. Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national, was also fired from his job at the ChatGPT maker, according to a government memo filed Sunday. His wife and young son left the country the day after his arrest on a one-way ticket booked and paid for by a Saudi military official, prosecutors said in the filing. "Ultimately, the defendant has little incentive to remain in the United States to see this case through," federal prosecutors wrote. "He has ample resources —including his significant compensation from a decade of high-tech employment in the Bay Area and at least two bank accounts in Saudi Arabia — and what appears to be considerable support from a foreign government." Prosecutors also noted Saudi Arabia has no extradition treaty with the U.S. as they seek to detain Alfozan until trial. A judge will consider the request Monday in federal court in San Francisco. Alfozan's lawyers didn't immediately respond to an email seeking comment ahead of Monday's hearing. But in their own court filings, they argued that Alfozan, who had worked at OpenAI since July 2025, had purchased one-way tickets for his family to Saudi Arabia more than two weeks before prosecutors allege the recording devices were installed. The defense said the couple planned to spend Alfozan's roughly two-month paternity leave in Saudi Arabia following the birth of their U.S.-citizen son. Prosecutors say after his arrest, Saudi officials purchased new plane tickets for the wife and son to leave the U.S. sooner than the Oct. 12 flight Alfozan initially booked. Alfozan's lawyers also argued that he was on track to become a naturalized U.S. citizen with an interview with federal officials scheduled next month. They said he has been a legal permanent resident since 2020, has lived in the U.S. for 15 years and attended MIT and the University of California, Berkeley. "This was a long-held dream for the Alfozan family, as it is for so many immigrants," his lawyers wrote. "His plan was always to return to the Bay Area, where his home, his career, and his community are." Rather than remain in federal custody, Alfozan's lawyers argue he should be confined to his family's home in the San Francisco suburbs, with GPS monitoring, travel restrictions and a requirement to surrender his passport. Prosecutors have not said what Alfozan might have wanted to do with the recordings, but say he was in "frequent communication" with a member of the Saudi royal family. They said the royal family member repeatedly tried to recruit Alfozan to an artificial intelligence venture being launched in Saudi Arabia. Alfozan told the unnamed person in WhatsApp messages that he wouldn't leave OpenAI until his stock was vested, even as he explored other career opportunities in the Middle Eastern kingdom, prosecutors wrote. Prosecutors say Alfozan concealed an audio recording device in toilet paper and plugged it into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room he wasn't authorized to access. They say security cameras captured him entering the room and checking behind the television after installing the device. It remained there for several days before being found Sept. 30. Prosecutors say the conference room was typically used for meetings involving company leaders, government officials and other executives and "discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, as well as nonpublic information." OpenAI has said the recording device Alfozan used was sophisticated, designed to evade detection and featured advanced encryption and audio-monitoring capabilities. They also said they had evidence Alfozan planned to place other listening devices elsewhere in the office. Alfozan has been charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. If convicted, he faces a five-year prison sentence. Marcelo reported from New York. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. (AP) — For many voters in Michigan, the U.S. Senate race has become about far more than which party controls Washington. In the Detroit suburbs, some Jewish Democrats are confronting deeply personal questions about faith and identity as they weigh whether they can support their party's nominee. Just miles away in Dearborn, Arab American leaders who backed President Donald Trump two years ago are growing increasingly alarmed by Republican rhetoric. Rogers has increasingly portrayed El-Sayed as an extremist and a threat to Jewish voters as the Republican tries to win over a traditionally Democratic constituency. The race has even divided close friends like Lori Goldman and Mimi Price-Miletic. Goldman, a Jewish Democratic activist, described Rogers' message as "a fear campaign." "It's spreading and it's not spreading slowly," she said. "It's spreading insidiously and widely and effectively." Price-Miletic, a member of the Michigan Democratic Jewish Caucus, sees things differently. She is not supporting El-Sayed and has not ruled out voting for Rogers. "Lori Goldman is my best friend," said Price-Miletic. "This summer I said we cannot discuss Abdul. I don't want to hear his name. We've agreed to disagree and we don't talk about it." Stevens represents much of Oakland County, just north of Detroit and home to a significant portion of Michigan's Jewish population. Rogers has focused heavily on the area and is holding an event later in October with U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, that's billed as "Who Will Keep Us Safe? Rogers vs. El-Sayed in the Wake of October 7th and the Temple Israel Attack." Vance Patrick, chair of the Oakland County Republican Party, said Rogers was "definitely making some headway" among Jewish voters and that the community is "listening to the Republican Party this time." Patrick added that Rogers has visited synagogues across the county, including Temple Israel in West Bloomfield, where a man rammed a truck loaded with fireworks and gasoline into the building and exchanged gunfire with a security guard in March. The attacker, a naturalized citizen originally from Lebanon who lived in Dearborn Heights, had recently lost family members in an Israeli airstrike in his native country. El-Sayed condemned the Temple Israel attack but drew criticism for saying "hurt people hurt people." He later apologized by saying "to anyone who feels like my comments might have been hurtful, I'm really sorry." Rogers and his allies have repeatedly invoked those comments, with Rogers claiming El-Sayed "can't condemn terrorism in our own country because he's so close to the people who are supporting the Muslim Brotherhood." Trump went further Wednesday, claiming El-Sayed was a member of the Muslim Brotherhood. There is no evidence that El-Sayed has any affiliation with the Muslim Brotherhood. His half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, wrote on social media in 2012 that "my family has long been MB" and described a conversation with her mother about involvement in the Muslim Brotherhood in the early 1970s. El-Sayed, who was born in Michigan to Egyptian immigrant parents and was raised by his father, told NBC this week the social media posts are "hearsay." The Trump administration designated the Egyptian, Jordanian and Lebanese branches of the Muslim Brotherhood as terrorist organizations earlier this year. Photo by Paul Sancya/AP Democrats are still struggling to unite behind El-Sayed after the primary exposed deep disagreements over Israel. 3196d3576b03.text: President Trump wants to hold a trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi and Russian President Putin in China next month to discuss "denuclearization" — but not necessarily Ukraine. Why it matters: Such a summit between the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia would be unprecedented. Trump has been talking for two years about his aspiration to reach a deal with Russia and China to reduce the number of nuclear weapons. But so far Putin and Xi haven't shown much openness to the idea. Driving the news: Trump is expected to travel to China in mid-November to participate in the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders' meeting in the city of Shenzhen. The Kremlin has been floating the idea of holding such a meeting since July. Putin raised the issue in two phone calls with Trump, including one last week. The Chinese government hasn't expressed willingness to hold such a summit. What he's saying: When asked on Monday whether such a summit could discuss ending the war in Ukraine, Trump said he wants to hold such a trilateral meeting, but in order to discuss other issues. "I would do it, not so much for Ukraine, we would have it to talk about denuclearization," he said.

e1dd86d307c1.text: By — Gisela Salomon, Associated Press Gisela Salomon, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/homeland-security-grants-temporary-deportation-reprieve-for-more-than-100000-ukrainians-and-sudanese Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Homeland Security grants temporary deportation reprieve for more than 100,000 Ukrainians and Sudanese World Oct 19, 2026 3:56 PM EDT MIAMI (AP) — More than 100,000 people from Ukraine and Sudan can stay in the United States without immediate risk of deportation, the Department of Homeland Security said, in what amounts to a temporary reprieve after their right to stay in the country was set to expire Monday. Temporary Protected Status was set to end Oct. 19 for about 101,000 Ukrainians and 1,800 Sudanese. But DHS said an announcement "will be made at the appropriate time." Until then, the department said in a written statement, Ukrainians and Sudanese in the U.S. covered by those temporary measures "retain protection." The Department did not indicate how long they could stay or when a final announcement would be made on their status. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. DHS did not respond to a question about whether they can keep their work permits, but TPS generally allows people to work while their protections remain in effect. The decision Monday marks another incident where the Trump administration, which has previously sought to end these temporary protections from deportation and send people back to their home countries, has allowed people covered by the temporary status to stay in the country but without giving any guidance as to how long. Yuriy Boyechko, CEO of Hope For Ukraine, a nonprofit that provides humanitarian aid in Ukraine and helps resettle newcomers in the U.S., described the government's announcement as "last-minute patches." It is a "bandage that has been placed on a wound that does not solve the real issue," he said. "It's time for U.S. to come up with some normal path to permanent residency for all these people," Boyechko noted. He emphasized that they cannot safely return to Ukraine. The context of the decisions to keep the protections Watch the segment in the player above. The Trump administration has already terminated TPS for more than 1 million people from 13 countries, including Venezuela, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, Afghanistan and Syria. But in a change in practice roughly a month ago, the administration kept protections in place for nearly 200,000 Salvadorans whose TPS was set to expire Sept. 9. In that case they also said that they were going to make a decision at the appropriate time and that in the meantime, people from El Salvador could continue to work and live in the U.S. Activists and a bipartisan group of lawmakers have been raising the alarm over the upcoming deadline for TPS to expire for Ukrainians, arguing that conditions remain unsafe for them to return home amid the war with Russia. Ukraine was first designated for TPS in April 2022, following Russia's full-scale invasion two months earlier. The Biden administration subsequently extended the designation, most recently in January 2025, when DHS authorized an additional 18 months of protection through October 2026. The TPS program for Sudan was established in 1997, and since then, successive U.S. administrations have extended it due to the armed conflict and political instability that have plagued the African nation. The decision Monday comes two weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, when Trump's hard line immigration policies will face a test at the ballot box. The TPS program has offered protections for decades but is controversial The U.S. Congress created TPS in 1990 to prevent deportations to countries suffering from natural disasters or civil strife. It allows people already in the country to remain and work, for renewable periods if the homeland security secretary determines conditions are unsafe for their return. But it doesn't give them a pathway to permanent residency. Supporters say that using this tool protects people from being returned to dangerous situations and that uprooting people covered by TPS after years of living in the U.S. is cruel. Critics, especially in the Trump administration, say successive administrations have extended these protections for years regardless of what has happened in the home countries. Federal rules say TPS is automatically extended for six months if the secretary doesn't make a determination at least 60 days before the designation expires. Advocates are grateful for DHS decision, warn about the war "We're grateful for an extension, however temporary, for TPS holders from Ukraine and Sudan," said Myal Greene, president and CEO of World Relief, an organization that has provided humanitarian assistance in both countries. "We encourage the administration and Congress to consider longer term relief for women, men and children trying to carve out stability while their countries of origin remain in upheaval." Krish O'Mara Vignarajah, president and CEO of Global Refuge, noted Ukraine and Sudan are not safe and meet the legal conditions for TPS to be extended. "Russia's war on Ukraine is nearing its fifth year, and Ukrainians are bracing for another winter under drone and missile strikes, driving civilian casualties and devastating critical infrastructure. Sudan remains locked in a brutal civil war marked by famine, widespread human rights abuses and the hallmarks of genocide," Vignarajah said. "It is not safe for these families to go home." Associated Press reporter Rebecca Santana contributed from Washington. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. b6eaabada8c6.text: By — Dan Gelston, Associated Press Dan Gelston, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/ap-source-eagles-qb-jalen-hurts-expected-to-miss-rest-of-season-after-blood-clots-found-in-lungs-and-leg Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter AP source: Eagles QB Jalen Hurts expected to miss rest of season after blood clots found in lungs and leg Nation Oct 19, 2026 3:42 PM EDT PHILADELPHIA (AP) — Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts is expected to miss the rest of the season because of blood clots in his lungs, a person familiar with the situation told The Associated Press on Monday. The person spoke to the AP on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of a health matter. Hurts was placed on injured reserve Saturday, two days after the Eagles revealed he has a blood clot in his calf. He missed the first of at least four games in Philadelphia's loss to the Carolina Panthers on Sunday. The Eagles and Hurts' agent, Nicole Lynn, released more information on his condition Monday. They said Hurts has deep vein thrombosis and a bilateral pulmonary emboli, meaning a blood clot has traveled from the legs to the lungs. His treatment involves blood thinners, and he will not be allowed to participate in any football activities until he is off them. The Eagles and Lynn said Hurts was expected to make a full recovery. "He is clinically stable and has no significant functional limitations," their statement said. The Eagles previously said Hurts was injured when he took a cleat to his calf area on Oct. 4 in a game against the Los Angeles Rams. Hurts informed the medical staff of the injury after practice on Oct. 8. The Super Bowl 59 MVP was back at practice the next day before the team left for London to play Jacksonville. Hurts was initially diagnosed by specialists in London with a left calf superficial vein thrombosis. Hurts hadn't missed more than two games in a season since becoming the full-time starter in 2021. He has led the Eagles to five straight playoff appearances, three NFC East titles and two Super Bowl appearances, beating the Chiefs 40-22 two years ago. Tanner McKee started for Hurts against the Panthers. McKee finished 26 of 45 for 215 yards and a touchdown in the Eagles' 25-14 loss to Carolina. The Eagles (2-4) have lost four consecutive games for the first time since 2020. Hurts has eight touchdown passes and three interceptions with 933 yards passing this season. He is in the middle of a five-year, $255 million extension, including $179.3 million guaranteed, that takes him through the 2028 season. The Eagles stunned fans when they drafted Hurts out of Oklahoma in the second round in 2020. They seemingly had Carson Wentz entrenched at QB and had more pressing needs. But Hurts supplanted Wentz and became one of the top quarterbacks in the NFL. AP Pro Football Writer Rob Maaddi in Tampa, Florida, contributed to this report. 5c6300d5d58b.text: By — Jocelyn Noveck, Associated Press Jocelyn Noveck, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/longtime-cnn-anchor-christiane-amanpour-leaving-network-after-a-storied-career-of-43-years Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Longtime CNN anchor Christiane Amanpour leaving network after a storied career of 43 years Nation Oct 19, 2026 3:35 PM EDT Longtime CNN anchor Christiane Amanpour, who began as an entry-level assistant and rose to become one of the most visible correspondents and anchors on TV, reporting from war zones and hot spots for decades, will be leaving the network after 43 years. Amanpour, the network's chief international anchor, will scale back her daily show, "Amanpour," on CNN International to once a week at the beginning of 2027, and end it in May, leaving the network the following month. She said in a statement Monday that she looks forward to "interesting new projects down the line." Amanpour, 68, also will end her PBS show, "Amanpour & Co," at the end of the year, she said in her statement, shared by CNN. She will continue her podcast, "The Ex Files," with her ex-husband, Jamie Rubin, a former U.S. diplomat. "After many months of thought and a few sleepless nights, I have decided to separate from CNN, my partner of 43 fantastic years!" Amanpour said. She added she would "always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism. Remember: Always be truthful, not neutral." No reason given for her departure Amanpour did not give a reason for her departure, nor did she specifically mention changes at her network. But her exit coincides with a new era at CNN as it comes under a new owner, Skydance. After a yearlong process, Skydance-owned Paramount closed its $81 billion buyout of Warner Bros. Discovery on Oct. 6. The merger unites under one roof two giants in TV news — CBS and CNN. On a personal front. Amanpour has spoken openly about her 2021 diagnosis of ovarian cancer and two later recurrences, calling it "the invisible killer." She has urged others to "get all the scans that you can." Amanpour joined CNN as an assistant in Atlanta in 1983. In his own message Monday, CNN's chief executive, Mark Thompson, wrote that at the time, her promise was not universally appreciated. "Famously, one of her bosses told her back then that she didn't have what it took to become a foreign correspondent — or to hold any on-air role at all," Thompson wrote. "Boy, did she prove him wrong!" Fame came during the first Gulf War Amanpour became a reporter, and an international correspondent seven years later. She earned fame in the early 1990s, covering the Gulf War, conflict in the Middle East and many other hot spots. War reporting is "a sense of mission, it's a sense of purpose, it's a sense of being able to tell a story," she said. She aimed to bring international news — including complicated stories — to American viewers. "I've never believed that things are too complicated to put on American television," she told The Associated Press in 2023. I've never talked down to an audience. I've never believed that they just want to know what's happening in their backyard." Amanpour also noted that her upbringing gave her a unique perspective. "Because of my upbringing — I'm half-Iranian and half-British — I've had the great privilege of being able to see the world from two very distinct perspectives," she said. "I've always spoken out about the need to bridge gaps. I know we can live in a world that's not 100% tribalized." In her remarks Monday, Amanpour thanked her field crews and show teams. "From my very first big exciting assignment covering the first Gulf War, to the horrors of the Bosnian War, Rwanda, Afghanistan, Ukraine and Iran and all the points in between, it's the teams and the camaraderie that counted so much," she wrote, "as we together battled to seek the facts, the evidence and the humanity, so that CNN could always broadcast the truth about the world and to the world, without fear nor favor." Across hundreds of miles of the northern Gulf of Mexico, a deep-water ecosystem collapsed after the massive 2011 Deepwater Horizon oil and gas spill, and recovery is uncertain, new research concludes.
The study, published Monday in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, found that animal populations, including octopus, krill, squid and shrimp declined by 60 to 85 percent in the three-and-a-half years after the spill, with few signs of recovery since. Krill and lanternfish, both foundational species in the Gulf’s food web, were among the hardest hit. The findings also suggest that the die-off is causing genetic bottlenecks that could further hinder ecosystem recovery.
The researchers identified it as the “fastest and most severe faunal decline reported for Earth’s largest ecosystem type” ever documented. The widespread die-off of marine organisms may also reduce the ocean’s ability to transport carbon dioxide from the atmosphere to the deep sea. After ruling out other factors, such as water temperature and oxygen levels, the researchers identified the Deepwater Horizon blowout as “the most parsimonious explanation” for the ecosystem’s collapse.
Comprehensive natural resource damage assessments and restoration efforts involving federal, state and tribal trustees are still underway. In 2016, BP agreed to a $20.8 billion settlement, including up to $8.8 billion for environmental restoration.
Remote ocean depths and habitats miles below the surface may seem buffered from the impacts of human activity, the authors wrote, but their findings suggest an industrial disaster pushed part of it into a diminished state with “limited resilience to facilitate recovery.” They said their findings also show that proposed industrial deep-sea mining could damage the ecosystem before baseline conditions are assessed.
A Transoceanic drilling rig, operating for BP about 50 miles southeast of the Mississippi Delta, exploded on April 20, 2010. The explosion and fire killed 11 people and triggered the largest accidental marine oil spill in history.
Oil and gas spewed uncontrollably from the broken well nearly a mile deep for 87 days, ejecting 4.9 million barrels of oil at a rate of about 400 tanker trucks per day, enough to fill up 1.2 million cars. The spill also released about 7.7 billion cubic feet of fossil gas into the deep sea at a rate of 88 million cubic feet per day, enough to supply about 820,000 U.S. homes. State and federal agencies, including the EPA, also authorized BP to apply 1.84 million gallons of chemical dispersants to try to reduce the impacts.
Some of the oil and gas dissipated and was transported out of the deep Gulf of Mexico region. Some coated barrier islands and devastated coastal wetlands and shellfish habitat and some settled onto the ocean floor, where currents can stir it back into the water. But enough hydrocarbon and chemical-dispersant remnants stayed suspended long enough to do almost immeasurable harm.
A series of studies since the spill have shown a wide range of toxic effects on marine organisms, from impaired development and reproduction to increased mortality and lasting health problems in dolphins and whales. The new paper suggests that lingering pollutants may interfere with some species’ ability to find mates in the dark by disrupting their highly developed sense of smell.
Scientists on Slippery Decks
The impacts continue to ripple through the ecosystem, said lead author Tracey Sutton, a professor of marine and environmental sciences at Nova Southeastern University in Florida. A 2024 study found an 80 percent decline in deep-diving toothed whales, he said.
“We used to have a big resident population of sperm whales right off the Mississippi River, but we haven’t seen a sperm whale in 10 years,” he said. Large predators need big, occasional dense patches of prey, and those have disappeared, he added.
Scientists have developed accurate ways to count fish. For this study, they started with a baseline from nine months of sampling in 2011 and compared it with nine subsequent surveys between 2015 and 2023. The researchers sampled deep-pelagic habitat along a large grid around the spill site from about 650 feet below the surface to about a mile down. The deep-pelagic zone accounts for about 90 percent of the Gulf’s total volume.
Across a grid of stations, scientists on slippery decks lowered and hoisted nets that open and close at different depths, with experts from different species groups to identify the catch. They sampled around noon and midnight to account for species that migrate vertically each day. Ship-mounted scientific echosounders provided an independent check, measuring sound reflected by marine life in the water column.
The research is “comprehensive and carefully composed,” marine biologist Bruce Robison, a senior scientist at the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute, said via email. “There is no other study that I know of with such an incredible number of net samples,” added Robison, who did not participate in the new study.
The research focuses on species that are not commercially fished and shows for the first time that human impacts can deplete marine life even in very deep ocean water, he said.
“It is important for the public to understand just how disastrous this oil spill was,” Robison said. “The Gulf has not recovered and it’s been over 15 years.”
Robison said other activities, such as deep-sea mining, could also have severe negative consequences for deep-water pelagic ecosystems by discharging wastewater containing metals or lubricants.
Three lines of evidence—net hauls, acoustic surveys and genetic sampling—corroborate each other, which is “unusually strong evidence to support his conclusions,” said Jeffrey Drazen, a marine ecologist at the University of Hawai’i at Manoa, who did not participate in the new study.
The study examines all possible causes of the decline and shows only one aligns with the scientific evidence, he said.

He voted for the costly Iran war and spiking gas prices." In Nebraska, Democratic candidate Chris Backemeyer says families are drowning. "And Mike Flood opened the gates. Flood voted six times for Trump's tariffs and the Iran war, flooding us with higher prices on groceries, gas, cars and medicine, costing us a thousand dollars more a year." Please check your inbox to confirm. And in Iowa, a group called Vote Vets Action Fund said Republican Senate candidate Ashley Hinson voted five times for the Iran war, "giving us record prices for gas and fertilizer." Those ads are but a few examples of how Democrats and aligned advocacy groups are using an unpopular war as they challenge Republicans, aiming to win back power in the House and Senate. It's the culmination of a strategy Democrats launched in the spring, when they began to repeatedly bring up war powers resolutions aimed at ending the conflict. The votes had little practical effect, but forced lawmakers to go on record and take a stand. READ MORE: 13 races that will determine control of the Senate Now those votes are being highlighted in campaign ads across the country, according to an Associated Press analysis of data from AdImpact, which charts media spending. In some cases, the Republicans targeted have never served in Congress before, so they couldn't possibly have voted on the various war powers resolutions. Even then, Democrats are portraying them as destined to be rubber stamps for President Donald Trump when it comes to the war. Tying the war to the cost of living The Associated Press analyzed data on broadcast and cable ads aired from Sept. 1 through Oct. 14 in the most competitive midterm races. The analysis focused on House and Senate races rated as either tossups or leaning Democratic or Republican by the Cook Political Report. A smaller number of streaming ads were also examined. At least half of the 50 races featured Iran-related ads, most of which included household cost-of-living messages. All told, the ads aired on TV more than 43,000 times since Sept. 1, costing an estimated $42 million. The AP used both AdImpact's own issue designations along with additional analysis of the ads' language to identify them. Of the 65 unique Iran-themed ads identified by the AP, 61 of them stressed household cost-of-living messages such as rising prices for fuel and other items. The Republican playbook Republicans are largely ignoring the Iran war in their ads. Their best strategy is to go after Democratic weaknesses so voters say "this guy is worse," said Ron Bonjean, a Republican strategist. "In the end, you're trying to get as many Republicans out to vote for you as possible and bring over some independents," Bonjean said. "And talking about the Iran war is really not a winning message because you're playing on the Democratic turf." The major themes addressed in the Republican advertising since Sept. 1 are taxes and crime, followed by issues tied to character, healthcare and immigration. Watch the segment in the player above. Some Republicans have sought to distance themselves from the Iran conflict outside the airwaves. In Michigan, Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers has said the "war with Iran needs to end — and end quickly." His opponent, Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, has run ads saying that a billion dollars a day is going to a war "we have no business fighting" and he was running to "invest our tax dollars here in Michigan." In Maine, Republican Sen. Susan Collins emphasized in a recent debate that she voted nine times to end the conflict, prompting Democratic challenger Troy Jackson to say she voted five times to "make it happen." In all, the Senate has voted 14 times on resolutions seeking to halt or restrict Trump's military action against Iran. The House has held six such votes since the conflict began in late February. In the latest House vote, seven Republicans ended up siding with Democrats in voting to end the war. That includes four Republicans seeking reelection in highly competitive districts: Tom Barrett of Michigan, Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania and Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Zach Nunn in Iowa. Barrett and Fitzpatrick had voted previously to remove U.S. troops from hostilities, but the yes votes were the first for Miller-Meeks and Nunn, reflecting the growing weariness with the war. Where Iran ads are most prevalent While the Iran war ads made up about 5% of the total TV spots aired across the competitive races, some contests leaned into the topic heavily. The highest concentration was in California's 48th Congressional District in the San Diego area. Roughly a third of the 12,000 aired ads touch on Iran. Democrats are seizing on a remark that Republican Jim Desmond made in the early days of the war, in which he said "no pain, no gain" as part of an interview on Real America's Voice. He also said in that interview he believed the higher prices were just "a spike" and would come down once the U.S. eliminated Iran's nuclear capability. e8c07bb6cef2.text: By — Bill Barrow, Associated Press Bill Barrow, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-trump-and-first-lady-unveil-new-task-force-on-womens-health-research Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH: Trump and first lady unveil new task force on women's health research Politics Oct 19, 2026 3:16 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Monday directed the federal government to bolster federal research into women's health, a move pushed by his wife, first lady Melania Trump. Watch the event in the video player above. The Republican president signed an executive order that creates a new women's health division at the National Institutes of Health and a White House task force to focus on the issue. That panel was set to hold its first meeting Monday after the Trumps held a Rose Garden signing ceremony. WATCH: How abortion politics is blocking progress in women's healthcare "Beginning today we will change the reality of women's health," Melania Trump said. "Previous generations fought for women's rights. Our generation will fight to discover the cures that will ensure a woman can live her life in health and to the fullest." Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The president, who spoke after his wife, said the order will "promote new research and really go after the understudied diseases affecting women." The order is also intended to promote diagnostic technology and improve treatment. White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, who recently completed treatment for breast cancer, and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. will lead the White House task force. Donald Trump said the task force will coordinate with various federal agencies and programs. The order does not include specific funding goals. WATCH: Documentary explores why U.S. mothers lack support systems found in other countries The initiative comes after a series of meetings the first lady had with federal health officials. The president called it a "historic action" and praised the first lady's work. "She's accomplished so much," he said before pivoting into unscripted commentary on White House renovations, including the patio stone that now covers what was once the Rose Garden lawn. Shifting back to women's health, the president expressed surprise that some of the order's requirements had not already been imposed. "Who the hell wouldn't have a women's health division?" he said, after recalling that he'd asked Melania Trump, "Are you sure they don't have that?" The executive order calls for targeting maternal health, mental health and endometriosis. It also mentions other health concerns and diseases, including Alzheimer's, osteoporosis, heart disease and stroke. Melania Trump helped shape the order and the task force in consultation with physicians, White House officials, Kennedy and the Republican president. The initiative adds a new dimension to her policy portfolio as first lady. In Donald Trump's second term, the first lady has focused on improving foster care systems and expanding technology and artificial-intelligence access in education. In Trump's first presidency, the first lady's signature initiative, Be Best, focused on child well-being, safe social media use and reducing drug abuse. The White House ceremony comes weeks before Nov. 3 elections and as Donald Trump's job approval ratings have declined, including among women. About 4 in 10 independent women supported Trump during the 2024 election against Democrat Kamala Harris and in the pre-presidency period, according to AP-NORC polls. That dropped to around a quarter in the opening months of this midterm election year, the period marked by Trump's hard-line immigration crackdown in U.S. cities and the opening weeks of the Iran war. Cooper, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/democrat-marie-gluesenkamp-perez-fights-to-keep-a-foothold-in-conservative-pacific-northwest-district Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Perez fights to keep a foothold in conservative Pacific Northwest district Politics Oct 19, 2026 2:48 PM EDT CHEHALIS, Wash. (AP) — Democratic Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez carried a dull kitchen knife and two pairs of rusty scissors through a county fairgrounds south of Seattle. She handed them to Beverly Phoenix, who sat hunched over a table in the back of an exhibit hall, volunteering to help neighbors breathe new life into old tools. Now she offered advice to a member of Congress on using a Dremel, a handheld oscillating device, to sharpen the blades. It was an unassuming campaign stop that reinforced Gluesenkamp Perez's message of self sufficiency. The owner of an auto repair shop with her husband, Gluesenkamp Perez has positioned herself as someone who can help her party bridge the divide between urban and rural, blue collar and white collar, left and right. If Democrats are going to take back control of the U.S. House, they need to hold districts like this one in Southwest Washington, which twice elected Gluesenkamp Perez while also supporting President Donald Trump in all of his campaigns. Although the party has been fixated on whether to accommodate the burgeoning progressive movement, Democrats' willingness to make room for more moderate and unorthodox members could be even more important to winning and maintaining a durable majority. "We are a really independent community. What we want is respect for our priorities, for our values," Gluesenkamp Perez said. When that causes friction with party leaders, she said, her job is "explaining my community to D.C., not letting D.C. try to define my community's priorities." To prove herself, Gluesenkamp Perez, 38, will have to win a very different kind of campaign this year. In her last two elections, she faced Republican Joe Kent, who had connections to extremists. Now she's up against a more mainstream opponent in John Braun, a businessman and state legislator with a better shot at appealing to the district's moderate voters. Gluesenkamp Perez is a lightning rod for progressive criticism The Pacific Northwest has a reputation as a bastion of progressive politics, but Washington's 3rd Congressional District is more complex. It includes both the northern portion of the Portland, Oregon, metro area and expansive rural territory with economies centered around fishing, logging and manufacturing. By balancing those competing interests, Gluesenkamp Perez sometimes finds herself in a lonely group of Democrats siding with Republicans. She opposed President Joe Biden's student debt relief and voted for a Republican election proposal backed by Trump. She supported the Laken Riley immigration bill and defense legislation that included restrictions on abortion and climate change initiatives. She voted to censure fellow Democratic Reps. Al Green of Texas and Rashida Tlaib, and she introduced a resolution to reprimand Democratic Rep. Chuy Garcia for quietly maneuvering to essentially hand his seat to a trusted aide. Tensions flared again last month when Gluesenkamp Perez twice voted with Republicans on procedural issues, an apostasy in the traditions of Capitol Hill, where lawmakers are expected to stick with party leaders when it comes to such matters. As a consequence, Republicans were able to force a vote on a resolution condemning socialism, putting some Democrats in an awkward spot in an election year. "I get upset with her too at times, but you know, I also understand that she represents 800,000-plus people and that's 800,000-plus opinions for differing views," said Dale Benjamin, a 66-year-old retiree and self-described "Bernie progressive" who lives in Battle Ground. "I'm very thankful to her that she's willing to do that, especially in such a divisive place and time that we're in right now." Gluesenkamp Perez has prioritized legislation that bolsters her blue collar identity and the specific industries in her district. She's a strong proponent of "right to repair" legislation that would ensure consumers and independent businesses can repair things like tractors, cars and digital devices without going to the manufacturer. And she's gone to legislative war against the sea lions that congregate around Columbia River dams, feasting on salmon and steelhead before they can reach fishermen. She has pushed for legislation that would make it easier to kill animals that she calls "Corolla-sized vermin." "People sometimes treat my agenda like it's like quirky, and I'm like, this is actually very normal where I'm from," Gluesenkamp Perez said. More moderate Democrats are likely headed to Washington Democrats can't take control of the House without winning at least a dozen districts that voted for Trump. If they pull it off, many of the party's newest members of Congress — the ones who could deliver the majority — could resemble Gluesenkamp Perez more than the democratic socialists who won a string of primaries in blue districts this year. Democratic leaders will need an agenda that speaks to moderates if they want to stay in power, said Jim Kessler, executive vice president for policy at Third Way, a Democratic group that advocates for centrist policies. "What Democrats need to realize, when you win these seats, you're in rental property. You don't own them," Kessler said. "You can keep them as long as you tend to them, but it just takes one bad cycle and they're gone." Speaking of Gluesenkamp Perez, Kessler said "she's carved out her own brand and she is able to survive in a hostile environment." f615783b8ed4.text: By — Dee-Ann Durbin, Associated Press Dee-Ann Durbin, Associated Press By — Anne D'Innocenzio, Associated Press Anne D'Innocenzio, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/consumer-concerns-grow-as-retailers-adopt-ai-assisted-pricing-tools Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Consumer concerns grow as retailers adopt AI-assisted pricing tools Economy Oct 19, 2026 2:35 PM EDT U.S. consumers aren't just frustrated with high prices. They're angry and confused about the increasingly high-tech ways that restaurant chains and major retailers are setting those prices. Digital price tags are rapidly replacing paper ones in grocery aisles. Artificial intelligence tools help businesses decide what to charge by predicting how customers might respond. Terms like "dynamic pricing" and "surveillance pricing" are stirring anxiety on social media, where users wonder if different people are getting different prices for the same product. Americans have grown accustomed to changing prices when booking flights, hotel rooms and rides, but the prospect of everyday spending shaped by algorithms they don't understand and personal data they may not realize they're sharing has touched a nerve. "There are major tensions happening right now between who's really going to have the power with some of these algorithms and usage of bots and AI: the companies or the shopper," said Katie Thomas, who leads an internal consumer behavior think tank at the management consulting firm Kearney. Companies using the technology say some concerns stem from misconceptions about how their pricing tools work. Walmart CEO John Furner said in a blog post last month that digital price tags save workers' time and keep prices up to date. He said the labels aren't used to raise prices based on the weather, time of day or individual shopper. "We price the product, not the person," Furner wrote. But companies aren't always transparent about the customer data they collect and how it's used, which has made consumers suspicious and led to speculation. For example, social media posts falsely imply that electronic shelf labels Walmart plans to put in all its U.S. stores scan shoppers' faces or cellphones to set individualized prices, Thomas said. Lawmakers and regulators are taking action. Legislators in at least 30 states have considered pricing bills this year, including measures addressing algorithmic and personalized pricing, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. The Federal Trade Commission has proposed an enforcement policy warning businesses that failing to disclose their use of personal data to set individualized prices could violate consumer protection law. Here are some of the pricing practices and technologies drawing scrutiny. Dynamic pricing can raise and lower prices What it is: Dynamic pricing means adjusting prices in response to changing market conditions, including supply and demand. An airline that adjusts ticket prices as departures approach is using dynamic pricing. Uber's practice of lifting fares when demand outstrips the supply of available drivers, such as during rush hour, is a type of dynamic pricing known as surge pricing. Why it matters: Frequent price changes extend well beyond food. Decodo, a web data company, tracked price changes in 2025 across products ranging from electronics to clothing and home improvement supplies. About half the U.S. changes it recorded were decreases, contrary to consumers' assumptions that dynamic pricing only raises prices, said Gabriele Vitke, a senior product marketing manager. Digital price labels are coming to more US stores What they are: Digital displays that let stores update shelf prices electronically instead of replacing paper tags. Why it matters: Digital price labels, long used in Europe and Asia, are drawing more attention as they spread to major U.S. retailers like Walmart and Whole Foods. Consumer advocates have argued that digital labels could eventually be used for surge pricing or personalized pricing. Labor unions also have opposed the technology. READ MORE: Inflation worsened last month to 3.7% as midterm elections near The electronic shelf labels make frequent changes easier but don't necessarily lead to higher prices during periods of strong demand. Retailers typically update electronic shelf prices on a regular schedule, often weekly, because shoppers value consistency, said Asa Farquhar of Relex Solutions, a retail technology company. Researchers who tracked prices at an unnamed grocery chain found "virtually no surge pricing" after the labels were introduced. "Changing prices throughout the day, the way airlines or rideshare apps do, is exceedingly rare in grocery and general merchandise today," Farquhar said. Personalized pricing, also called surveillance pricing, draws on customer data What it is: Personalized pricing means offering customers different prices and discounts based on their locations, incomes, web-browsing habits and other information about individuals or groups of shoppers. Some advocacy groups and regulators use the term "surveillance pricing" for the same practice. Why it matters: It's unclear how widely businesses use personal information to customize prices. An FTC staff report released in January 2025 found that intermediaries offering tools that can tailor prices and promotions worked with at least 250 clients, including grocery and clothing retailers. Lawmakers in Maryland, New Jersey and Connecticut recently enacted restrictions on using shoppers' personal data to determine what they pay. The Maryland and New Jersey laws focus on groceries, with exceptions for certain loyalty discounts and other promotional offers. Connecticut's legislation covers a broader range of retail purchases. California prosecutors sued Target in 2022, alleging that the retailer's app displayed lower prices before shoppers entered stores and raised them once they were ins
