Millions of people across India are marking Dussehra, one of the country's most widely celebrated Hindu festivals, with processions, prayers and the ceremonial burning of giant effigies to symbolise the triumph of good over evil.
The festival is observed with different rituals and traditions across different parts of the country but with grand celebrations everywhere.
It commonly marks the deity Lord Ram's victory over the mythological 10-headed king Ravan.
The festival coincides with Vijayadashami, celebrated in eastern, southern and other parts of India, to honour goddess Durga slaying the buffalo demon Mahishasura.
Hindus follow a lunar calendar, and Dussehra falls on the 10th day after Navratri, a nine-night festival of worship and celebrations.
In the days leading up to Dussehra in northern India, performers wear elaborate costumes and make-up to stage Ramlila, the dramatic retelling of the ancient Hindu epic Ramayana. They recount Lord Ram's exile and his wife Sita's abduction by Ravan, culminating in the battle that symbolises the victory of good over evil. The final act is followed by the ritualistic burning of the effigies of Ravan, his brother, Kumbhkaran, and son Meghnath.
The vibrant stage is usually accompanied by a carnival-like atmosphere with food stalls, rides and smaller performances.
In the east and some other parts, as well as among Hindus in Bangladesh, the festival sees devotees worshipping the divine feminine power with Durga Puja celebrations.
Temporary tents housing idols of Goddess Durga and other deities are set up across cities and towns. People visit these structures, known as pandals, where Durga is often depicted slaying the buffalo demon Mahishasura.
Current affairs often make their way into the traditional celebrations, like theme-based decoration of tents in Kolkata city, which is famous for its Durga Puja celebrations.
Dussehra also marks the beginning of preparations for Diwali - the festival of lights - which is held 20 days later.

05690acd2668.text: One issue is breaking through even among the most loyal Republican supporters: gas prices . Why it matters: Republicans promised to slash gas prices. But the Iran war sent them soaring, up 37% since President Trump took office . Republicans call it temporary. But there are limits to what voters will accept. On recent campaign trips with House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) and Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.), gas prices were the most frequent concern raised at events attended by Axios. These weren't rooms full of undecided voters. They were GOP donors, activists and supporters who had turned out to help Republicans win in November. Zoom in: The first question Scalise fielded at a campaign event for Republican Marty O'Donnell in Nevada was about high gas prices. "Everyone's always worried about gas prices," the attendee said, asking whether Republicans could do more to promote Trump's efforts to expand domestic energy production. Another attendee pointed to the gas-price difference between California and Oregon on a recent trip, and asked whether Congress could intervene to ease state restrictions. Scalise acknowledged the impact of the Iran war on gas prices — and said they'd fall once it's resolved — but blamed Democratic energy policies for making the U.S. more vulnerable to rising costs. Zoom out: Emmer faced similar concerns during a recent campaign trip through North Carolina and Virginia. "Four-dollar gas, five-dollar diesel, six-dollar diesel, totally unacceptable," Emmer told supporters at a North Carolina fundraiser. "But it ain't enough to make me vote for communists." "[Democrats] are talking about affordability. That's the problem. We need to be sensitive to the fact that gas and diesel are way up. Just sensitive to it because people are struggling," he told Axios in an interview. The big picture: Republican candidates are feeling the pressure too. Texas Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton privately blamed the Iran war and gas prices for his campaign struggles, according to audio obtained by Axios. "It's the war, it's gas prices, it's diesel," Paxton told donors at a closed-door fundraiser last month, calling affordability "by far our biggest problem." The bottom line: "I don't think gaslighting works," House GOP conference Chairwoman Lisa McClain (R-Mich.) told Axios in an interview last month. "I think if you meet voters where they're at and you have an honest conversation with them ... that's pretty refreshing to them."

cfffb25dab62.text: House Majority Leader Steve Scalise won't talk about defeat, even as his outside GOP allies are pulling money anyway. Why it matters: Republicans face brutal political headwinds, but Scalise (R-La.) stands out from his fellow leaders for refusing to even contemplate losing the House. Zoom in: At an event for Republican Marty O'Donnell, who's challenging Rep. Susie Lee (D-Nev.), Scalise argued that his presence in the district was evidence Republicans are still on offense. "If it's some horrible cycle for Republicans, then why am I here?" Scalise told supporters at a Las Vegas country club Thursday. "This is a winnable race," he said. But MAGA Inc., a super PAC allied with President Trump, pulled nearly $1 million in advertising from the race last week. The big picture: House Democrats lead the generic ballot by eight points in new Washington Post-ABC polling . Trump's approval is at a record low of 31% ( Reuters/Ipsos ) and 72% say the country is on the wrong track (Post/ABC). He's making 56 campaign stops between August and Election Day as part of what he's dubbed the "Save America Tour," complete with T-shirts featuring a map of his travels. "This is like better than a rock band," Scalise told Axios during an in-flight interview while campaigning in Arizona and Nevada last week. Scalise identified 35 competitive districts , including 15 Democratic-held seats Republicans believe they have a chance to flip. He pointed to Reps. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.), Juan Ciscomani (R-Ariz.), Rob Bresnahan (R-Pa.) and Ryan Mackenzie (R-Pa.) as races he'll watch closely as bellwethers for how the night could unfold. The pro-Scalise super PAC Save American Freedom is also launching a $3.5 million get-out-the-vote and digital advertising blitz to help 52 House Republicans, Axios' Alex Isenstadt reports. Among the Republicans benefiting are Reps. Brad Finstad (R-Minn.), Mike Carey (R-Ohio) and Rob Wittman (R-Va.), along with GOP candidates Ralph Alvarado (KY-6), Alex Mealer (TX-9) and Jenny Costa Honeycutt (S.C.-1). The intrigue: The GOP's pullback in some districts has fueled speculation that Republicans are giving up on the House to save the Senate. But Scalise argued it will still benefit his members. He pointed to Iowa, where the Congressional Leadership Fund, a super PAC allied with House Republicans, pulled financial support from Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks' district. Senate Republicans subsequently bought the airtime for Ashley Hinson. "You actually get a three for one, " Scalise said, arguing that shifting the ad time to Hinson will benefit Miller-Meeks, Rep. Zach Nunn and the Republican running to succeed Hinson in her House district. "You're going to probably see that in some other areas too," Scalise said. He pointed to Senate races in North Carolina and Texas, where he acknowledged "challenges" at the top of the ticket. The bottom line: Scalise isn't ready to look beyond Election Day, even as Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) publicly weighed in on that very scenario last week. Johnson said he intends to remain the top House Republican even if Democrats win the majority. The race for the top job could become a three-way fight among Johnson, Scalise and Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio). Scalise repeatedly declined to say whether he would endorse Johnson for minority leader or consider running himself. "Anybody who's thinking about planning for us losing is in the wrong business," Scalise told Axios.

5a872c7ebc66.text: The war of words between President Trump and Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelenskyy reached another fever pitch on Monday. Trump again excoriated the embattled Ukrainian leader, putting more pressure on Zelenskyy than on the man in Moscow who started this war, Vladimir Putin. The president's comments come after the U.S. has limited a key technology that Ukraine relies on. Nick Schifrin reports. Geoff Bennett: The war of words between President Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy escalated again today, with Mr. Trump sharply criticizing the Ukrainian leader and directing more pressure at him than at Russia's Vladimir Putin, who launched the war. Zelenskyy is set to meet with U.S. negotiators this week. But the latest tensions come as Washington has restricted Ukraine's access to critical technology it relies on in its fight against Russia. Nick Schifrin starts our coverage. Nick Schifrin: In Kyiv's shattered windows and downtown debris, the impact of what Ukraine says is blocked U.S. support. Today, Russian drones and missiles hit the capital without warning, leaving walls slashed by shrapnel, blowing out residences, a shopping mall, and a school, part of Russia's attempt to make Kyiv unlivable. MAKSYM MAKSYMOVYCH, Kyiv, Ukraine, Resident (through translator): It's one thing to observe this happening elsewhere in other places or other cities, but now it's getting closer and closer. That's a bit chilling. Nick Schifrin: The chill is between President Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who today suggested the U.S. stop the intelligence that has for years fed into Ukraine's air alert system. Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukrainian President: Only the United States has this unique intelligence to say, to tell us, to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles. Nick Schifrin: What Zelenskyy did not say, the U.S. warning system is not perfect and can miss certain Russian missile launches, especially in bad weather. But Ukraine is having to physically slow down and is losing connection to its drone interceptors and mid- and long-range drones because of speed caps by the American SpaceX system. That threatens Ukraine's ability to bring the war to Russia and defend itself. On Sunday on "Meet the Press," Zelenskyy said the intel sharing was on and off. Kristen Welker, Moderator, "Meet the Press": Is that accurate? Has the United States cut off intelligence sharing with Ukraine? Volodymyr Zelenskyy: It was blocked for some period of time. And then it was de-blocked by American side. We are very thankful for this. Now it works. Nick Schifrin: Today, in Uzbekistan, Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied the U.S. had ever restricted intelligence. Marco Rubio, U.S. Secretary of State: I don't know where he's getting these things from or why he's saying these things to the press. You should go back and ask him. There's been no pause. The United States -- but, again, what he should be focused on and what we want to be focused on is bringing an end to this war. President Donald Trump: We've given a lot to Ukraine. They've given us nothing. Nick Schifrin: This afternoon, President Trump accused Zelenskyy of not wanting to end the war. Donald Trump: Zelenskyy is not helping matters much. I think he doesn't want to stop it. I think it's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine. Nick Schifrin: And President Trump said he might meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping next month to discuss arms control, but said this about the possibility of the three discussing Ukraine: Donald Trump: I would do it, not so much for Ukraine. I -- because Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. Nick Schifrin: That is not how Ukraine sees it, a war launched by Russia with enormous casualties, including a baby in Kharkiv today, some progress at enormous human cost, and now its most important supporter limiting its support. For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Nick Schifrin.

a27791c8a2bf.text: As Ukraine and Russia trade attacks, President Trump has exempted Russia from sanctions, widening his rift with Ukrainian President Zelenskyy. To discuss the latest developments, Geoff Bennett spoke with Denys Sienik, Ukraine's Deputy Ambassador to the U.S. Geoff Bennett: We turn now to Dennis Sienik, the charge d'affaires of Ukraine to the U.S. I spoke with him a short time ago and asked about the evidence Ukraine has that Washington is deliberately withholding intelligence with advance warning of the Russian missiles that hit Kyiv. Denys Sienik, Ukrainian Deputy Ambassador to the United States: Well, nobody is talking about any deliberate actions. What we are talking about is the mere fact that something has happened. So, last week, we had situations when Ukraine did not receive early warning, and we informed about it our partners and wanted to establish the facts. And then, unfortunately, it happened again. And we just hope that the technology will work and all the data will be provided later on, so that in the future we will be able to be notified about the future attacks. Geoff Bennett: And, specifically, as it relates to SpaceX's Starshield system that plays a critical role in Ukraine's military operations, including those interceptor drones and the longer-range strikes, President Zelensky said again today that access to that communication system has been restricted. Again, what evidence do you have that that has been deliberate? And do you believe that decision, if so, came from President Trump or Elon Musk, or both? Denys Sienik: Well, our specialists can track literally live the speed of the connection that Starlink is working on and the Starshield technology. And we can see that the speed that we used to have, which was unlimited speed, is no longer in place. And we can see that, when we are launching our drones to intercept Russian drones, and when they reach the speed of more than 100 miles, then the system says there is a failure and the maximum speed has been exceeded. Geoff Bennett: Does Ukraine believe the U.S. is acting as an honest broker in these peace negotiations, or do you increasingly see Washington as a source of pressure, rather than protection? Denys Sienik: Well, the fact that we speak on a daily basis with American team means that there is a clear desire to end the war, at least to start with the cease-fire. That's our priority. Geoff Bennett: When the president takes steps that effectively ease pressure on Russia and ramps up pressure on Ukraine, what message does that send to President Putin? Denys Sienik: Our position has never changed since day one. There must be additional pressure on Russia so that Russia stops this war. So, any message that Putin will receive that sanctions may be lifted or restrictions may be lifted or there will be less pressure on Russia, that will incentivize his attacks and actually move him to escalate in order to achieve even greater objectives that he has on his mind. We can see that the sanctions are working. Russian economy is staggering. The inflation rate, the consumption rate, the wealth fund in Russia has been depleted. The only thing is that every time Russia is adjusting itself to the existing sanctions. And that is why we are so actively advocating for putting more and more new sanctions, more pressure on Russia, so that it does not have the capability to adapt. Geoff Bennett: There are reports that President Putin wants to discuss Ukraine's future with President Trump and China's leader without President Zelenskyy at the table. Is Ukraine concerned that decisions about its future are being made or could be made without its consent? Denys Sienik: Well, nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine. And this has not changed. I cannot imagine how it is possible to discuss, like, anything which is related to the war without my president being present at the table. Geoff Bennett: What would you say to those Americans who believe the U.S. has done enough to support Ukraine, and it's time for Ukraine to make some difficult compromises to end this war? Denys Sienik: We are talking about our territory that we have been defending since 2014. You fought fiercely for your independence. We are fighting fiercefully for our independence. And we understand that, if you look into history, Russia will not stop. And I really want to draw your attention to the situation in Oleshky in Kherson region. About 2,000 people are trapped in that occupied town without access to food, to medicine. Russian soldiers are taking food away from Ukrainians, do not allow any access to Ukrainian side, to our partners, to Red Cross to enter the that town and to provide medicine. That's what Ukrainians are thinking about. My message to the American people is just gratitude. We are grateful for all the assistance that the United States has provided, that the U.S. Congress has provided to Ukraine. I am thrilled to see the Ukrainian flags flying in the streets. As long as there is a conflict and aggression, he will do his best to stay in power. In the contrary, he will have to focus on his domestic affairs. And they are not doing great at all. And that is why I have no doubt that Putin will continue doing what he is doing. But I hope that we will be able to sit down at the negotiations table and finish this war. Geoff Bennett: Charge D'affaires Denys Sienik, thank you for your time this evening. We appreciate it. Denys Sienik: Thank you.

d5ccad625fba.text: In our news wrap Monday, a federal judge clashed with Justice Department lawyers in the latest legal standoff over the fate of a Washington, D.C. golf course, the Supreme Court will review a Reconstruction-era ban on home distilleries and Israeli authorities say they've arrested at least ten people in connection with recent settler attacks in the occupied West Bank. Geoff Bennett: Also, today a federal judge clashed with Justice Department lawyers in the latest legal standoff over the fate of a Washington, D.C., golf course. The judge is demanding details on who's responsible for the recent cutting down of hundreds of trees at the East Potomac Golf Links. The government has argued that they were removed as part of routine maintenance. But President Trump told reporters today that he's aiming to, as he put it, build a better golf course after posting on social media that the site would be closed for a 15-month renovation. During today's hearing, the judge said -- quote -- "There is no universe in which all of this coincidentally happened all at the same time." The U.S. Supreme Court says it will review a Reconstruction era ban on home distilleries. The justices will decide whether Congress had the authority to ban the practice back in the 1860s in an effort to prevent distillers from avoiding taxes. The High Court will also revisit the issue of race and school admissions in a case involving Asian American parents and selective middle schools in Maryland. It comes three years after the justices restricted affirmative action in higher education. And the court rejected a bid by alleged 9/11 Mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed to revive a plea deal the government later withdrew. He and two accomplices are expected to stand for a military trial in the year 2028. Israeli authorities say they have arrested at least 10 people in connection with recent settler attacks in the occupied West Bank, including on European diplomats and Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine. Police released video today showing at least one suspect being arrested in a predawn operation. Authorities have not identified the suspects, but Israel's army radio reports that all are Israeli citizens. Meantime, Israeli settlers continued to move through Palestinian-owned olive groves today as local residents accuse Israeli forces of standing by, rather than intervening to protect them during the annual harvest. Mohammed Abu Rabee, Resident of Deir Abu Mash'al, West Bank (through translator): I do not believe the army. These people are one nation in two sides of one coin. They are the same. The settlers attack us when the Israeli army is here. Geoff Bennett: U.S. and European officials have condemned the violence. Meantime, President Donald Trump has endorsed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's reelection bid, calling him a great warrior. Mr. Trump's support comes just over a week ahead of Israel's first elections since the October 7 Hamas-led attacks. In Yemen, authorities say Houthi forces fired ballistic missiles at a military camp today, killing at least 53 soldiers and injuring 200 more. Video published on social media shows the aftermath of the attack. It was one of the deadliest strikes since a resurgence in fighting between the Iran-backed group and government forces this summer. It comes a day after Houthi health officials say an airstrike by Saudi-led forces killed at least nine people in rebel-held territory in Yemen's north. The Saudi government has not commented on that incident. On Wall Street today, stocks ended mixed to start the week. The Dow Jones industrial average slipped around 35 points. The Nasdaq rallied more than 1 percent following last week's losses. The S&P 500 also ended higher on the day. And journalist Noah Adams, who hosted NPR's "All Things Considered" for nearly two decades, has died. Noah Adams, NPR News: This is special coverage from NPR News. Geoff Bennett: To millions of radio listeners, Noah Adams was a steady, reassuring voice, guiding Americans through historic moments, from the fall of the Berlin Wall to the September 11 attacks. But Adams also had a gift for telling quieter, more personal stories, capturing the lives and experiences of everyday Americans. He wrote five books exploring subjects from the Wright Brothers to his own experience learning how to play the piano in his 50s. His wife says Adams died at their home in Ohio on Friday. Noah Adams was 84 years old.

The Scoop
As Waymo expands into new cities with its self-driving cars, the company plans to use the $5 billion it recently borrowed to massively increase its fleet.
The company, which currently has 4,000 cars, is looking to bring its total number to 8,000 by the end of the year and grow to 20,000 by the end of next year, according to people familiar with the matter.
Waymo declined to comment. The company said in a statement on its website that it raised the funds to grow internationally and in the US.
Waymo, which operates in 15 US cities, is also bringing its rides to locations such as Toronto. Waymo recently opened a facility in Nashville in partnership with Lyft to charge, clean and maintain cars.
Waymo has already ordered thousands of cars from China, to help expand its fleet, the New York Post reported. The company has also rebranded versions of a vehicle made by Zeekr, a unit of CCP-linked company Geely Holding Group.
Know More
Waymo recently raised debt for the first time, and it came without guarantees from Alphabet, its parent company. It borrowed the $5 billion from private credit lenders, and the deal allows the company to use its fleet in the future to borrow more by securitizing leases.

3488ab63c719.text: In recent presidential elections, Ohio has become a reliably Republican state. But in this year's midterms, it's once again a battleground. The races for governor and U.S. Senate are both seen as toss-ups by The Cook Political Report, and there are a handful of competitive House districts. Liz Landers reports on how national issues are affecting Ohio voters as they prepare to head to the polls. Geoff Bennett: In recent presidential elections, Ohio has become reliably Republican. But, this year, the state is once again a major battleground. The Cook Political Report rates both the governor's race and the U.S. Senate contest as toss-ups. Several congressional races are also competitive. And with just two weeks until Election Day, Liz Landers reports on how national issues, especially concerns about affordability, are shaping voters' decisions in Ohio. Liz Landers: Youngstown, Ohio, was built on steel. Today, abandoned factories still line stretches of the Mahoning River, a reminder of jobs that left decades ago and never fully came back. Ron Gay, Communications Workers of America: I was born right before the steel mill started to close, which was the late '70s. And it's been rough to see the neighborhoods go down, to see the income of people go down, to see the overall quality of the city go down. Liz Landers: And the losses keep coming. The summer, Youngstown bakery Schwebel shut down after 120 years. In nearby B Boardman, AT&T is closing a call center that once employed hundreds of union workers. A decade ago, Donald Trump won over working-class voters in Ohio by promising to bring jobs like these back. This year, with Republicans in charge in Washington and in Columbus, they're the ones being asked to answer for it. Chris Anderson, leads the Mahoning County Democratic Party. Chris Anderson, Chair, Mahoning County Democratic Party: They promised that, on day one, they were going to tackle inflation and affordability, they were going to make everyone's lives better. And I think you would be hard-pressed to find a single person who thinks that their life is better today than it was in 2024. Liz Landers: That argument now runs through two toss-up races. One could decide control of the U.S. Senate. The other could give Ohio its first Democratic governor in 15 years. Fmr. Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-OH): Ohioans don't have anyone in the Senate fighting for you until November. Liz Landers: In a region still waiting for its comeback, Sherrod Brown is attempting one of his own. He won three Senate races here before losing two years ago. His pitch? Republicans made life more expensive. Fmr. Sen. Sherrod Brown: Jon Husted stands with corporations, not with us, not with Ohioans, not with you. And we all pay for it. Sen. Jon Husted (R-OH): My team and I are here to serve you. Liz Landers: Republican Jon Husted, appointed to the seat last year, has his own story of the decline. He says his father was laid off when the Ohio factory where he worked closed. Sen. Jon Husted: And after 25 years of clocking in every day, he got laid off. Husted says the answer is the tax cuts he voted for and that Brown had three decades to fix things. Narrator: Thirty-two years in D.C. is enough for Senator Brown. Liz Landers: But the war with Iran and the gas prices that came with it have tested even Trump's allies. Last month, Husted broke with the president, saying the war needs to end so prices can come down. At Trump's recent rally here, some supporters said they're willing to wait. Gerald Carpenter, Republican Voter: Gas prices affect me a bunch. I own a pizza shop. So, I have got delivery boys. Everything that we -- cheese, flour, boxes, you name it, it can go up. But I have been doing it for 31 years. So it's not like there haven't been ripples in the past. And I believe Trump's a man of his word that, if we get these gas prices under control, we get Iran under control, and I think gas prices will come down. Liz Landers: It's a similar fight in the governor's race. Vivek Ramaswamy (R), Ohio Gubernatorial Candidate: Why is it that life feels so unaffordable? Liz Landers: Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, an entrepreneur and former presidential candidate, promises to roll back property taxes and eventually scrap the state income tax. Vivek Ramaswamy: So this question on property taxes, this is probably the number one issue in the state that a governor can fix relatively immediately. Amy Acton (D), Ohio Gubernatorial Candidate: As governor, I will take on the corruption that's raising our costs, cut taxes for the middle class. Liz Landers: Democrat Amy Acton, who led the state Health Department early in the COVID pandemic, is proposing tax credits for working families. She says Ramaswamy's tax cuts would come at the expense of schools and public safety. Amy Acton: My opponent says people are struggling because they're not working hard enough, because they're lazy and mediocre, which is not the Ohioans I know and that I have grown up with. Liz Landers: Early voting is already under way. With control of the Senate up for grabs, many voters see a choice that reaches well beyond Ohio. Rhonda Luetje, Columbus, Ohio, Resident: I feel like, Trump's first term, he had some people surrounding him that acted as kind of bumpers for him that kept him in the lane, but this time he is completely unchecked, and the House and the Senate are also not checking him and, to some degree, the Supreme Court. Bob Thompson, Mansfield, Ohio, Resident: I think that if we can keep everything red, after the midterms, he will do what he needs to do for the second half of his term. Liz Landers: Back in Youngstown, the stakes feel closer to home. Just ask the region's AFL-CIO Labor Council. Larry Fauvre, President, Mahoning and Trumbull AFL-CIO Labor Council: I have lived here all my life. I have watched the good times. I have watched the bad times. And my family grew up here, and some of my family have moved away because there was no jobs here that they could

463d4647c8c8.text: NPR’s Tamara Keith and Carrie Dann of the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter join Geoff Bennett to discuss the latest political news, including a new poll putting President Trump's approval rating at a record low, the amount of money being spent on Senate races, Trump escalating his feud with Ukraine's president and Trump's attempts to remake Washington. Geoff Bennett: A new poll puts President Trump's approval rating at a record low. Meantime, the president is escalating his feud with Ukraine's president. Our Politics Monday team is here to discuss that and more. We have got Tamara Keith of NPR and Carrie Dann of The Cook Political Report With Amy Walter. Amy Walter is away this evening. It's great to see you both. Tamara Keith, National Public Radio: Good to be here. Geoff Bennett: So let's start with this latest new national poll. You have got The Wall -- excuse me -- The Washington Post/ABC News/Ipsos poll. It's putting President Trump's approval rating at just 33 percent, the lowest of either term. And Democrats have an eight-point advantage heading into November. So, Tam, how much of a liability is that for Republicans on the ballot? I know you have some new reporting. Tamara Keith: Yes, so back in September, President Trump held a dinner in the Rose Garden with about 30 Republicans in competitive races. And, at that dinner, he promised he was going to go to all of their districts. He was going to go to 35 competitive districts and help those members by just showing up. Well, my analysis of his travel since that time is that he's gone to a fewer than a third of those districts, and instead he's gone to a lot of very red states and very red districts. Part of that is because he's a liability in swing races, and part of that is that he loves the warm embrace of a rally in a place where they actually love him. He claims he's going to say thank you. But part of it is just that the map has shifted so that areas that we weren't even really talking about a few months ago are now considered competitive races. Geoff Bennett: And, Carrie, where do you watching most closely to gauge where this election is headed and if all of this polling is actually true or accurate? Carrie Dann, Managing Editor, The Cook Political Report With Amy Walter: One of the numbers I found the most fascinating in that Washington Post poll was among Republicans. And the way The Post broke it down was MAGA-affiliated Republicans and then Republicans who say, I affiliate as a Republican, but I'm not really into the MAGA movement. Among MAGA Republicans, Donald Trump's approval rating is 94 percent. Like, basically, all of those people are huge fans of the president. But among that other group of Republicans who are not into the MAGA movement, he's barely breaking even. Almost half of those voters disapprove of him. And, to your point, I think one of the trickiest things that Republicans are trying to do is to tell those people, disaffected Republicans, hey, you got to hold your nose and show up in November and vote for a candidate, even if you're not crazy about the president, without deactivating that 94 percent approval rating among MAGA people, which is I think why he's going to these very red areas to juice every single one of those voters that he possibly can, while also quietly singling to other Republicans in the state, hey, you might not love the president right now, but you need to show up for your team. Geoff Bennett: And, Tam, Democrats appear to have momentum, even in states -- as Liz just reported, states like Ohio, that have shifted toward Republicans in recent elections. How do you interpret that? Tamara Keith: Yes, Ohio is a fascinating state. It is, according to AdImpact data, the most expensive state in that Senate race among all of the Senate races starting September 1 through Election Day. Just truckloads of money are being dumped on that state. What is fascinating about it is you really have, in some ways, two incumbents and then also two non-incumbents at the same time, because Jon Husted didn't win the seat. He was appointed. And a lot of people still think Sherrod Brown is a senator from Ohio. Geoff Bennett: Well, let's shift our focus in the time that remains to Ukraine, because President Trump is escalating his confrontation with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. There's this dispute over access to important satellite communications that are used for the military there. The president has blamed Ukraine for rising gas prices in this country. What's driving the president's increasingly hostile posture toward Ukraine and its leader? Carrie Dann: Well, I think you justified that he's trying to draw a line between Ukraine and high gas prices. I think it may be a little bit late to do that credibly with voters. I think voters have drawn a very bright line between the Iran conflict and the high gas prices. He may be trying to deflect that by talking about this other conflict. But I looked back. You mentioned AdImpact. I looked at the ad spending around the issue of Ukraine and Russia this cycle, $2 million. For Iran and gas prices, we're at like $80 million. So, clearly, the politics of this are not that voters really care about this issue. I think what he is trying to do is tie it to gas prices and tie the high gas prices to Joe Biden, instead of the decisions that his administration has made. Geoff Bennett: How do you see it, based on your reporting? Tamara Keith: Well, voters very clearly tie it to the Iran war. Like, they draw that direct line. The president certainly -- I have covered him for years. He has often been looking for reasons to escalate or to fight with Zelenskyy. This isn't really new. This is certainly a new front in this, but he's often been feuding with Zelenskyy. And so this is a moment where he is just throwing a lot of spaghetti against a lot of walls. In this case, doing a deal or announcing that Russia will sell diesel to the United States, no one is expecting this

a281cba852a5.text: Electric aviation is still in the very early stages of its development. But a number of companies are moving forward with more ambitious plans. In contrast to its approach with other forms of electric transportation, the Trump administration seems willing to embrace a bigger rollout. Aviation correspondent Miles O'Brien reports on the promise and the challenges of the budding industry. Geoff Bennett: Electric aviation, or e-aviation, is still in its infancy infancy, but a growing number of companies are developing plans to bring electric aircraft into wider use. And unlike its approach to other forms of electric transportation, the Trump administration has so far embraced the industry's expansion. Our aviation correspondent, Miles O'Brien, became the first journalist to pilot one of these aircraft and reports on the promise and the challenges of this emerging technology. Miles O'Brien: It wasn't very graceful, but that's me stepping into the future of aviation, a more sustainable future. Kyle Clark, Founder and CEO, BETA Technologies: As we get rolling on the runway, stay on the center line. Miles O'Brien: The pilot in command is Kyle Clark, founder and CEO of BETA Technologies, a start-up focused on developing electric aircraft. Kyle Clark: Give it to me. I will go off the center line, come back. Just feel it out, because, when you land you're going to want to have that muscle memory. Miles O'Brien: We taxied toward the runway, held short, and then it was suddenly silent. It's just weird how quiet it is. Kyle Clark: I know. (LAUGHTER) Miles O'Brien: When the motor is all electric, it only turns when you need it. Kyle Clark: Three, two, one gentle back. There we go. And just feel that... Miles O'Brien: Yes, yes. Kyle Clark: Perfect. And fly like you have got a glass of wine in your hand there, kind of. Miles O'Brien: As we flew over Vermont's Green Mountains, Kyle gave me an update on the company he founded nine years ago here in his hometown, Burlington. They are designing and building planes, batteries, and motors, marching through an FAA certification process that isn't plugged in to this kind of transformation. What takes up most of your time? Kyle Clark: Regulatory. It's the interpretation of the rules that were written for turbine aircraft applied to electric aircraft. Miles O'Brien: Right. Kyle Clark: It's not an easy task to write a rule that's applicable. Miles O'Brien: While the Trump administration has pulled back federal support for electric cars, it appears to be charged up about electric aviation. In May of 2026, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy flew with Kyle Clark in the plane we were in. He also got some time in the electric vertical takeoff and landing, or eVTOL, version, and then gushed about it on social media. Sean Duffy, U.S. Transportation Secretary: People and products are going to move more efficiently, more cost-effectively. Kyle Clark: We burned $3. Sean Duffy: Three fricking dollars on that flight. Kyle Clark: Yes. Sean Duffy: This is not "The Jetsons." This is actual real life. Miles O'Brien: There is some real-life testing under way. In June of 2025, the White House launched a program to accelerate the deployment of eVTOL operations in the United States. The FAA has carved out some airspace for eight projects spanning 26 states. Beta is among at least eight companies that will test-fly still uncertified electric and hybrid aircraft in demonstration missions, ranging from cargo delivery to passenger service, a three-year pilot program in more ways than one. Chriss Rocheleau, Former Deputy FAA Administrator: What we want to be able to do is make sure they're able to actively operate in the national airspace system. That's something that we hadn't done before. Miles O'Brien: Chriss Rocheleau was the FAA deputy administrator when we spoke with him. When do you think there will be electric vertical takeoff and landing air taxis flying in the United States with paying passengers? Chriss Rocheleau: I think we are right around the corner from certifying an aircraft. We certainly have made it clear and the secretary of transportation and the administrator of the FAA has made it clear we will be operating commercially by L.A. '28, by the Olympics. Miles O'Brien: San Jose-based Archer Aviation is the official air taxi provider for the 2028 Olympic and Paralympic Games. The company plans to carry as many as four paying passengers at a time on 10-to-20-minute flights across greater Los Angeles. It will be an important P.R. milestone. But the Jetsonian vision of skies filled with air taxis has yet to arrive. Kyle Clark: I think we should go over to the battery line. Miles O'Brien: Kyle Clark gave me a factory tour with a special focus on the bottleneck to practical, affordable electric flight, the batteries. The plane we flew has 13,000 lithium-ion cells bundled into 55 modules, five times the energy of a Tesla Model 3. But Clark says they exceed automotive and even FAA safety standards. Kyle Clark: We use advanced materials like carbon and titanium, aluminum. Of course, it costs a little more to do it like this, but we also have twice the number of battery management systems in here and a whole lot more quality control coming in. Miles O'Brien: BETA engineers are running batteries through accelerated life cycles to see how they perform over time. They deliberately drop them, overheat them, and otherwise push them to failure, working toward a design that ensures even the worst-case scenario does not become catastrophic. COO Sean Donovan earned his battery chops at Tesla. Sean Donovan, COO, BETA Technologies: E.V.s on the ground have pushed battery technology really far that have really enabled electric aviation. Miles O'Brien: But batteries designed for electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft must meet a challenge nothing in your garage will ever face. They need to deliver very high power at the beginning and the end of their discharge time. Venkat Viswanathan,

911e12b0767c.text: As cultural institutions across the country face growing pressure to avoid issues of race, a major new exhibition is confronting them head-on. The work of artist Arthur Jafa spans two floors of New York’s New Museum in his largest exhibition to date. Senior arts correspondent Jeffrey Brown met with Jafa for our arts and culture series, CANVAS. Geoff Bennett: As cultural institutions across the country face growing pressure to avoid issues of race, a major new exhibition is confronting them head on. The work of artist Arthur Jafa spans two floors of New York's New Museum and his largest exhibition to date. Senior arts correspondent Jeffrey Brown met with Jafa for our arts and culture series, Canvas. Jeffrey Brown: Everywhere you look in Arthur Jafa new exhibition, one image is placed next to another, whether still or moving, each affecting the other, each changed by its proximity to the other. Arthur Jafa, Artist and Filmmaker: This is the Big Bang, the beginning of the universe. That image has never existed next to that image. One picture here, another picture there, you put them next to each other, boom, we got something else. Jeffrey Brown: At New York's New Museum, the boom of Jafa's exhibition, titled I Am Tony, a reference to jazz drummer Tony Williams, extends over two floors. Photographs and sculptures, wall plaques, and installations of cutout figures, music and soundscapes everywhere. (MUSIC) Jeffrey Brown: Most of all, his films, including "Love Is the Message, The Message is Death" from 2016, a seven-minute montage or visual poem made from more than 100 video and archival clips, portraying the pain and joy, the hatred and celebration of Black life in America. Arthur Jafa: I'm less interested increasingly in making work about Black people and more interested in making work like Black people. Jeffrey Brown: What does that mean? Arthur Jafa: It means I'm not trying to declare anything about Black people. I'm just trying to make things that in some way parallel or reflect the complexity of Black being or what a Black person, how a Black person might be understood. Jeffrey Brown: Jafa was born and raised in Mississippi. He started out in the film world, notably a cinematographer on "Daughters of the Dust," the 1991 movie directed by his former wife, Julie Dash. He would work with Spike Lee and Stanley Kubrick. His turn to the art world came later. He's always been a collector and creator of images. Here, he's constructed a kind of maze of them that visitors can walk through. Arthur Jafa: It's a different way to structure them, like you're moving through the relationship of images, as opposed to standing outside of them. Jeffrey Brown: Another display here, a series of photographic notebooks. Arthur Jafa: Yes, I have just been fascinated with that. All of my life, just I have been gatherer, a hoarder, maybe even of images and stuff. I consume images, so I'm also interested in cooking, just to take the analogy. Jeffrey Brown: Cooking them? Arthur Jafa: Yes, I mean, you know what I'm saying? You -- if there's something you're interested in, you don't necessarily just want to consume it. You want to produce it as well. Jeffrey Brown: His art films can be quick-cut still images, as in "SloPEX," playing in the room where we talked, or extended scenes, as in "The White Album," another meditation on race and racial attitudes. "Akingdoncomethas" is an hour-45-minute portrait of the Black church with sermons and singing, while "Aghdra" is a computer-generated ocean, lava-like, accompanied by a soundtrack of slowed-down soul music. Arthur Jafa: A lot of it is just leaning into an aspect of moving images that I think is musical. Jeffrey Brown: Music, culture, history, the full variety of lived Black experience and all its complexities, as in one of Jafa's newest works, "M.J.," for Michael Jackson, the mesmerizing performer, the troubled individual. There's the moment in "Love Is the Message, The Message is Death" where a woman says, what would America be if it loved Black people as much as it loves Black culture? So you are looking at the both the beauty and the violence. Arthur Jafa: Yes. Sometimes, I say we like the canary in the mine shaft, a Western civilization, but the mine shaft is an incredible place to be. Black culture exists in a perpetual state of emergency. And I mean that in both senses of it, like crisis and the pressure of crisis, but also constantly emerging, constantly coming up with new things. And that coming up with new things, this sort of inventiveness, the improvisation, all that, it is -- and it's strictly bound up with the pressure of Black life. You can't separate the two. Jeffrey Brown: And you're capturing that in these films. Arthur Jafa: I'm capturing it. I'm trying to -- like I said, I'm trying to make a thing that's like it, that is modeled on in some kind of way, so is a rich enough proxy of the actual thing, you know? Jeffrey Brown: You have said many times you don't think of yourself as a protest artist or... Arthur Jafa: I'm definitely not. Jeffrey Brown: Yes. So it's not a political artist. This isn't -- it's not... Arthur Jafa: It's not, not political either. If you make a rendering of a Black anything, Black child, Black grandmother, it's going to be inherently political just because this is an anti-Black environment, but it doesn't mean that's necessarily what your motivations are. It's like we exist, we continue to exist, we have a very complex relationship with our continued existence, and we recognize that other people have a complex relationship with our continued existence. So they say you make art about what you know, and this is what we know, so I'm trying to make art about what I know. Jeffrey Brown: Arthur Jafa's exhibition I Am Tony continues through January 3. For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Jeffrey Brown at the New Museum in New York.

f6ad6a10269a.text: Film critic Ann Hornaday has died. As chief film critic for The Washington Post, she was a respected and passionate voice in the world of cinema. She was also a longtime regular on the News Hour, sharing her love of film with our viewers. Senior arts correspondent Jeffrey Brown has our remembrance. Geoff Bennett: Some sad news now for all of us here at the "PBS News Hour." Film critic Ann Hornaday has died. As chief film critic for The Washington Post, she was a respected and passionate voice in the world of cinema. She was also a longtime regular on this program, sharing her love of film with our viewers. Senior arts correspondent Jeffrey Brown is back now with a remembrance. Ann Hornaday, Film Critic, The Washington Post: I mean, this has been such a great year for first-time filmmakers. Jeffrey Brown: Sometimes, it was the excitement of a creative new voice. Ann Hornaday: And one of them is this woman named Celine Song. Jeffrey Brown: Sometimes the thrill of watching how a director makes decisions. Ann Hornaday: It's just a superb exercise in restraint on almost every level, written and directed by Tom McCarthy, who's just a fantastic filmmaker, and just his choices throughout this film are at spot on in terms of never really putting too much spin on the ball. Jeffrey Brown: Often, it was the sheer joy of movies. Ann Hornaday: Listen, I will tell you something. My number one movie of the year was "Top Gun: Maverick." And I was utterly disarmed almost immediately. Those elbows that had been sharply out collapsed. And it was just so much fun to see it, and the audience was having such a good time. Jeffrey Brown: Ann Hornaday was one of the nation's leading film critics, a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize for Criticism in 2008. She also regularly shared her views with us on the "News Hour." Marty Baron, then-executive editor at The Post, characterized her work this way: Marty Baron, Former Executive Editor, The Washington Post: She writes with great intellect. She always writes with great heart. Jeffrey Brown: And she loved sharing her passion with young people. She met Benjamin Price when he was just six and encouraged his love of movies. Today, he studies film in college and is interning with a studio. Ann Hornaday: And so what I have done with the book, I hope, is to guide readers through my process in evaluating a movie as a professional critic. Jeffrey Brown: The way you think about it as a critic. Ann Hornaday: Exactly. Jeffrey Brown: Hornaday's 2017 book, "Talking Pictures," offered stories and tips for the rest of us on how to watch and talk about movies. Ann Hornaday: Well, I have actually learned to watch movies sort of on the job, and in many cases that means through my interviews with filmmakers like writers and directors and actors and different craftspeople, and they have really taught me a great deal about this medium and how to appreciate it. Actor: Woodward, Bernstein, you're both on the story now. Jeffrey Brown: She was at work on a book about one of her favorite films, "All the President's Men." But after leaving The Post last year, she was diagnosed with glioblastoma. She died today. Ann Hornaday was 66 years old. For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Jeffrey Brown. Geoff Bennett: And our thoughts go out to Ann's family and friends.

8a4e88f98f5c.text: By — Ellen Schmidt, Associated Press Ellen Schmidt, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/minnesota-teen-accused-of-plotting-terror-attack-at-mall-of-america-to-remain-jailed Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Minnesota teen accused of plotting terror attack at Mall of America to remain jailed Nation Oct 19, 2026 6:18 PM EDT MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — An 18-year-old from Minnesota who prosecutors say planned a terror attack at the Mall of America and who was arrested after buying an AK-47 from an undercover FBI employee must remain in custody, a federal judge ruled Monday. Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud, an American-born U.S. citizen of Somali descent, won't be released because he's a risk to the community and a flight risk, U.S. Magistrate Judge Dulce Foster said. Mohamud had been on the FBI's radar since December 2024, when he began trading messages with a confidential informant. He was arrested Oct. 6 after meeting with an FBI employee posing as a member of the Islamic State group and paying $600 for the rifle, 200 rounds of ammunition and four 30-round magazines, authorities said. "This was as close to committing a terrorist attack as he could have gotten," Assistant U.S. Attorney Benjamin Bejar said during the hearing. "He was 100% committed to doing this crime and he was 100% committed to doing it on behalf of ISIS." Mohamud's attorney, Manny Atwal, said during Monday's hearing that he was just 16 when the confidential informant began speaking to him, and that his only access to weapons was through those supplied by the FBI. She had asked that he be held in a halfway house where he would be monitored by GPS and have no access to the internet. Mohamud was arrested at a public park in Richfield, the Minneapolis suburb where he lived, several miles northwest of the mall. Authorities said Mohamud said he planned to attack the mall on Oct. 24, when there was a scheduled arts celebration by the Hmong community, Minnesota's largest Asian ethnic group. "He wanted to harm as many people as possible," FBI Special Agent Keegan Rupenthal testified at Monday's hearing. The teen's "ultimate goal was to become a martyr," and during his arrest he pledged allegiance to the Islamic State group's leader, Rupenthal said. Mohamud initially expressed interest in messages about traveling to Somalia to fight for al-Shabab militants, according to Rupenthal's affidavit in support of the criminal complaint. But Mohamud, who expressed admiration for terror attacks that had happened in the U.S., eventually said he didn't have enough money to travel overseas and decided to carry out an attack in Minnesota, according to the affidavit. Rupenthal said during the hearing that on multiple occasions, the confidential informant told Mohamud that the attack was a serious thing, and that he could back out. "He said that he was 100% committed to doing it and that he wasn't being pressured," Rupenthal testified. The FBI has foiled several alleged attacks through sting operations in which agents posed as terror supporters, supplying advice or equipment. Critics say the strategy can amount to entrapment. In May 2025, FBI agents were concerned enough that they went to Mohamud's home. His mother told them he wasn't home from school yet and called the boy's father, who declined to speak with them and said he would give their contact information to his lawyer, the complaint said. Tens of thousands of people of Somali descent live in Minnesota, dating back to when refugees began arriving in the 1990s. Over the years several have been charged with attempting to join militant groups. Schmidt is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues. Associated Press reporter Jamie Stengle in Dallas contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Donate now By — Ellen Schmidt, Associated Press Ellen Schmidt, Associated Press

e09a3c98e14f.text: Social media lets us share our lives with family, friends, and strangers. But how do people decide what to post, what to leave out, and what do those decisions say about them? On "Settle In," Geoff Bennett discusses that with Kathryn Jezer-Morton, author of "The Story of Your Life," a new book about how the incentives of social media platforms have narrowed the kinds of stories we tell. Geoff Bennett: Social media has become the main way we share our lives with family, friends, and strangers alike. In this week's episode of "Settle In," I spoke with Kathryn Jezer-Morton, author of the new book "The Story of Your Life" about how the incentives of social media platforms have narrowed the kinds of stories we tell and shapes how we see ourselves. You write about what you call the redemption narrative, the pressure to turn whatever difficulty one is going through into this story of personal growth or triumph. Why are we so drawn to that? Kathryn Jezer-Morton, Author, "The Story of Your Life: How Social Media Shapes the Way We Experience Everything": You know, I think that's something that is really at the core of American identity. I mean, I think that the project of the United States was sort of built on this idea of starting something in a new place and overcoming the odds in order to make it work. And I think that's the story of capitalism. It's the story of economic progress as we know it today. So, to me, this is just an extension of that. But it's just not the only story. And I do think it makes sense to tell a story about redemption when you're talking about a business, when you're talking about an enterprise. I think it makes less sense to lean on that narrative when you're talking about a family or an individual, just because a family's life is always going to have ups and downs. Geoff Bennett: There's something almost radical these days about saying, yes, this experience was difficult, and it didn't necessarily make me a better person. (LAUGHTER) Geoff Bennett: It was just something I had to go through. Kathryn Jezer-Morton: Yes, right. That's right. That's -- to kind of just let it land on that kind of unresolved note is really dissonant, I think, to the contemporary ear. People want to hear a resolution. They want to hear the takeaways, what I learned from. And this is really, I think, a product of this narrative orientation that we have towards redemption. Make it better. Learn something from your troubles. And I just don't believe that that's always the path that we take. And the people that I spoke to in this book really reinforced that idea for me that it's not always just better and better and better. Geoff Bennett: Well, say more about the people with whom you spoke for the book and how you determined who you would speak with and what stories you would include. Kathryn Jezer-Morton: Yes, I mean, it really just started leaving my bubble, trying to find strangers. I joined like Meetup.com groups, just any place where I could go where I would be able to talk to strangers without making people uncomfortable. I went on Facebook and community groups, and I asked if I could talk to people. I really just kind of tried everything. And I just spoke to a lot of different kinds of people, mostly millennials, I would say. And I heard a lot of stories. Basically, if someone told me a story that really stuck in my head, I would be like, I'm going to build a chapter around this, and then I would find other stories, and I would just kind of put them together. But I kind of let the data lead the way, and I was just looking for people to surprise me. And it was not hard to find people to surprise me, I have to say. It was a lot easier than I thought it was going to be. Geoff Bennett: One of the real paradoxes you identify in your book is that social media promises individuality and self-expression, but actually produces an enormous amount of conformity. What did you find when you were sort of researching and stitching together that part of your book? Kathryn Jezer-Morton: Yes, I call it like a small-C conservatism. People want to replicate ways of being that they have already seen, which is a fundamentally conservative orientation. Like, I want it to be the traditional way. And I think a lot of that is just because people -- not everyone is like a natural-born storyteller with a huge creative well of ideas, and they just figure, hey, that looked cool, I'm going to do it that way. So, I mean, that's just a basic human orientation. But I also just think that we -- this is now our version of success. When we see someone taking a cool-looking vacation, we're like, that's what success is. I want to do that. If I'm able to do that, I will have succeeded. And so, yes, it does sort of funnel us into these ways of telling our story that are really, really similar to each other. Geoff Bennett: And you can watch all episodes of "Settle In" on our YouTube page or wherever you get your podcasts.

b2abafddbfba.text: By — Sophie Bates, Associated Press Sophie Bates, Associated Press By — Jack Brook, Associated Press Jack Brook, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/mississippi-attorney-general-says-officers-force-was-justified-in-death-of-1-year-old-kohen-wiley Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Mississippi attorney general says officer's force was justified in death of 1-year-old Kohen Wiley Nation Oct 19, 2026 6:10 PM EDT JACKSON, Miss. (AP) — Mississippi's attorney general says a Senatobia officer was justified in using force when he responded to a shoplifting call and fired at a moving vehicle that investigators said was driving toward police, killing a 1-year-old boy who was inside the car. The conclusion of the state's investigation into the shooting death of Kohen Wiley follows months of mourning and calls for justice, both nationally and in the small town where the shooting took place, about 40 miles (65 kilometers) south of Memphis, Tennessee. The shooting occurred in mid-June as Senatobia officers responded to a shoplifting call at a Walmart, where they saw Vellesiya Wiley, Kohen's mother, carrying her son as she and a friend left the store, got into a car and began driving away. Wiley and her friend are both Black. Police believed they stole diapers and baby clothes. Kohen's mother has denied she or her friend stole anything, and neither of them have been charged with shoplifting or any other counts, according to online state and county court records. According to a statement released shortly after the shooting by the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation, officers attempted to stop the vehicle, but the car drove toward law enforcement, prompting an officer to fire into the car, striking Kohen and his mother's friend. Martin Zummach, an attorney who represents the officer who fired the shot that killed Kohen, says the attorney general's findings cleared his client of criminal wrongdoing. He said the driver of the vehicle "tried to kill" his client and other officers who were present. "He had no choice but to fire his weapon," Zummach told The Associated Press. In a video released days after the shooting, Vellesiya Wiley disputed that her friend, who was driving, headed toward the officers. Lawyer calls for release of body-worn camera footage Ben Crump, a nationally renowned civil rights attorney who is representing Kohen's family, has said results of a preliminary independent autopsy indicate Kohen was shot from the side of the car, not the front, contradicting officers' claims that the car was heading toward them. Crump on Monday pointed out that authorities have yet to release video footage of the encounter to support the attorney general's finding that the shooting was a justified use of force. "How can anyone accept that conclusion when Kohen's family and the public still have not been allowed to see the body-camera footage?" Crump said in a statement. "If the footage supports the state's decision, release it. We will not stop fighting until this family gets the truth." A photo of the car after the shooting shows that the passenger window was shattered and an apparent bullet hole pierced the windshield on the passenger side. The other woman in the car was badly wounded, authorities said. John P. Gross, an expert on police use of force on moving vehicles, said that if the vehicle had been moving toward officers, the best practice would have been for them to get out of the way. "This shooting was almost certainly unjustified," Gross told the AP. "In terms of both officer safety, the safety of the occupants of the vehicle and general public safety, you don't shoot vehicles." Charles "Joe" Key, a firearms and ballistics expert and former Baltimore police lieutenant who typically testifies in defense of police, said the image of the vehicle after the shooting suggests that the officer fired from the side. "That indicates that the officer who did the shooting was not personally at risk at the time he shot," Key said. "The only way it would have been justified is if officers had been in the path of a car driving directly at them." "The body-worn camera's going to have to tell if anybody was in danger," he added. Marquell Bridges, an activist who has been working with Kohen Wiley's family, called for the release of video footage of the shooting in a statement. "His family deserves the truth. The public deserves transparency," Bridges said. "We will not be silent. We will not look away. And we will not allow the life of a Black child to be treated as though it means nothing." Child's death stokes simmering tensions The shooting is the latest in a string of incidents that has eroded trust between the Senatobia police department and the city's Black residents. Last year, a Senatobia officer threatened a Black woman with a Taser, pulling her from her car and onto the ground and arresting her during a confrontation over an accessible parking space in the same Walmart lot where Kohen was shot. Two years earlier, a Senatobia police officer was fired for arresting a Black 10-year-old for urinating in public. More recently, former Senatobia Police Chief Harold Vanderford was fired by the city's board of aldermen, after reporting by The New York Times, Mississippi Today and Verite News alleged he used racist slurs in private text messages. Brook reported from New Orleans. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. cc44a04292e4.text: By — Teresa Medrano, Associated Press Teresa Medrano, Associated Press By — Suman Naishadham, Associated Press Suman Naishadham, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/from-france-to-albania-how-social-unrest-is-fueling-protests-across-europe Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter From France to Albania, how social unrest is fueling protests across Europe World Oct 19, 2026 6:00 PM EDT MADRID (AP) — Rising fuel costs, discontent with the state of schools, declining public services and a housing crisis have created perfectly stormy weather for an autumn of protests in Europe. Crowds have taken to the streets for weeks in major cities, resulting in arrests, looting, injuries, and violence across France, Italy and Albania. In Spain and Portugal, tent camps have sprung up in protests against unattainable rents and housing costs. Young Europeans are experiencing "a strong sense of uncertainty and a lack of control," said María Silvestre, professor of sociology at the University of Deusto in Spain. "And when specific situations come together, a spark suddenly ignites that is capable of channeling that discontent and driving people into the streets." Cities have turned into battlefields as top EU economies, including France, Italy and Spain, approach pivotal elections, while far-right parties have made electoral gains in Germany and could do so elsewhere. It also comes as Europe faces a critical moment in its support for Ukraine, with President Donald Trump making overtures to President Vladimir Putin even as Russia is blamed for increasingly frequent hybrid attacks in NATO countries. Right-wing politicians have seized on the chaos. While protests in France have appeared broad-based, Trump portrayed immigrants as responsible for the destruction, writing on his Truth Social platform: "The migrants have taken over France. They must CLOSE THE BORDERS, FAST!" on Monday. Watch the clip in the player above. Many of the protests have been fueled by frustrated young people. Other elements including black-clad, masked agitators have fomented violence, but French authorities and police have not blamed immigrants. Here's a look at what's driving the unrest: Students say education resources are dwindling In France, which has a centuries-old tradition of popular protest, high schoolers have staged blockades and demonstrations for more than three weeks, demanding more resources for schools they call understaffed and dilapidated, especially in lower-income neighborhoods. The protests then broadened as France's CGT labor union and other activists joined in while students paused for a fall break. The movement now includes demands over rising living costs and public services. Despite hundreds of thousands of people marching peacefully, the weekend's unrest led to 2,400 arrests and serious disturbances in parts of France, including looting in Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Bordeaux. In Limoges, flames engulfed the 19th-century City Hall and nearly destroyed the building. Some schools were set on fire. As students and rioters threw firebombs and law enforcement responded with tear gas, hundreds have been injured. French President Emmanuel Macron condemned Saturday's violence, accusing far-left activists of trying to foment chaos by attacking buildings and police. "Those who looted will have to pay for the damage, and those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable," Macron said Sunday in a rare televised address. In Spain, elementary and secondary schoolteachers began an indefinite strike in Madrid last week to demand better pay and working conditions. Discontented teachers staged similar walkouts elsewhere in Spain this year. Unaffordable housing stymies young people A man sets up a roof cover at a makeshift camp set up by protesters demanding stronger laws to protect renters in Puerta del Sol square in Madrid, Spain, on Friday. Photo by Bernat Armangue/AP In Madrid's central Puerta del Sol, tarpaulin tents have blanketed the square for weeks to protest rising housing costs, sparked by the eviction of Maricarmen, an 87-year-old woman who later died while hospitalized. Smaller protest camps followed in other Spanish cities. The public pressure led the ruling Socialist government to approve affordable housing measures, but they lacked support in Parliament, triggering a snap election announced by Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez for November. A general strike also was called for November — the first in 14 years. Similar housing protests have sprung up in Portugal's largest cities, Lisbon and Porto, and in Barcelona, a focal point of Spain's overtourism and housing challenges. Spain's minimum wage is 1,221 euros ($1,370), while the average monthly rent for an 80-square-meter apartment is around 1,130 euros (about $1,270), according to an analysis by the business newspaper Expansión. "Most of my paycheck goes to the rent. My roommate struggles to make ends meet just like I do," said Diana Manzanares, a 20-year-old waitress at the Madrid encampment. "This is my reality and the reality of most of us living in this city." Untenable living costs as inflation rises in Italy Police confront "Italia in Piazza" protesters in Milan, Italy, on Saturday. Photo by Stefano Porta/LaPresse via AP "Italia in Piazza," or Italy in the Streets, has galvanized thousands of demonstrators, voicing demands for better employment, healthcare, education, and access to housing, as well as higher wages. Inflation in Italy rose to 4.2% in September, surpassing the eurozone's 3.8%, according to government data. Regulators in Texas did not stop processing permits for data center projects when Gov. Greg Abbott ordered a pause last month, according to an analysis of public records released Monday by the oil and gas watchdog group FracTracker.
Amid an upswell of public opposition to the booming buildout of digital infrastructure in Texas, Abbott directed the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality in a Sept. 21 letter “to halt all permits sought by data centers.”
But FracTracker, in collaboration with Public Citizen, identified 35 permitting actions taken by the TCEQ for data center projects in subsequent weeks.
“TCEQ has continued reviewing applications and issuing approvals that allow data center development to proceed,” the groups said in a press release Monday. “These actions do not signal an agency trying to pause.”
Abbott’s office and the TCEQ did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Abbott has described his moratorium on data center projects as an opportunity for state agencies to evaluate the facilities’ impact on water resources and grid stability.
“No other state agency shall move forward with regulatory approvals related to data centers until this information is acquired,” Abbott wrote in his Sept. 21 letter to TCEQ executive director Kelly Keel.
Since that letter, the TCEQ has fast-tracked or assigned engineers to 14 permits, approved stormwater coverage for 11, certified emissions estimates for seven and issued public notice for three, according to permitting documents collected by FracTracker and Public Citizen.
The permits regard construction of gas power generation facilities for energy-hungry facilities. All of the largest gas power projects currently proposed in Texas are specifically intended to serve data centers, which are primarily planned to run artificial intelligence.
The projects would release tens of thousands of tons of regulated pollutants, according to permitting documents, as well as more than 100 million tons per year of greenhouse gases—an enormous amount roughly equal to the annual emissions of a mid-sized industrialized country.
The day after Abbott’s pause on data center permits, on Sept. 22, FracTracker and Public Citizen found that TCEQ mailed notices of preliminary approval to three major projects: NRG Prairie Energy Center, VoltaGrid’s ABI-1 power plant and Nexus’s self-powered data center in Hubbard.
The agency opened public comment periods on two of those projects in following days.
FracTracker and Public Citizen found approvals of stormwater management permits for data center construction issued after Sept. 21, including for Caldwell Valley Technology Park in Caldwell County, Crusoe’s Abilene campus and EdgeConneX’s Cedar Creek campus.
The report identified numerous other projects that continue to advance through permitting. For example, records show the TCEQ received a permit application for generators at Edged Energy in Dallas on Oct. 6, and an engineer completed an initial review on Oct. 9.  
“Our research uncovered glaring inconsistencies between regulatory actions and Governor Abbott’s directives,” said Sam Law, manager of communications at FracTracker Alliance and author of the report. “We need an actual pause to study the threats posed to the land, water and livelihoods of Texans.”

In papers filed with the high court, Khalil asked it to overturn a ruling earlier this year by the 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Philadelphia that found federal courts do not have jurisdiction to review the legality of the detentions until immigration courts had fully considered each case. Khalil, a lawful permanent U.S. resident, was detained by immigration authorities last year because of his participation in pro-Palestinian demonstrations at Columbia University in the spring of 2024. The U.S. government argued at the time that Khalil's presence in the U.S. was harmful to the country's foreign policy interests. As a result, the former Columbia graduate student spent over three months in detention before a federal judge in New Jersey ordered him freed after finding that the federal government had acted unconstitutionally. The Trump Administration acted well within its statutory and constitutional authority with respect to Khalil, as it does with any alien who advocates for violence, glorifies and supports terrorists, harasses Jews, and damages property. We would encourage him to use the CBP Home app and self-deport." The 3rd Circuit has put its ruling on hold so that Khalil could appeal to the Supreme Court. He remains free. Although the Supreme Court typically agrees to grant only a small percentage of appeals requests, the U.S. government has already asked the high court to overturn a federal appeals court decision that upheld a judge's decision to release Georgetown University scholar Badar Khan Suri. That ruling by the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Richmond, Virginia, directly conflicted with the 3rd Circuit decision in the Khalil case. Sometimes, conflicting appeals court rulings can increase the chances that the Supreme Court agrees to hear a case.
