When Israel's far-right National Security Minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, reached voting age, he was rejected from Israel's army for being too politically extreme.
His views have not changed much in the 30 years since then - but Israel has. Once shunned by the political establishment, he is now part of the government's inner sanctum of ministers.
On the campaign trail ahead of Israel's general elections next week, Ben Gvir is often surrounded by a jubilant pack of fresh-faced young fans, waving huge party flags over the heads of his numerous security guards.
At the covered market in Ramle - a mixed city of Jewish and Arab Israelis - he told us his message to young voters was to get out and vote.
"We see the support, we see the love [and] we want to win!" he said.
More than half a million first-time voters will cast their ballots in this election, which many Israelis see as existential for Israel's future security and identity.
Polls suggest it will be a tight race, and the new young voters could help decide the result.
More than 16% are planning to support far-right parties - either Ben Gvir's Jewish Power or the Religious Zionism party of his far-right ally Bezalel Smotrich - according to a poll for one of Israel's most popular newspapers, Yedioth Ahronoth.
And almost three-quarters see themselves as "right or centre-right", according to another survey for Israel's leading Channel 12 television network.
"Itamar Ben Gvir gives me a sense of security," said 20-year-old Mordechai, one of the young fans accompanying the politician to Ramle.
"Like everyone in history, from Trump to Moses, there are slips of the tongue that are a bit less good. So what? 90% of the things by Itamar are amazing."
"Itamar will give us safety, and when we go to the army, someone will have our backs and be behind us," said 18-year-old Nadav.
"I think he's trying to show that we're a strong country. For many years, we couldn't show we're strong in our beliefs. We couldn't express our ideology."
Meir Schreiber, an ultra-Orthodox 23-year-old who grew up in London, said the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attacks on Israel, which triggered the Gaza war, also convinced him that Ben Gvir was the right choice.
"Young people understand that peace isn't something we can do," he told me, "because what happens to you when you're young shapes your personality - we saw October 7."
Ben Gvir is a divisive candidate in a divided nation: his political positions include annexation of the occupied West Bank, Jewish settlement of Gaza, and the "voluntary emigration" of Palestinians - positions and rhetoric that are widely condemned by liberal Israelis.
Several Western countries have imposed sanctions or travel bans on Ben Gvir and Smotrich for incitement against Palestinians. Both men are powerful ministers in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's governing coalition.
As he and his entourage pushed their way between the stalls, some shopkeepers threw sweets; others, dark looks.
"I don't like him, he sows discord," one stallholder said. "Ramle is a mixed city - Jews and Arabs. There's no problem here, even after 7 October, but his message preys on young uneducated people."
The fact that he appears more popular with 18 to 22-year-olds than with their parents' generation is often put down, at least partly, to the impact of the 7 October attacks.
But political analyst Dahlia Scheindlin, who previously ran many Israeli political campaigns, said it was more than that.
"For about the last 20 years, we've seen young Israeli Jews are more right wing than average, and significantly more right-wing on many measures than the 55+ group," she told me.
"They have grown up under a series of wars with no personal experience of efforts to achieve peace. But for the most part, they have been socialised into the most extreme terms of the debate [as] legitimate to discuss: annexation, settlement expansion and - after 7 October - annexation of Gaza. And now they're voting for the first time."
A series of classroom debates filmed by Israeli satirist Lior Schleien recently highlighted the extreme views of some young Israelis.
The debates, in which he challenges racist or extreme views, drew a lot of attention in Israel, and included one exchange in which a student advocates killing all Arab citizens of Israel. That particular video has since been removed from Schleien's website.
Surveys suggest that first-time voters here are highly motivated to cast their ballots, with more than 80% saying they are likely to do so. But the same research suggests they are also more sceptical about democratic institutions and less engaged by political protests or petitions.
In a race that is largely deadlocked between two stable blocs of pro-government and anti-government supporters, getting new voters to the polling stations could make all the difference.
Opposition parties have been engaging younger voters with warnings about threats to democracy, new social media videos and younger candidates.
"In 2022 [in the last election], only 59% of the citizens living in Tel Aviv voted - in the most liberal city in the whole Middle East! In places where they voted for Ben Gvir, they voted at around 90%," said Yonatan Shalev, a 24-year-old candidate with the centre-right opposition party, Beyachad ("Together"), led by former prime minister Naftali Bennett.
He told me that Ben Gvir had understood the power of social media faster than other politicians.
"The liberal politicians didn't believe in TikTok, didn't believe in Instagram, and he took advantage of that arena."

It’s been more than three decades since Democrats held a trifecta in Pennsylvania, but the prospect of a blue wave in next month’s elections has Gov. Josh Shapiro and party leadership optimistic that their time could come in Harrisburg.
After flipping the state House of Representatives in 2022, Democrats now have a chance to take advantage of flagging support for President Donald Trump and Shapiro’s positive favorability to gain control of the state Senate for the first time since 1993. If the gridlock breaks, legislators and environmental advocates see an opportunity to advance long-stalled proposals on renewable energy, data centers and greenhouse gas reductions.
“I think of it as a tectonic shift in Pennsylvania environmental politics,” PennEnvironment executive director David Masur said about a potential trifecta. “It’s a generational shift, and it really changes the playing field with the opportunity to move toward a green majority in the legislature.”
For years, Democratic legislators have operated with an “imaginative constraint” because of their inability to move bills through both chambers, said Sen. Nikil Saval, a Democrat from Philadelphia who is a member of the environmental resources and energy committee. If they secure the trifecta, quick action is possible on several House bills that have been blocked by a Republican-controlled Senate for the past four years, addressing solar power, siting reform for energy projects and guard rails for data center development.
Given the recent price hikes ratepayers have seen in their energy bills, offering relief would likely be among Democrats’ first priorities if they control the state government. One in four Pennsylvania families are struggling to pay their energy bills, and one in 20 carries significant utility debt.
“Energy has become a kitchen-table issue,” said Elowyn Corby, senior regional director for the Mid-Atlantic at nonprofit Vote Solar.
In this environment, community solar is the type of “low-hanging fruit” that should quickly move through the legislature, Saval said. Legislation that passed the House with support from more than a dozen Republicans would allow Pennsylvanians to subscribe to a local array and cut costs on their electricity bills. Several neighboring states have already opened the door to the practice.
Similarly, Democrats and advocates point to battery storage as a sensible solution with a clear path to law. Earlier this month the House passed a bill with bipartisan support that would require electric utilities to store energy for use during peak periods to lower overall costs and improve reliability. A proposal to make warehouses solar-ready has also sat in the Senate after clearing the House and could complement other actions on energy policy.
Rep. Elizabeth Fiedler, a Democrat from Philadelphia and chair of the House energy committee and co-sponsor of the battery storage bill, highlighted another idea to lower ratepayers’ bills: her proposal to rein in utilities’ profits by ensuring that their rates of return equal their demonstrated capital costs. That bill passed the House unanimously in June and has been stuck in the Senate since.
“Regardless of the election’s outcome, I believe our mission remains to do everything we can on the energy committee to lower peoples’ utility bills, generate more energy to meet demand, and hold big corporations accountable,” Fiedler said in a statement.
In the interest of energy generation, Rep. Mandy Steele, a Democrat from Allegheny County, has proposed a bill that would prevent municipalities from passing blanket prohibitions against renewable energy projects. This bill could be a “starting point,” Saval said. Pennsylvania is among a small number of states that lack a statewide energy siting policy, making it a target for reform.
“It would lower our energy bills in noticeable ways,” said Alex Bomstein, executive director of nonprofit Clean Air Council. “It would make our air cleaner. It would be a huge deal.”
Democrats could also approach renewable energy by updating the Alternative Energy Portfolio Standard, which sets requirements for the portion of the energy grid composed of renewable energy. Pennsylvania ranks 47th nationally in renewable energy growth, in large part because the standard has “flatlined,” allowing utilities to maintain the status quo, Masur said.
Of course, skyrocketing utility bills are inextricable from the proliferation of power-hungry data centers. There are already 70 in the state, and 93 more projects are proposed, according to the Data Center Tracker, heaping unprecedented demand on a grid already forecast by the Public Utility Commission to face 13 annual outages by 2030. Legislators and advocates said a House-approved proposal to regulate data centers and limit their impact on electricity bills could pass in a Democratic trifecta.
The environmental concerns around data centers go well beyond electricity. Rep. Danielle Friel Otten, Democrat from Chester County, said the Pennsylvania Water Resource Act, which she introduced in May, would be an important companion to any legislation, imposing a fee on users withdrawing more than 10,000 gallons per day.
“There’s an opportunity there to hold these large water users accountable and make it more expensive to do consumptive use in Pennsylvania,” she said.
Data centers are a key issue for Pennsylvania voters. Nearly three-quarters said they would oppose having one built in their community, according to a recent Quinnipiac poll. The stiff public opposition has given rise to calls for a moratorium on new data center construction.
“We should push pause until and unless the industry can show that their negative effects on the environment and public health and our pocketbooks can get resolved,” Masur said.

The Orionid meteor shower, which is capable of producing bright fireball meteors, is set to peak in UK skies this week.
While it has been active for most of October, the celestial spectacle will be at its best in the early hours of October 22.
Clear skies permitting, skygazers could be able to spot as many as 10-20 meteors per hour.
Where the weather is less cooperative, there will still be chances to catch a glimpse of the shower until 7 November.
Where do the Orionids come from and how can I watch them?
The Orionids are an annual meteor shower caused by debris left by Halley's comet in its journey around the Sun.
Every year, Earth passes through the comet dust and the debris burns with the friction caused by the atmosphere, creating a bright streak of light through the sky.
The Orionids are fast and bright, entering our atmosphere with speeds of around 41 miles per second. They can often produce long glowing trails and fireballs.
To spot them, find a dark spot with wide open skies, away from city light pollution and let your eyes adjust to the night sky for 20 minutes.
The meteors are visible to the naked eye so you won't need any specialist equipment like binoculars or a telescope.
The meteors will appear to originate from the constellation of Orion, near the red supergiant star Betelgeuse. This is known as the radiant.
Between midnight and dawn the constellation will climb higher in the sky to the south and then the south-west.
It is best to view the meteors slightly away from the radiant as they will be more visible.
Unfortunately, the Moon will be in the waxing gibbous phase on the night of the 21 October, throwing extra light into the night sky and reducing visibility.
However, conditions will improve once the Moon sets around 03:00 BST on Thursday morning.
What is the forecast for the peak?
Meteor showers are best seen in cloudless skies. Unfortunately for skywatchers, this week looks to be the wettest and windiest week so far this autumn with a strengthening jet stream propelling low pressure systems across the UK.
All is not lost, however.
While Wednesday is looking wet and windy for many parts of the UK, a brief ridge of high pressure could mean that there is a chance of clear spells for many parts of England, Wales and Northern Ireland for the second half of the night into Thursday morning.
There may also be some clear skies for a time for western Scotland.
Eastern Scotland looks cloudy and wet with a lingering front and the far south coast of England could also see outbreaks of rain.
Keep an eye on the latest forecast here or on the BBC Weather app.

a7e32b985bbb.text: By — Tom Nouvian, Associated Press Tom Nouvian, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/curfews-bring-calm-to-paris-as-france-cracks-down-on-weekend-rioters Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Curfews bring calm to Paris as France cracks down on weekend rioters World Oct 20, 2026 12:45 PM EDT PARIS (AP) — Paris returned to calm on Tuesday after its first quiet night since a weekend marred by France's most destructive rioting in years, as authorities imposed curfews in several cities in an effort to prevent another round of rioting and looting. At least 2,400 people were arrested after rioters in cities across France on Saturday clashed with police, set cars on fire, stormed public buildings and engulfed a historic city hall in flames, during nationwide protests against rising living costs and poor conditions in schools. READ MORE: French Prime Minister Lecornu calls for localized curfews in cities to curb rioting and looting On Sunday evening, small groups set fire to trash bins, bicycles and other objects in the streets and looted businesses in Paris, Lyon, Marseille and other cities. Please check your inbox to confirm. In the capital, a curfew ran from 11 p.m. on Monday to 6 a.m. Tuesday, and a police helicopter circled over Place de la République overnight, a central point in the weekend clashes, sweeping the square with a searchlight to check that the order was being respected. Early Tuesday morning, workers used a crane to remove a giant fluorescent yellow vest draped over the statue at the center of the square, a reference to the " yellow vest " protests over fuel prices that began in 2018 and shook the first term of President Emmanuel Macron. READ MORE: From France to Albania, how social unrest is fueling protests across Europe Workers then used pressure washers to blast graffiti off the monument. "The targeted curfews helped keep last night calm," Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu wrote on X on Tuesday, adding that new curfews would be imposed that night "wherever the situation requires," decided locally by prefects, the state's representatives in each region, together with mayors. Speaking in Lille, northern France, Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said 149 people had been jailed nationwide as of Tuesday at noon. According to the Justice Ministry, of the roughly 2,500 people arrested since Saturday, more than 800 have been sent before prosecutors, most of whom were either put on trial immediately or ordered to appear at a later hearing. READ MORE: Macron condemns those who 'sought to bring down the Republic' after rioting mars nationwide protests In Paris alone, about 300 people have been sent before prosecutors following the Oct. 17 protests, the city prosecutor's office said in a statement. Darmanin said he asked prosecutors to appeal any sentence they considered too lenient. "People with no criminal record ending up in prison for property crimes is extremely rare, if not unheard of," he said, arguing that the French justice system will be "extremely firm." In Lille, he said, three men aged 20 to 25 with no criminal record were each sentenced to 10 months in prison and imprisoned immediately for looting a video game store in the city's old town. The National Assembly, France's lower house of parliament, is launching an inquiry into the Oct. 17 violence and the authorities' policing strategy, its speaker, Yaël Braun-Pivet, said, with findings expected "by the end of the year." Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar said that they discussed ways to strengthen bilateral ties in trade, energy, technology and defense, along with talks on regional developments. Under a framework agreed upon in February, the tariff rate was reduced to 18%, but the negotiations have since stalled. Earlier this month, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said that the talks had "plateaued." Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal, however, said last week that the first tranche of a trade deal was in its final stages. India says its final tariff rate should be similar to those of competing manufacturing countries such as Vietnam. India's purchases of discounted Russian crude since the start of the war in Ukraine in February 2022 have strained ties with the United States at times. The Indian government has said that it would expand energy imports, including from the U.S., while diversifying suppliers to maintain market stability and keep prices affordable. "But they're also an important ally and partner of the United States." Rubio is scheduled to visit a refinery in the city of Jamnagar in Gujarat state on Wednesday and meet with business leaders, according to the U.S. State Department. The Jamnagar facility, operated by Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani's Reliance Industries, is the world's largest refining complex. Sudan's army has been accused of launching several drone strikes that have reportedly killed more than 300 people, including dozens travelling to a funeral.
The death toll from strikes in two areas of West Kordofan state on Sunday evening was 150, sources told the Sudan War Observatory, which tracks the conflict that erupted in 2023 between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
In Abyei, a disputed border area between Sudan and South Sudan, 153 people were killed when drones hit a market on Monday, the region's information minister said.
A military source told the BBC the army had carried out the Abyei attack, saying the market was a fuel supply site for the RSF.
The attack has raised tensions between South Sudan and Sudan, which jointly administer Abyei, as they both claim ownership to the oil-rich region in a dispute that has remained unresolved since South Sudan ceded in 2011.
South Sudan has summoned Sudan's ambassador to lodge a formal protest. There are fears the conflict could spill across the border.
Despite a partial arms embargo on Sudan, foreign countries have been supplying both the army and the RSF with drones and they are increasingly becoming the weapon of choice in the conflict.
The war has created one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world, killed hundreds of thousands of people and forced more than 14 million from their homes.
"We are alarmed by the continued deadly drone strikes across the country that are killing civilians, including children, and that are disrupting essential services," UN spokesperson StÃ©phane Dujarric said on Monday, external.
The rising use of armed drones came as 20 million people faced acute hunger, with a rising risk of famine in parts of the western region of Darfur and Greater Kordofan, he said.
Greater Kordofan comprises three states and is a vital axis linking Darfur, controlled by the RSF, to the capital, Khartoum, now in army hands.
The wave of drone attacks started on Sunday evening and, according to the Sudan War Observatory, it is likely they were launched from the army-held city of Kadugli in South Kordofan state.
A truck carrying around 200 mourners which had travelled from an area north of Abyei was hit as it arrived in the town of Al-Dabab in West Kordofan, the monitoring group said.
Sources told the group that 145 people were killed and a tent where mourners at the funeral had gathered was also hit, killing five others. A further 150 people were injured in the attacks, it said.
Army drones also bombed a market in the town of Al-Mujlad in West Kordofan on the same evening, according to the Sudan War Observatory, which said the exact number of deaths and injuries were not yet known.
Sudan's army has not responded to the allegation it carried out these strikes, but said it did not attack civilians even if they believed there were RSF fighters amongst them.
The attack in Abyei, which borders West Kordofan, took place on Monday around 11:30 local time (09:30 GMT) targeting Amiet Market around 10km (six miles) from Abyei town, the region's Information Minister Yohana Akol Ngor told Radio Tamazuj, which broadcasts from the Netherlands to audiences on the Sudan-South Sudan border.
On Tuesday, the minister confirmed to the Associated Press and Reuters that the death toll had risen from 73 to 153 people.
"It is a horrible and shocking situation," AP quotes him as saying.
BBC Verify has studied satellite images that show extensive burnt buildings in the north-east corner of Amiet Market, which is also known in Arabic as Al-Na'am Market. Older images from the area show it is usually full of trucks.
It has also verified footage filmed near the market that shows a large plume of smoke, at least one petrol tanker and someone talking about five missiles being fired. Another verified video shows two massive, separate fires coming from buildings near that section of the market.
Earlier, Ngor told Reuters that emergency workers had struggled to retrieve the bodies because of fires caused by the strikes.
On Monday, medical charity MÃ©decins Sans FrontiÃ¨res (MSF) said it had also received people wounded in the attack at Ameth Bek Hospital in Abyei town.
"So far we received over 20 patients, including several critical cases. Patients with burns were also admitted. We are providing surgical services and wound dressing, along with other emergency care," MSF's Christian Lindauer, the charity's manager at the hospital, said in a statement.
Meanwhile, a drone strike near the airport in Khartoum on Monday has killed four people, including three children, the AFP news agency reports, quoting a medical source.
It also cited a military source as saying air defences in the Sudanese capital had downed several other drones launched by the RSF towards the airport.
Fighting in Kordofan, a strategic area rich in gold and oil, has intensified over the last year after the army regained control of Khartoum from the RSF.

The world’s development banks continue to finance expansions of large climate-polluting livestock operations, but environmental advocates are notching a victory after they say the World Bank’s private lending arm has withdrawn funding for a controversial feed mill in Brazil.
A coalition of environmental groups said the International Finance Corp. will not go forward with a $20 million loan to Brazil’s Grupo Agronorte after activists and the Indigenous Apinajé community called for the IFC to halt the funding.
In May more than 100 advocacy and Indigenous groups, organized by the Stop Financing Factory Farming coalition, wrote to the IFC—the world’s largest development finance institution focusing on private sector investments in lower-income countries. The groups asked it to cancel the loan, which the IFC announced in March.
The IFC did not respond to questions from Inside Climate News, but it has removed the Agronorte loan from its disclosure portal.
The Agronorte operation, which mills soy for livestock feed, is more than 1,000 miles south from the Apinajé territory, but the groups argue that it would ramp up pressure for soy production in their region.
Soybean plantations have spread across the Amazon and neighboring Cerrado, now the most productive soy-growing regions of the world, largely to feed growing global demand for livestock feed. Much of that expansion has occurred on illegally deforested swaths of the Amazonian rainforest, the most climatically critical landscape on Earth, and has increasingly crossed into the Cerrado, a grasslands region that researchers say is among the most at-risk ecosystems on the planet.
The groups note in their letter that the founder and majority owner of Agronorte, Gilmar Gonçalves Carvalho, is facing a federal lawsuit in Brazil, accusing him and his associates of illegally cutting down nearly 5,000 acres of rainforest bordering Indigenous lands.
“For many years, we have been fighting against Agronorte’s owner,” said an Apinajé chief in a written statement provided by the Stop Financing Factory Farming coalition, withholding their name because of security concerns. Environmental defenders are among the most targeted activists in the world, including in Brazil.
“The area he claims, which overlaps with our territory, is now completely deforested,” the chief added. “We were deeply concerned that, if he obtained this funding, he would continue to deforest the area around our territory without consulting us. That is why it was so important for the IFC to stop this project.”
The groups pointed out in their letter that the IFC has acknowledged Agronorte has no systems in place to ensure the soybeans it processes aren’t grown on illegally deforested land. “Funding a company involved in land conflicts and accused of illegal deforestation is not aligned with IFC policies, nor with the objectives of the Paris Agreement or the Global Framework for Biodiversity,” the groups wrote, adding that large-scale, monocultural grain farming does little to contribute to the bank’s mission of eradicating hunger, given that most of what Agronorte produces would be animal feed for export.
The World Bank and other multilateral development banks have long maintained that funding large-scale agriculture projects, including livestock, adheres to their missions of boosting economic conditions in developing regions. In 2018, three years after countries signed the Paris climate agreement, these banks agreed to align their funding to meet the goals of the historic accord.
But watchdog groups and researchers have found that the banks continue to fund livestock operations, despite the greenhouse gas impacts.
The production of livestock globally accounts for somewhere between 16.5 percent and just under 20 percent of total greenhouse gas emissions. Researchers have determined that, even if the world stopped using fossil fuels, the largest source of heat-trapping gases, it would be impossible to control global warming without reducing emissions from the food system, largely from cattle.
Livestock accounts for one-third of man-made methane globally, roughly the same as the oil, coal and natural gas industries combined. Methane, though short-lived, has roughly 80 times the climate warming potential over a 20-year period of carbon dioxide, the most prevalent greenhouse gas.
Yet, the World Bank Group, which includes the IFC, poured about $1.4 billion into livestock production in developing countries between 2023 and 2024. The IFC approved 38 industrial livestock investments worth nearly $2 billion between 2020 and 2025, according to a recent Stop Financing Factory Farming analysis.
Another of the group’s analyses found that, in 2024, development institutions significantly cut their investments in animal agriculture, but that spending on large-scale livestock facilities and related supply chains still outstripped investments in smaller-scale operations 5 to 1.

A South African woman has been killed in a shark attack off the country's east coast, in what is the first recorded such fatality this year.
Janine Lochrenberg was swimming off a beach in KuGompo City (formerly East London) on Tuesday morning when she was attacked.
Witnesses said the 65-year-old was bitten in two places and died before she was brought to shore.
Shark attacks are rare in South Africa, with about 10 fatal ones since 2012, according to the Florida Museum's International Shark Attack File.
Lochrenberg was out on a daily morning swim with her local open water swimming club when she was attacked at around 08:00 (06:00 GMT). Fellow swimmers brought her to shore, but it's believed she died before they could get her out of the water.
She was bitten on her thigh and her upper arm, one of her fellow swimmers told the BBC. They also said she had been wearing a magnetic shark repellent band on her ankle at the time.
Lochrenberg's sister Margot said she was holding her sister's head as they brought her to shore but believed she bled out in the water.
She told the BBC that her sister had "loved the water so much" despite knowing there was an "elevated shark presence in East London".
"She'd made peace with that. She had a deep affinity with the water and was a remarkable person," she said.
Barbara Briceland, Lochrenberg's partner, told the BBC the retired medical physicist was a good swimmer, who often swam far out into the breakers, and described her as very brave.
"She was highly intelligent, lots of fun, kind, in a quietish way, thoughtful, well-loved with a love of life."
Briceland added they were looking forward to retirement and were about to leave for a three-week road trip together.
Orient Beach, where the attack took place, has been closed alongside another nearby beach, authorities confirmed.

7ef07c909f9c.text: The AI boom is sucking up all the capital. The Federal Reserve is raising rates to try to cool inflation. And one sector is bearing the brunt of the pain from both: housing . The big picture: The situation is lose-lose for both homebuilders and homebuyers. Builders are facing more expensive capital and bidding for scarce construction-related resources. Would-be buyers are being quoted some of the highest mortgage rates of this century. New September housing starts data out Tuesday morning puts an exclamation point on what has been a slow-moving disaster for a sector that plays an outsized role in the economic cycle and in Americans' basic living standards. By the numbers: The number of housing units started by builders fell 5.2% last month, the Census Bureau said , to 1.22 million. It's down 7.4% year over year and near post-pandemic lows. Starts of single-family homes fell 4.6% to their lowest level since March 2023. Pending home sales fell 7.3% last month, the National Association of Realtors said Tuesday morning, to the lowest since the data was tracked going back to 2001. Homebuilder sentiment fell this month to its lowest level since 2012, the National Association of Home Builders said Monday. State of play: The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate was 7.4% earlier this month, Freddie Mac said in its most recent weekly reading. The rate was briefly higher than that in 2023, but has not been consistently above that level since the fall of 2000. That has kept homebuyers on the sidelines — while a parallel rise in borrowing costs for developers has made it harder for new projects to pencil out. In effect, the bottomless demand for capital from AI hyperscalers and the U.S. government has to squeeze something, and that something has been the housing sector. Residential investment has subtracted from overall GDP for five of the last six quarters. Zoom out: Housing affordability is the crux of Americans' broader dissatisfaction with economic conditions, and all signs point to it getting worse, not better. For all the bipartisan emphasis on increasing housing supply — most prominently in the passage of a law to encourage more building earlier this year — conditions are weighted against a building boom. Housing developers are competing with data center builders for labor and materials like copper, concrete and HVAC equipment. Of note: Restrictionist immigration policy has also crimped the supply of construction workers . "Nationwide, more than one-third of builders reported immigration enforcement activity in their market areas during the past month, causing construction delays and discouraging legal workers from reporting to work," said NAHB chairman Bill Owens, an Ohio homebuilder, in the sentiment release . Between the lines: An unfortunate side effect of relying on Fed interest rate policy for macroeconomic stabilization is that interest-sensitive sectors, particularly housing, take it on the chin when the economy shows signs of overheating. It's particularly problematic now, when persistent undersupply of housing is a defining economic challenge of our age. The bottom line: The current alignment of interest rates, housing supply and construction costs isn't making anybody happy. Builders can't afford to build, buyers can't afford to buy, and even the people sitting pretty with pre-2022 mortgages can't afford to move.

033740f42391.text: As the French right-wing National Rally is seizing on fiery protests in the country for its pre-election pitch, so are President Trump and his Republican allies in the U.S. The big picture: The Trump administration has used the unrest, which began over education grievances , to bolster its messaging on immigration and the threat of "communists," a group Trump has repeatedly claimed is threatening American civilization. Driving the news: "When you see burning steeples and raging fires in France, just remember that is what the radical 'Dumocrats' want to do to America," Trump said before a Kansas rally crowd Monday. He claimed France was being "conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists and communists who hate Christianity" and "the Western civilization itself." Speaking earlier to reporters, the president claimed, without evidence, that the situation in France was about "immigration, not schools." He's repeatedly blamed immigration for the protests. The White House referred Axios to the president's Truth Social post echoing that rhetoric. Catch up quick: Localized demonstrations by high school students that began in Paris last month have broadened into a massive nationwide movement over poor school conditions and costs of living, sparking thousands of arrests and clashes between police and protesters, Axios' Bec Falconer reports. The civil unrest gave way to rioting and looting, leading French President Emmanuel Macron to condemn "unrestrained violence" by "insurrectionist elements from radical far-left groups, joined by numerous criminals," per the AP . Some 550,000 people demonstrated in France Saturday, per the interior ministry, though Reuters reported that a key union estimated 800,000. On the sidelines, "thugs" chose "violence," per a translation of the interior ministry's statement , which added that some 500 police officers and firefighters were injured. The forceful police response to student demonstrators has also been scrutinized , sparking dozens of probes into officer conduct. Zoom out: Other U.S. Republicans have followed Trump in evoking the protests, which have spread to other countries , to rally voters and condemn immigration . Vice President Vance wrote on X, " Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion," sharing a video of a historic town hall reportedly set ablaze by masked protesters, per AFP. "This is the future congressional Democrats seek for your country," Vance contended. Yes, but: Macron, per a translation of his nationwide address over the weekend protests, said the hundreds of thousands of demonstrators had " legitimate demands" and should not be conflated with violent rioters. He said those concerns included the cost of living and fuel price spikes triggered by the war in Iran. The bottom line: The spiraling violence has created global shock that Trump is harnessing as a boogeyman ahead of an uphill midterm battle. Christina Applegate thought she was living with multiple sclerosis (MS) for five years, until recently discovering she had been given a wrong diagnosis.
The actress, known for hits like Anchorman and Married With Children, said she was "not happy at all" about the news and in tears when she found out.
"You don't get misdiagnosed and then all of the sudden I'm better," Applegate said in an episode of her Messy podcast released on Tuesday. "If anything, I've gotten worse."
The two-part episode, co-hosted by Jamie Sigler, ends a recent break she took to process the information. An investigation into what is causing her debilitating symptoms - which she experiences daily - will begin next week.
"I'm back at square one where I don't know what's going on with me," she said.
In the podcast, Applegate said that "all of a sudden, a few years ago", her doctor suggested ending her infusion treatment for MS to see how her body reacted.
During the time off, her body did not respond in a way that would indicate she had MS.
Doctors then looked into her case further and concluded she in fact did not have the autoimmune disease, which can cause muscle stiffness and problems with walking and talking.
"She came into my room and said, 'Congratulations, you don't have MS,' " Applegate said, recalling the moment.
"I was, like, not happy at all," she continued. "Everybody else was so happy."
Dr Marwa Kaisey, a guest on Tuesday's episode, said MS misdiagnoses are not uncommon because symptoms are inconsistent and there is no universal testing. One in five people people who were told they had MS "didn't actually have it".
"It's not like we have something like a pregnancy test that says 'yes, you have it. No, you don't,'" Kaisey said. "It's a list of criteria."
Applegate was first diagnosed with MS in August 2021, after experiencing symptoms for a while, saying at the time: "It's been a tough road. But as we all know, the road keeps on going."
Years later, she described being in a "real depression" and said in a 2024 episode of her podcast that "I don't enjoy living. I don't enjoy it. I don't enjoy things anymore".
She had said in a New York Times interview that she could not walk without a cane and used a wheelchair during filming of the Netflix series Dead To Me.

99a6a8bf9a88.text: The manosphere stars who helped mobilize young men for Donald Trump in 2024 are losing their shine with that very audience. Why it matters: Trump and Republicans rode a wave of cultural cachet to reach young male voters. Now, the president and some of his most influential online allies are showing signs of losing their grip on that audience ahead of the 2026 midterms . Driving the news: New polling from the Democratic project Speaking With American Men suggests some of the most prominent influencers during Trump's 2024 campaign have lost their luster with young male voters, per Puck News , Joe Rogan's favorable rating among young men dropped from 11 points, while Elon Musk's popularity dropped 14 points and Tucker Carlson lost 12 points. Andrew Tate, who was arrested on sex trafficking and rape charges, had "a -30 net approval rating," per Puck. Between the lines: Economic pressures and the Iran war have become major concerns for young men heading into the midterms, Puck reported. Those issues have caused tension between Trump and the influential voices who bolstered his last campaign. State of play: Young men are turning on politicians, podcasters and influencers, many of whom may have influenced recent political outcomes. They're becoming more skeptical and turning their backs on politicians, especially Trump. The 2026 Young American Men Survey from Cygnal similarly found that among 18- to 30-year-old American men, Trump, Vance and the Republican Party all were viewed unfavorably. Trump's numbers among young voters dropped precipitously. Marquette Law School national polling shows that Trump's approval dropped from 40% in January 2025 to 19% in April 2026, before rebounding to 28% in June. The law school hasn't polled on the question since then. Yes, but: Young men aren't especially enthusiastic about Democrats, either. Former President Barack Obama, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), and NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani were the only Democrats showing upticks in favorability ratings, per Puck. Context: Several prominent manosphere personalities have been critical of Trump in his second term, particularly on the Iran war and the Epstein files release. Rogan , like many MAGA influencers, has criticized the war and the Trump administration's handling of the Epstein files. Tucker Carlson has chastised Trump over many issues, including his partnership with Israel in going to war. Vice President Vance has even admitted the White House "screwed up" on its communications about the Epstein files. Reality check: Researchers question how influential podcasters and personalities actually were in 2024. A September working paper from the NYU Center for Social Media, AI and Politics found that podcast exposure did not necessarily cause Trump's gains among young men. Researchers, who reviewed 36,659 podcast episodes from 2024 alongside two survey datasets, found podcasts explained only a small portion of the widening youth gender gap. The other side: Influencers still have enormous reach among young voters. A survey from Morning Consult published on Oct. 16 found that nearly two-thirds of Gen Z adults say they get news from creators, while 62% trust creator recommendations. Business Insider reports that one in four U.S. adults feel influencer content has affected their voting decisions. Separate Marquette polling found that 54% of adults who consumed podcasts for political news approved of Trump's job performance in June, compared with 38% of adults overall. The bottom line: The manosphere's biggest personalities still have sway, but the direction of the country isn't helping them — or Trump — with young men.

Known for their distinctive black-ringed eyes, lipstick-like mouth markings and timid, elusive nature, the vaquita is the world’s rarest marine mammal. Last year’s survey—carried out by a team of international scientists and state environmental officials—estimated just seven to 10 remain in the waters of Mexico’s Upper Gulf of California.
Yet Mexican authorities announced last week that they were rolling back 2020 protections for the globally adored porpoise. Having declined from more than 550 in 1997 to just a handful today, conservationists warn the vaquitas’ future hangs in the balance.
“We’ve reached the point where every single vaquita matters. With such a small population remaining, even losing one individual has serious consequences for the future of the species,” said Heidy Martínez, a shark scientist and science communicator who has spent years on board vaquita-monitoring vessels in the Upper Gulf.
“I really hope that years and years of effort working on protecting the vaquita are not going to get diminished because of this,” said Martínez.
New regulations, announced last Wednesday, reduce the regional area where gillnets are prohibited by almost 86 percent, from around 4,300 square miles to just 600.
Mexico previously banned the use of gillnets in the region to bolster vaquita populations and combat criminal activity. Though used legally for decades by fishermen from the town of San Felipe to catch shrimp and sharks, the vertically hanging, curtain-like fishing gear is known for snaring high levels of indiscriminate bycatch.
The gear is also the poaching tool of choice for those hunting large silvery totoaba. A similarly endemic and endangered fish with a highly valuable swim bladder that sells on the Chinese black market for between $20,000 and $80,000 per kilo, totoaba is prized for its alleged medicinal and aphrodisiac benefits.
In addition to allowing gillnets back into vast swathes of the Sea of Cortez, the “Zero Tolerance Area”—where fishing and all boat traffic were previously banned—will also open up an 1,100-foot wide vessel transit corridor.
While conservation advances have been made in banning commercial fishing between the hours of 7 p.m. and 5 a.m., and requiring local fishing boats to have satellite vessel-monitoring systems on board, the latter will not be required for a further 12 months.
“With only a handful of vaquita left, it’s absolutely shocking that the government is gutting protections rather than stepping up to help these little porpoises,” Alex Olivera, the Mexico representative at the Center for Biological Diversity, said in a press release. “It’s heartbreaking because if this isn’t reversed it will almost certainly lead to the vaquita’s tragic extinction, which could’ve been prevented.”
Beyond international conservation concerns, however, lies a story of local struggle. For residents in San Felipe, a town built on fishing, vaquita protections have often been seen as a barrier to their own economic survival.
In December 2020, this conflict came to a head when a collision between Molotov cocktail-hurling fishermen and a 150‑ton cutter operated by the ocean nonprofit Sea Shepherd resulted in the death of 56-year old local fisherman, Mario García Toledo. In the weeks that followed, trucks were scorched, a Navy patrol boat was set on fire and local police and army units were called into the region to restore order.
Mexico—pressured internationally to protect the vaquita but locally to look after the 17,000 residents of San Felipe—appears to finally have chosen a side. On Thursday, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum defended the lifting of regulations by emphasizing the need to let local people earn a living from the ocean.
Marina del Pilar Ávila, the governor of Baja California, similarly welcomed the move on social media, describing the development as “great news for the fishing community of the Upper Gulf of California.”
Counterintuitively, some local fishermen were dissatisfied with the change.
Following the government announcement, fishermen blockaded the road out of San Felipe, unhappy that the “Zero Tolerance Area”—one of the most productive shrimp areas—remained in place. With previous gillnet bans poorly enforced, they contended that the reconfiguration of fishing zones will actually restrict them further.
“The whole new agreement was very controversial,” said Valeria Towns, a National Geographic Explorer and field coordinator for Pronatura Noreste, who has spent years trying to build relations between conservationists and the community.
“Since the former agreement was never applied, for the fishers, anything new that implies real enforcement is obviously a threat to the way they’ve been doing things for years,” she said.
While the blockades were lifted over the weekend, talks about government compensation for fishermen who avoid the restricted zone will continue: “It’s the most just and fair thing to do considering the fishers, and also the most effective way to ensure that Mexico can comply and actually enforce a polygon where we know vaquitas are,” added Towns.
Indeed, among some conservationists, there is a recognition that maintaining harmony with local communities is paramount to protecting vaquitas.
“My biggest question is whether these changes will actually result in more or fewer nets in the water, because ultimately that’s what determines whether the vaquitas are safe or not,” said Martínez, noting that more stringent restrictions on an already struggling fishing community haven’t always been enough to protect the species.

It was a decisive result in a referendum that could have strained the bonds of national unity.
But preliminary results show that more than two-thirds of Alberta voters sent a clear message that they want to remain in Canada.
It's possible that once the final tally is counted, the rejection by a comfortable majority of voters to pursue separation through a binding referendum could halt Alberta's separatist sentiment in its tracks.
This would push the idea that had been discussed quietly for decades back into the political fringes.
For leaders of the Alberta separatist movement, while the result was expected given the polling, it was still disappointing after more than a year of campaigning and pushing for a vote on separation.
Asked by the BBC how he felt in one sentence after the results, separatist leader Mitch Sylvestre simply said: "Not happy".
The outcome was celebrated almost immediately by Prime Minister Mark Carney, who said in a statement that "Albertans made a clear choice".
But the movement's leaders say their battle is long from over and that the issue could dominate Alberta politics for years to come.
Jeffrey Rath, a Calgary-lawyer and one of the main spokespeople for Alberta separation, said he and others "plan to roll up our sleeves and work harder".
Keith Wilson, another separatist, told supporters in Calgary that while the vote is over, "the conversation about Alberta's future in Canada and our place in Canada and our role in Canada will continue".
Smith, who openly supported and campaigned for the unity vote, thanked voters for the result.
The Alberta premier has been criticised for taking a "dangerous" gamble that the independence push would likely face defeat while still giving her restive base what they wanted.
She lowered the petition threshold needed to get the citizen-led campaign the ballot in the first place.
By making Monday's result non-binding, she got around a court decision blocking the pro-separation petition because it failed to consult indigenous First Nations whose land would be affected if the province separated.
That gamble could test her leadership of the United Conservative Party, which she has led since 2022.
"She's lost the confidence of the (party) base," said Rath.
Albertans who voted against an independence referendum told the BBC throughout the campaign that they were motivated by a desire to keep the country united, especially as Canada grapples with tariff threats from the US, its longtime ally.
They also feared that an independent Alberta could be vulnerable to outside influence - or even annexation.
Thomas Lukaszuk, a prominent pro-unity campaigner, told a crowd of supporters on Monday night that the early results made him proud to be Albertan.
At a pro-unity results watch party in Edmonton, Lukaszuk appealled directly to separatists, saying that "some of the issues they have raised are legitimate", and that the province must do the hard work of healing the divisions laid bare by this debate.
"I don't want to see us doing another referendum like this ever again," Lukaszuk said.
Premier Smith told CBC earlier in the week that she would not hold an independence referendum if Albertans vote against it as long as she is premier.
Some of the rifts can't easily be smoothed over.
The separatist sentiment has its roots in "western alienation" which is a term that has been used for decades by some in Canada's western provinces to describe a feeling of being ignored or overlooked by the federal government in central Canada.
Alberta independence supporters - and many on the unity side - believe that Ottawa has long undermined the province's oil and gas industry, most recently through environmental policies.
That anger later deepened as some Albertans grew frustrated with the response by former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau to the Covid-19 pandemic and vaccine mandates, viewing them as yet another example of government overreach.
Carney, who was raised in Alberta, has worked with Smith to address some of these issues, signing an agreement that would see a new pipeline from Alberta built to Canada's pacific coast.
He nodded to that in his statement on Monday night, saying that his plan is to unlock Canada's "full potential as a global energy superpower with Alberta at its core".
But there are signs that there could be tension in the future between Carney and Smith, an able politician and a survivor - so far - of Alberta's rough and tumble politics.
She also put nine other questions to Albertans on Monday, most that seek to give the province more autonomy from Ottawa, including on matters like immigration.
The (very) preliminary results suggest that many might pass.
Some who voted in favour of a second binding separation referendum have said they didn't want outright independence, but some leverage over Ottawa. Smith has said these other nine questions help give her just that.
Quebec, another province with similar sovereigntist sentiments, could offer clues on where Alberta's separation movement might end up.
They held two separation referendums, in 1980 and 1995, both of which were defeated by a close margin.
Alberta independence supporters don't hide the fact that they gain inspiration from the majority French-speaking province.
They view Quebec as having successfully used the threat of separation to gain significantly more autonomy over provincial affairs.
And despite support for Quebec sovereignty being at historic lows, a newly elected provincial government has pledged to hold a third referendum on independence by 2030.
Rath made a note of that as he pondered his side's defeat.
The sovereigntist Parti Quebecois "has just formed the government of Quebec with 28% of the vote," he said.
"It's not out of the realm of possibility", he added, that Alberta separatists could do the same in the future.

31e2619f9cc7.text: The Iran war and the Ukraine- Russia conflict are creating a "multidirectional squeeze on world agriculture" that could spiral into a crisis, a new report finds. Why it matters: Wars and extreme weather are colliding to threaten global food supplies and drive up prices, especially in vulnerable economies. The report explores how the El Niño phenomenon could compound the problems of restricted supplies of key fertilizer ingredients, higher fuel costs on the farm and more. The S&P Global Institute report is an unusually holistic look at the topic. Driving the news: The analysis comes alongside new warnings about food from the International Monetary Fund. Its World Economic Outlook last week sees an overall 10% increase in fertilizer prices this year and food costs rising by 5% in 2026 and 2.4% in 2027, though it depends on the region. "Higher energy and food prices could have severe effects on poverty and food security" and threaten political stability in vulnerable economies, the IMF warned. State of play: Food producers need steady supplies of natural gas and sulfur for fertilizer, diesel for farm machinery and food transport, and open sea lanes for trade, S&P notes. "Conflict is now testing all of them at once, just as El Niño tests the harvest," states the report from the research and consulting firm. "The risk is increasing, especially for low-income countries, where food costs amount to about half of household spending," it states. Zoom out: The disruptions could affect agricultural production worldwide, from soybeans and corn in Brazil to wheat in Australia, S&P finds. The intrigue: The S&P report also warns of something that has received somewhat less attention. The diesel supply crunch doesn't just raise costs for farmers. It also works alongside pro-biofuels policies to make biodiesel production more attractive. "The knock-on effect is that, in some regions, crops for fuel become more valuable than crops for food." Zoom in: A few stats via S&P illustrate the overlapping threats. Middle Eastern prices for exported sulfur, a fertilizer ingredient, reached a record $1,000 per metric ton in July, after starting the year at a historically high $500 per metric ton. 47% of the global sulfur trade normally goes through the Strait of Hormuz. In Indonesia, industrial use of palm oil, largely for biodiesel, is expected to be roughly five times its 2015-16 level. The bottom line: A global food crisis is by no means certain. But if wars keep disrupting energy and fertilizer supplies, and weather cuts harvests in key regions, "the elements of such a crisis will be falling into place," S&P warns.

The eldest son of Kenyan cult leader Paul Mackenzie, convicted of murdering 191 people, says his younger siblings were still being forced to fast as recently as two weeks ago.
Dan Mackenzie, 27, said he reported the case to police, who rescued eight children, including his five younger siblings from their grandmother's house, and took them to a rescue centre.
"They were basically forcibly fasted because they were denying food to them for almost three days," he tells BBC's Newsday.
His father was found guilty on Monday of murdering 190 children and one adult who starved to death in Shakahola forest, near the Kenyan coast.
He had ordered members of his doomsday cult to starve themselves and their children to death so they could "meet Jesus".
Twenty-eight other cult leaders were also convicted of murder.
Dan Mackenzie, who had initially defended his father, said at first he had struggled to understand the allegations against the cult leader, but came to realise the scale of the tragedy during the court proceedings.
"When I was 12, I was forced to fast for almost a week," he says. He also remembers church members beating him for hours to make him attend a service as a child.
Now, he says he felt he had to report family members who still believe in the teachings in order to free his siblings. "I had to report my grandmother."
The cult leader's doctrine said that education was forbidden and modern medicine was "evil".
"I left school when I was seven," says Dan.
Now living in the coastal town of Malindi, Dan earns a living as a motorcycle taxi driver, supporting himself and his younger siblings.
He said some people in the town had been angry with him because of his father's crimes, but others "had accepted him because he had distanced himself from that life".
"I hope the verdict would bring some comfort to those who had lost friends and relatives," Dan tells BBC's Newsday.
On Monday, Stephen Mwiti, 48, who said he had lost all six of his children to the cult, welcomed the verdict.
"I'm a happy man, that all persons have been convicted," he told the BBC outside court.
His former wife was one of those convicted of murder alongside Mackenzie.
Delivering her eight-hour judgment in the port city of Mombasa, Justice Diana Mochache said Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece".
One of his co-accused told the court that Mackenzie had said anyone who resisted fasting must be forced to go to heaven "through kicks and blows".
Burials in the forest where the cult was based were described as "weddings", with those who died celebrated as having "wedded with Jesus", the judge said.
Mackenzie and other cult leaders also face separate cases involving terrorism, radicalisation and denying children an education.
The murder verdict is the first ruling on the most serious charges against the pastor, who was arrested in 2023 after more than 400 bodies were discovered in shallow graves in Shakahola forest, near Kenya's coast.
He is due to be sentenced on 6 November.
Additional reporting by Thomas Mukhwana

Quantum computers capable of doing a million reliable operations could bring about a new stage of quantum calculation. That “megaquop” regime — as it’s called — isn’t here yet. But scientists just took a significant step toward it.
A quantum computer built by the company Quantinuum has error rates so low that it could perform a million operations with only about five errors, researchers report in a paper posted October 19 on the company’s website and arXiv.org.
“These statistics are consistent with this being a good building block for that megaquop machine,” says quantum physicist David Hayes of Quantinuum, who is based in Broomfield, Colo. In order to reach that regime, however, such computers will need to be scaled up.
Quantinuum’s computer, known as Helios, is made of electrically charged atoms, called ions, hovering over a chip. Those ions serve as the 98 quantum bits, or qubits, of the computer. But, like all qubits, those ions are finicky. Their states are delicate and can flip unintentionally and mess up calculations, like a 0 randomly switching to a 1.
A technique called quantum error correction tackles this by combining multiple error-prone qubits into one, forming a supercharged unit called a logical qubit that is less prone to mistakes. (For those who grew up on 1990s TV, it’s a bit like how Captain Planet is born from the combined powers of the gang of Planeteers.)
Logical qubits come in different sizes, integrating a given number of physical qubits — the ions, in this case. Each time a logical qubit is scaled up, going, say, from seven physical qubits to 19, the error rate drops by a factor called lambda. A previous demonstration of error correction by Google, reported in Nature in 2024, had a lambda of about 2, meaning errors were cut in half each time the logical qubits were scaled up.
Quantinuum’s computer has a lambda of about 10. So errors dropped quickly when the researchers made larger logical qubits. A logical qubit composed of 37 physical qubits had just 5 errors in a million operations — close to what would be needed for the megaquop regime. However, that experiment involved only a single logical qubit. Reaching the megaquop regime could possibly involve around 50 to 100 logical qubits.
The large value of lambda means that achieving a desired error rate takes fewer physical qubits, says Ken Brown, a quantum engineer at Duke University and a scientific adviser for the company Logiqal who was not involved with the research. “That’s a huge savings in the overall number of qubits you would need. So that’s what’s exciting.”

Lizâs view
One rule of investing is âdonât fight the Fed.â Playing the contrarian to the Federal Reserveâs plans to stimulate or dampen the economy only ends badly.
But Big Tech is not run by rule-followers.
AI giants have been almost willfully indifferent to the rising cost of money. Rates go higher, and they borrow more. Itâs a problem for the Federal Reserve, which is trying to tamp down inflation that, as Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee told us last week, is âjumping out of its laneâ â spreading from AI-linked sectors into unrelated parts of the economy. The Fedâs main lever, at least so far, isnât working.
Mark Zuckerberg and Dario Amodei arenât giddy consumers whose spending cools when borrowing gets expensive. They see themselves as great men of history, securing super intelligence for the West and ushering in an age of intergalactic abundance. They also believe customer spending on AI has only just begun, and so the coming revenue can justify their investments. That kind of existential drive canât be discouraged by an extra 75 basis points of bond interest.
Both the AI companies and the Fed are desperate for goodwill and credibility. If mortgages cost 15% and hyperscalers are still spending like thereâs no tomorrow, people are going to be very mad at both of them.
Notable
- Speaking at the IMF annual meeting in Bangkok last week, Warsh recognized that AI investment was creating a âshockâ on prices, but reiterated his conviction that the technology would bring wealth and productivity in future.

There are more signs that Qatar is ramping up liquefied natural gas exports as prices surge and inventories dwindle ahead of the Northern Hemisphere winter. One tanker is now sailing toward Poland through the Red Sea, according to Bloomberg, and at least 20 more shipments have passed through the Strait of Hormuz to other destinations since early September. The gas could help halt the surge in consumer prices and slow the decline of Qatarâs $200 billion economy, which the IMF expects to contract by 15.6% this year.
Itâs unclear how the LNG is getting out: Qatarâs prime minister said last month that buyers had negotiated passage with Iran for the few cargoes that made it through during the first six months of the war. But Doha also seems to have adopted the âHormuz shuttleâ strategy Gulf crude exporters are using.
Tracing the journey of Al Rayyan, one of Qatarâs oldest LNG tankers, Bloomberg tracked the vessel transferring its cargo to another ship in the Gulf of Oman before returning to Ras Laffan to reload. LNG ship-to-ship transfers are more complex than oil transfers, requiring cryogenic hoses to handle gas chilled to minus 162 C (minus 260 F). The effort is paying off, however: QatarEnergy restored LNG exports in September to about a third of prewar levels, Bloomberg reported.

Lufthansa has suspended flights until Nov. 18, Cathay Pacific until the end of January, and Delta has pushed back the launch of its Atlanta route to March 2027.
Attacks on Riyadhâs airport damaged six aircraft with a combined insured value of about $375 million, The Wall Street Journal reported, prompting Saudi carriers to evacuate aircraft worth up to $4 billion from the city. Many travelers are now driving to Bahrain, Qatar, and the UAE to catch commercial flights, while the wealthy are paying a premium of more than 50% compared to prewar rates to fly private out of al-Qassim airport, an almost four hour drive north of Riyadh, according to the Financial Times.

f273d5774339.text: Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in a phone call Tuesday that President Trump hasn't issued any kind of order to harm Ukraine. Why it matters: The call was an effort to prevent the crisis between the U.S. and Ukraine from escalating further — and to push back on Ukrainian accusations that Trump is trying to coerce Zelensky into making concessions to Russia. The 45-minute call took place several hours ahead of a new round of peace talks with White House envoy Steve Witkoff aimed at reaching a unified position with European allies on an updated peace proposal to present to Russian President Vladimir Putin. Driving the news: The crisis broke out 10 days ago when Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia at the same time his envoys were in negotiations with Ukrainian officials in Miami. Zelensky on Monday lobbied a bipartisan group of senators to press the Trump administration to remove what he says are restrictions on intelligence sharing and weapons supplies. Behind the scenes: Rubio told reporters on Tuesday that he clarified to Zelensky that the Pentagon hasn't changed anything when it comes to intelligence sharing with Ukraine, weapons sales or restrictions on the use of the Starshield satellite system. "No change was ordered. It is not true that we restricted it," Rubio said. Rubio acknowledged to Zelensky that there could be a delay in sending Patriot interceptors that have already been paid for by NATO countries. But the reason, he said, is that the U.S. needs to make sure it has enough to protect its own military bases around the world. "Nothing is being deliberately denied. We balance between our obligations to partners and our own needs," he said. "There hasn't been a deliberate political directive to harm Ukraine." Rubio also asserted that the several cases in which Ukraine didn't get advance warning of Russian ballistic missile attacks were a result of technical failures, not a U.S. order. What he's saying: "No doubt there are tensions," he said. "That is why we had the call. The president is frustrated. The president is responding to the insinuation that he is doing things to deliberately harm Ukraine, which is not fair and not true." Rubio said Trump is "angry and frustrated" about the lack of progress in peace talks between Russia and Ukraine after two years of efforts. The other side: Zelensky wrote on X after the call that he is "grateful" for Rubio's "readiness to help and his clear position." He said Ukraine needs ballistic missile interceptors and early warnings to protect Ukrainian citizens and stressed that "the situation with Starlink and Starshield needs to be restored." State of play: Witkoff arrived in Oslo on Tuesday for talks with Zelensky and European leaders. The talks there are expected to include Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, President of Finland Alexander Stubb, representatives of the E4 nations (the U.K., France, Germany and Poland) and officials from the EU and NATO. Following Oslo, Witkoff plans to travel to Russia to meet with Putin and present ideas developed in consultation with Ukrainian and European leaders.

Thunder and lightning have boomed across Marseille following the weekend's mayhem, illuminating the cracked windows and boarded-up doors of hundreds of businesses that were smashed as protests gave way to disorder.
France's second city saw some of the worst violence as chaos gripped the country on Saturday. Local business leaders say more than 500 premises were damaged, and the majority looted.
A police union boss told the BBC that the weekend had been an "apocalyptic" hell for his colleagues. 118 officers were injured, representing more than a tenth of the national figure.
So far, 101 arrests have been made in the port city, a quarter of them children.
But by Monday, it was police who were most conspicuous on the city's streets, not protesters. For eight hours, demonstrations and gatherings were banned in an effort to avoid a third consecutive day of disorder.
It seemed to work; the largest central gathering we witnessed was a posse of weather-beaten tourists trudging around the quayside.
Nonetheless, an overnight curfew for minors will come into force in parts of the city from Tuesday evening. An overnight curfew in parts of Paris, which came into force on Monday, has also been extended.
Marseille is one of France's most ethnically diverse cities â a place where generations of new arrivals have landed.
18-year-old student Maryame only arrived in the southern city a few weeks ago, albeit from the countryside not too far away.
"It was very scary because it's my first time in a big city, and also my first time demonstrating," she said.
Maryame said violence engulfed the student demonstration her friends had joined as looters began attacking shops.
She said the solidarity of the earlier march was "beautiful" and the subsequent disorder "terrifying", but went on to say that she was conflicted as to whether even more violence would make the government sit up and listen.
"It is a very complicated question if violence is legitimate," she began.
"But the thing is, France, our history is really based on revolution, and sometimes we really have to make a really big impact.
"Sometimes it goes too far."
'An unheard-of level of violence'
For the police, the extent to which order disintegrated was a shock, according to one organisation representing rank and file officers.
"It was a war," said Arnaud Blaise from the UN1TE police union. "An unheard-of level of violence. Unprecedented."
Looting was reported across the city centre, including along La CanebiÃ¨re - Marseille's equivalent of Paris's Champs-ÃlysÃ©es - Rue Paradis, and at the Centre Bourse shopping centre. Businesses were also hit further afield, such as in the Grand Littoral and Le Merlan shopping malls to the north.
Blaise said he was concerned that future protests could follow the same destructive pattern as Saturday, with young people from the deprived northern suburbs seizing the opportunity to steal amid chaos that, in his view, was stirred up by far-left agitators - referred to in France as the Black Bloc.
"The Black Blocs provoked, and the youngsters took advantage to start looting," Blaise said. "That created chaos, with police officers running right, running left, and in effect, we got overwhelmed."
I put it to Blaise that the police had been accused of heavy-handedness with peaceful students but sitting back as the most violent protesters pillaged local businesses.
"That is not the case at all," he replied, arguing that more police than students had been injured.
"Four thousand tear gas grenades were fired and then we ran out of ammunition. So at a certain point, you have no choice but to retreat."
France's Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez - whose resignation in the wake of the riots was rejected by President Macron - travelled to Marseille on Monday evening.
He came to the City Hall, which was briefly occupied by protestors on Saturday, and met Marseille's Socialist Mayor BenoÃ®t Payan.
Payan said he wanted answers from the government as to how the chaos was allowed to happen.
"Order was lost, and an attempt was made to restore order. I believe that from start to finish, it was a fiasco," he said on Monday.
He said under-staffed and poorly deployed police needed to change their tactics.
"If there isn't a radical change of approach on this issue - if, by chance, the only target remains high school students - then we will see looting scenes again."
He continued: "I don't know what's left to loot in Marseille, but for the little that remains, it will be looted."
While the ban on public gatherings in Marseille and partial overnight curfews in other French cities have brought some temporary calm, more demonstrations are planned for the weekend.
At a smashed out tram stop, 79-year-old grandmother Chantal Bellanger said she had been "worried - but then, I've been worried for a long time".
"We can clearly see that France has lost its grip on many things. Public services, hospitals, education is in a horrible state, the peripheral neighbourhoods are dilapidated, they are abandoned."
She said she used to work in these deprived northern suburbs, where poverty and crime rates are very high, and feared a whole lost generation was criminalising itself through anger and despair.
"It tugs at your heartstrings," she said.
"To see children whose actions are going to place them completely outside of society. It's painful to watch."
Additional reporting by Paul Pradier and Pol Reygaerts

This is the moment the planet's second largest living creature opens its giant jaws and swallows thousands of gallons of water during feeding.
The fin whale was filmed by videographer Rhys Morgan off the Pembrokeshire coast in Wales, and it shows the mammal's expandable pleats take in up to 18,000 gallons of water and krill.
Morgan said "it was complete luck" that he captured the whale feeding and swimming with dolphins on his drone while fishing with a friend.
Second only to the blue whale, the fin whale is one of the largest animals ever to have lived, reaching up to 24m in length and weighing up to 70 tonnes.
Despite its enormous size, the fast-swimming creature is elusive and spends much of its life in the open ocean and often surfacing only briefly before disappearing beneath the waves.
The mammal can be found all over the world's oceans but is most at home in cooler waters.
Morgan, from Houghton, Pembrokeshire, works at an oil refinery by day, and said he was "brought up on the water", but became interested in marine videography after using his friends drone to capture footage of sea creatures across the surface of the ocean.
"It's pretty incredible really," Morgan said.
"It makes you feel very small out there."
To avoid causing harm to the whales while recording out at sea, Morgan said: "We do what we can to keep our distance in the boat but unfortunately nature can have a mind of its own sometimes.
"There's been times when we've been anchored up fishing with nothing happening in the area and a whale has popped up next to us.
"The wildlife will approach you sometimes."
Dr Marianna Chimienti is a lecturer in marine top predator ecology at Bangor University and said Morgan experienced a "rare and fortunate encounter".
Chimienti, who specialises in animal behaviour added: "It is normal that the fin whale comes and feeds at the surface, as it is part of the species foraging strategy but being in the coastal water is quite spectacular.
"In theory, they should have migrated."
Little is known about fin whale migration but their movements are believed to be quite different from other baleen whales such as blues and humpbacks.
Scientists have found that fin whales are more abundant in higher latitudes in warmer months of the year, and more numerous in lower latitudes during colder months, but this can vary.
What do fin whales eat?
Fin whales have a pretty simple diet which is usually made up of krill, small schooling fish and squid.
Due to the small size of its prey, fin whales have to eat a lot to survive and can spend several hours each day feeding, consuming up to 2,000 kilograms of food.
