Nestled within a rebuilt inkjet printer, droplets of ink hang suspended above a page. Seen through a microscope, the droplets reveal how an inkjet printer produces crisp, uniform letters.
Ole Bielfeldt, a design student in Cologne, Germany, has been photographing the microscopic world since about 2021. His interest began as a quarantine hobby, when an old school microscope from his attic gave him a way to explore while stuck at home during the pandemic.
His printer image won first place in the 2026 Nikon Small World photomicrography competition. To capture the winning photo, he built a custom rig that moved the paper instead of the printer’s ink nozzles, keeping the nozzles stationary and in focus.
The mini side of ‘macro’
Ole Bielfeldt created this custom rig to catch impossibly fast ink droplets midflight. The contraption is only a bit larger than his head. Swipe through to see what word the printer was spitting out ink to spell.
Bielfeldt estimates that the droplets traveled at nearly 20 meters per second — too fast for even his best slow-motion camera to resolve. To freeze their motion, Bielfeldt worked in darkness, illuminating the scene with a single brief flash. He instructed the printer to repeatedly spell out “macro,” a nod to his social media handle, macrofying.
Before this project, a printer was “like magic,” Bielfeldt says. Photographing its inner workings helped him understand how it operates.
Bielfeldt no longer takes the magic printers spit out for granted. “It’s so, so advanced technically, but at the same time it’s so, so common,” he says.
His photograph is one of 86 images recognized in this year’s competition, whose winners were announced October 21. Here are some of our other favorites.
Did you capture my jumping side?
This pollen-dusted jumping spider offers a close look at the bristling hairs and some of its eight eyes that are easy to miss with the naked eye.
John-Oliver Dum’s fascination with spiders began as a childhood fear. Dum says he suffered a particularly painful arachnid-inflicted bite when he was young. Several years ago, when he was inspired to study the movements of a curly hair tarantula (Tliltocatl albopilosus), Dum became passionate about capturing their beauty.
Preparations for his photographs can begin years before he submits them to a competition. His wife grows plants selected for their pollen, which Dum uses in his images.
“The biggest challenge was finding a spider like this on the right plants, with the right pollen attached to it, at exactly the right time of year and at exactly the right moment,” he says. “You need to understand not only the spider’s behavior, but also the surrounding insect and plant life and their seasonal rhythms.”
Dum hopes the photograph, which won second place, encourages viewers to look more closely, too. “We first have to see the beauty of this largely unknown world before we can truly understand what we may be destroying,” he says.
Seeing a mouse eye in a new way
It’s not a leaf and it’s not a flower. This cross section of a mouse eye is crisscrossed in fractals of blood vessels and tethered by the optic nerve.
Cell biologists Sinem Karaman and Satu Paavonsalo at the University of Helsinki visualize vascular networks, like blood vessels, to study how they work within tissues. The arrangement, Paavonsalo says, could even point to mechanisms underlying how these systems stop working in obesity and diabetes.
Paavonsalo says the duo set out to capture a mouse eye in 3-D, different from the flattened retinas typically used in her research. After meticulous mounting which required several attempts for an arrangement she was satisfied with, Paavonsalo still didn’t know for certain the image would turn out right.
“I had to hope that the sample was correctly positioned and that the staining was detected throughout the sample,” Paavonsalo says, which made her excitement upon seeing the image even more pronounced. The image won 19th place in the competition.
A tardigrade Easter egg
A water bear emerges from its shed cuticle, and oh! What’s that left behind? This egg will be protected by its mother’s discarded skin.
The tardigrade (Hypsibius exemplaris) is one of nature’s toughest creatures, able to survive space by going into a state of suspended animation. This species, emerging from its former skin, is only about two-and-a-half times as wide as a strand of hair. Evolutionary developmental biologist Gonzalo Quiroga-Artigas captured the image during his studies of these tiny wonders at the University of Montpellier in France.
In the tardigrade life cycle, “egg laying is closely synchronized with molting,” says Quiroga-Artigas. Tardigrades can lay up to about a dozen eggs at once, and the moment one sheds its old cuticle happens quickly enough that it’s easy to miss.
Snapping this image demanded painstaking mounting and imaging of many specimens. Quiroga-Artigas chose this particular one, which won 12th, because “the egg looks almost like a precious gem being left behind by its mother.”
The stretch of a slime mold
This slime mold (Hemitrichia sp.) was found in the heart of Brooklyn, N.Y., sprouting from a decaying log in Prospect Park. The image features the mold’s gelatinous fruiting bodies, which release spores as part of reproduction. To bring the delicate structures into sharp detail, Eric Epstein stacked 240 images.
First, Epstein searched local parks for slime molds to photograph, carefully cutting pieces of waterlogged wood free without disturbing his subjects. “In this liquidy state, any touch would demolish” the fruiting bodies, he says.
One species of slime mold closely mirrors the cosmic web of gas and dark matter connecting galaxies, which helps scientists to more accurately map the cosmos. Another species has fascinated researchers for its ability to pack a store of bacteria to feed the next generation, when it’s near death.

The family of a senior Irish prison officer murdered by the IRA has received a state apology on Wednesday for failings in investigations into his killing.
Brian Stack, a father of three, was crossing a street in Dublin, after leaving a boxing match in 1983, when he was shot in the back of the neck.
Stack, who was the chief prison officer at the high-security Portlaoise Prison, was left paralysed and died 18 months later, aged 49.
There were three separate garda (Irish police) investigations into Stack's death, but no-one was brought to justice for his killing.
The Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) MicheÃ¡l Martin offered an apology on behalf of the state during a sitting of the DÃ¡il (Irish parliament).
Stack's wife Sheila and her sons Austin, Kieran and Oliver were in the chamber for the apology.
Martin said the Provisional IRA is "still in the possession of all the facts" on this case.
Apology means 'an awful lot'
Speaking to BBC Radio Ulster's Good Morning Ulster programme Brian Stack's son, Austin Stack, said the apology "means an awful lot to us".
"It's a great sense of comfort, to particularly my mother and to myself and my two brothers, because the state is officially owning up to the errors and the missions that happened," he said.
He went on to say that the serious crime review team looked into the first investigation and "they found 194 errors and omissions".
"So I have, and my family have, met with several ministers for justice down through the years and we have a requested sight of that report.
"And every time we've requested it, we've been told that it's an internally valid document and that we cannot see it."
Austin Stack said that Wednesday would be a very emotional day for his family.
"My dad was doing a very difficult job at a very difficult time in our history," he said.
"He was awarded the Irish Prison Service's highest bravery award for that work that he was doing. And this is further vindication of him and his good name."
Prior to the DÃ¡il proceedings, the Stack family held a private meeting at government buildings with the taoiseach and Minister for Justice Jim O'Callaghan.
'Utterly unacceptable'
In 2007 the Garda Commissioner directed a review of the case by the Garda Serious Crime Review Team. Over 200 recommendations were made relating to the cases.
This review led to "serious failings" being found as well as "the shortcomings in the management" of the earlier Garda investigation.
These failures, listed by Martin in the DÃ¡il, are: failure to keep a map made of the crime scene, a failure to keep a motorbike helmet found near the crime scene and linked to the crime, a failure to keep custody of material exhibits, including various fingerprints, samples and debris gathered during the investigation.
The taoiseach also said there was a failure to document some potentially important aspects of the original investigation, including whether Brian's colleagues at Portlaoise Prison were interviewed and whether prisoners at the prison were interviewed.
There was also a failure to interview the Stack family and to interview Brian's wider group of friends.
"It is plainly and utterly unacceptable that material that was potentially of evidential value to the investigation can no longer be located by An Garda SÃochÃ¡na.
"It is admitted by An Garda SÃochÃ¡na that these are serious matters that had an impact on the investigation," Martin said.
He formally apologised to the Stack family for these failings.
Speaking in the Commons during Northern Ireland questions on Wednesday, Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant said he "warmly welcomed" the apology.
Asked about the matter by Democratic Unionist Party leader Gavin Robinson, Sir Chris said Dublin doing so was "entirely right and proper" and went to the heart of discussions MPs had been having this week as they debated the UK government's Troubles legacy bill.
He added that it was "incumbent on all of us to make fulsome and not mealy-mouthed apologies".
'Regret'
The IRA admitted killing Stack in 2013 after his family mounted a long campaign to secure the admission, and met Sinn FÃ©in's Gerry Adams and a former IRA commander.
Adams, at that time, expressed his "regret" to the Stack family over the killing.
A Sinn FÃ©in spokesperson said that "in a 2013 statement, a former IRA leader acknowledged that IRA volunteers were responsible for Brian Stack's killing".
"The statement said the shooting had not been authorised by the IRA leadership, accepted IRA responsibility for his death, said it should not have happened and expressed sorrow for the pain and hurt suffered by the family."
The spokesperson added: "As republicans, we acknowledge the hurt caused by republican actions. That suffering cannot be disowned. We are sorry for all the lives lost during the period of conflict on this island, without exception."
Irish foreign affairs minister Helen McEntee also spoke during the State apology, she said: "The State failed you during their investigation into Brian's killing."
She said Brian was "targeted" by the Provisional IRA and said "they are responsible".
"To Sheila and to all of the Stack family, we are deeply sorry for all that you have endured, for the failures of the investigation and the additional suffering they have caused you, we are deeply sorry. I hope today's formal apology brings some measure of peace and comfort."
Donegal Sinn FÃ©in TD (member of Irish parliament) Pearse Doherty said the Stack's family "long search for answers deserves respect".
"No apology can restore Brian Stack's life or return the years spent seeking answers but it can recognise the wrong done."
He said the failures of the garda investigation "compounded" the suffering of the Stack family.

a5a72c78bef8.text: By — Dasha Litvinova, Associated Press Dasha Litvinova, Associated Press By — Eric Tucker, Associated Press Eric Tucker, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/russia-frees-american-stephen-hubbard-after-over-4-years-in-prison-during-a-visit-from-u-s-envoy-witkoff Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Russia frees American Stephen Hubbard after over 4 years in prison, during a visit from U.S. envoy Witkoff World Oct 21, 2026 9:15 AM EDT Russia on Wednesday freed an American who had been jailed for more than four years on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine, in a deal completed during a visit by a top U.S. envoy and at a time when President Donald Trump has taken a series of actions meant to benefit Moscow. Trump said in a Truth Social post that he had asked Russian President Vladimir Putin during a phone call last week to free Stephen Hubbard, and that, unlike previous releases, his had not required the U.S. to give up anyone in return. READ MORE: Zelenskyy says early warning system for Russian missile attacks resumes after call with Rubio "Welcome home, Stephen, it's great to have you back," Trump said. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Hubbard, a 74-year-old former teacher from Michigan, was on his way home following a visit to St. Petersburg by U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, who also held talks with Putin about Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, as Trump pushes Kyiv to make a deal that stops the fighting. WATCH: Evan Gershkovich reflects on arrest in Russia and reclaiming his life after release Hubbard was sentenced in 2024 to nearly seven years in prison following a closed trial. Prosecutors said he had signed a contract with the Ukrainian military after Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, and that he fought alongside Kyiv's forces until being captured two months later. The U.S. government under the Biden administration designated Hubbard as wrongfully detained. The release came amid Trump moves to benefit Russia Witkoff, a key Trump administration figure who has tried without success to steer Russia and Ukraine toward a settlement to end a war that will hit the five-year mark in February 2027, thanked Putin for releasing Hubbard, telling him, "Because of you, he's going home to his family." "You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir," Witkoff said. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian media on Wednesday that Hubbard's release was "raised by the American side for a certain time," and Putin decided to free the man out of "humanitarian considerations." WATCH: Families reunited as Americans who were detained in Russia arrive home He added that general contacts "continue on a regular basis between the intelligence services." The release occurred at a dynamic moment in relations between the United States, Ukraine and Russia, with the Washington-Kyiv relationship being roiled by fresh tensions at the same time that the Trump administration has advanced policies that aid Putin. Those include Trump's decision last week to waive sanctions on Russia imposed by a bill that Congress overwhelmingly passed to support Ukraine. Named after the late South Carolina Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, the legislation targeted the flow of financial resources fueling Moscow's war. That reversal followed Trump's announcement of a deal to import Russian diesel fuel in a long-shot effort to curb high gas prices ahead of next month's U.S. midterm elections. Witkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway on Tuesday. He was expected to exchange ideas from that meeting, as well as proposals from European and American colleagues, in his talks Wednesday with Russian leaders in St. Petersburg. Other Americans remain jailed in Russia Hubbard is the second American freed by Russia in roughly two months, following the release in August of Marine veteran Robert Gilman, who had been gravely ill and was imprisoned on disputed charges of assaulting a police officer. Other Americans, including some with serious illnesses, remain jailed in Russia. Hubbard was the only one designated as wrongfully detained, although advocates say that label should be applied to other prisoners. WATCH: Zelenskyy seeks to mend ties with Trump ahead of Witkoff-Putin meeting Global Reach, a group that works to free Americans detained abroad and currently represents five American held in Russia, praised the release but called for the other prisoners to come home as well. "We are grateful to the Trump Administration for reuniting Stephen Hubbard with his family, but at the same time, we know that there are five other families of Americans held in Russia who are going to have a hard time understanding why their loved one was not included in the deal," Eric Lebson, the group's chief strategy officer, said in a statement. Hubbard had been imprisoned since 2022 on charges that Hostage Aid Worldwide, a hostage advocacy group, has called bogus. The organization in August posted an open letter to Trump that it said was written by Patricia Hubbard Fox, Hubbard's sister, in which she offered praise for Trump but also said her brother had been subjected to "constant beatings, torture and starvation" while in custody. "Even so, everything that you're doing isn't going to matter to my kidnapped, American Veteran brother, Stephen James Hubbard (soon to be 74) if Putin won't cave and let him come home and he dies up there in a Nazi prison (crying)," the letter said. Tucker reported from Washington; Litvinova reported from Tallinn, Estonia. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 869ea0495591.text: Data: Columbia University Center on Global Energy Policy; Table: Ben Geman/Axios The push to pass a sweeping permitting bill is gaining powerful allies and encountering fresh resistance as Congress prepares for a post-midterms showdown. Why it matters: It's the most important energy bill in a long time. Cutting hurdles for projects is a top priority for fossil fuels and renewables sectors. But some environmentalists say it badly weakens crucial protections in the name of speeding reviews. Driving the news: A new, interactive analysis out on Wednesday projects potentially huge time savings if the bill becomes law. Transmission projects could see the biggest acceleration, per Jack Andreasen Cavanaugh, a researcher with Columbia's energy think tank. He based it on historical data about a large number of specific projects, then estimated how much quicker they would have proceeded under the bill. Columbia's Center on Global Energy Policy doesn't have an institutional position on the bill. But founding director Jason Bordoff, a prominent voice in energy policy circles, is urging environmentalists not to oppose it. State of play: A who's who of economic and national security officials spanning six presidents (including Trump) are linking arms behind the bill in a new letter to Capitol Hill leaders. What's next: The effort goes beyond signatures for some of the former officials, according to letter organizer Arnab Datta of the Institute for Progress, a nonpartisan think tank. "Some folks are engaging beyond the letter itself with stakeholders across the board, and some have made themselves available for members briefings or conversations," he tells me via email. Catch up quick: The letter from 19 officials includes Biden-era Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen and Trump 1.0 Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin, among five people who held the job. The list also features Trump 1.0 Secretary of State and CIA boss Mike Pompeo, and Leon Panetta, who had top Obama-era defense and CIA gigs, to name just two others. Friction point: The last 24 hours has also brought new signs of simmering opposition to the bill, or at least parts of it, adding to existing concerns among tribal leaders and some green groups. Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) posted on X that it would be "tone deaf if Congress makes it easier to build data centers." That drew pushback from backers who emphasized provisions to ensure data center companies cover grid costs. What we're watching: The Edison Electric Institute, a powerful group of for-profit utilities, still hasn't weighed in. But David Pomerantz, who's with the progressive Energy & Policy Institute obtained an Oklahoma Gas & Electric document criticizing the transmission provisions. The bottom line: The Senate is expected to hold a procedural vote on the bipartisan permitting bill immediately after lawmakers return from recess. - Published
Nigeria has recorded a case of Ebola in a female patient who travelled from Uganda in East Africa to Abuja, capital of the West African state.
Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate said the diagnosis had been confirmed by laboratory tests.
The patient, who health sources have told the BBC is not Nigerian and is the wife of a diplomat, is in isolation and receiving medical care after being admitted to a hospital in Abuja.
She developed symptoms on Wednesday 7 October, four days after arriving in the country, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
Health authorities have begun contact-tracing to prevent further spread, with 44 close contacts of the woman identified.
Nigeria, the first West African state to report a case linked to the current Ebola crisis in East Africa, successfully stopped a previous outbreak in 2014.
Uganda's Ministry of Health has stressed there are currently no confirmed active Ebola cases in the country.
"We urge the public to remain calm, vigilant and to practice regular handwashing and sanitising," it said.
Ebola is a rare but deadly disease, external caused by a virus. As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.
The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
The outbreak in Democratic Republic of Congo, which began in May, has claimed at least 4,600 lives, with more than 9,500 cases recorded, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control reports, external.
It was caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.
Shortly after the outbreak was announced, it was also reported in Uganda, where at least two people died. Uganda declared itself free of the disease in August after its last patient was discharged.
Following the latest case in Nigeria, Uganda's health ministry said preliminary information indicated that the patient had transited through Uganda without symptoms.
In a statement on X, Uganda's Director General of Health Services Charles Olaro said the woman had travelled to eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo for business before passing through Uganda in early October.
He said her symptoms had only developed after arriving in Nigeria.
The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks.
The woman's exact travel history - key to tracing contacts - appears to be unclear at the moment.
"The location of exposure remains under investigation. The government of Nigeria is yet to provide detailed information on her travel itinerary and clinical history which will guide further investigations and any necessary contact tracing," Olaro said.
Nigeria's health minister confirmed the woman had had no symptoms when she arrived in Nigeria, but he said the patient had not confirmed travel to DR Congo.
"We presume that it was likely picked in Uganda," Pate told the national broadcaster Nigerian Television Authority (NTA) on Tuesday evening.
Her travel documents will be used to trace contacts and the authorities have urged the public to co-operate with health officials carrying out contact tracing.
The disease has also recently spread to Kenya, which has reported at least nine infections.
On Monday, the US advised its citizens to reconsider travel to Kenya because of health risks and raised its travel advisory level for the country.
Since the outbreak, Nigeria has stepped up disease surveillance, with the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control issuing public health advice to travellers.
The agency says travellers from countries with active or relevant Ebola transmission may be required to complete a health declaration form. Those arriving from other countries are currently exempt.
It has also urged travellers to remain vigilant and seek medical attention promptly if they develop symptoms of Ebola.
In 2014, Nigeria managed to beat an outbreak of Ebola which caused at least eight deaths.

The News
Elon Muskâs companies, SpaceX and Tesla, have begun exploring a merger that would create a $3.5 trillion corporate giant spanning key sectors of cutting-edge technology. Musk argued that combining the companies would allow them to deepen cooperation on chip design, robotics, software, and other technologies; both firmsâ share prices rose following the announcement.
Lizâs view
The outlines of MegaMusk Inc. are starting to emerge, where special committees of SpaceX and Tesla directors will now have to bless the merger. Combining the two would bring the tech and infrastructure parts of Muskâs empire together (the Wall Street pitch) and a hyperconcentrated bet on the billionaireâs inventions, politics, and personality (the actual pitch).
Musk already rolled up X, xAI, and SpaceX, whose June IPO paved the way for the Tesla deal. Many of Muskâs projects already bleed into each other â the new Roadster has SpaceX thrusters â and Muskâs employees often work interchangeably across his companies, so thereâs some business and governance sense in formalizing whatâs already happening. But itâs clear Musk is again using Teslaâs shareholders â and its massive retail investor base â to fund his other exploits, just as he did in 2016 when Tesla bailed out his cash-strapped solar company, SolarCity, and, more recently, when he reallocated Tesla talent and GPUs to xAI.
While Musk says heâll recuse himself from the decision, his companiesâ boards donât have a history of pushing back. Tesla Chair Robyn Denholm told Semafor last year she was skeptical of Tesla investing in xAI; four months later, it invested $2 billion. And a combo would further strengthen Muskâs control over Tesla: Super-voting shares give him roughly 84% of the vote at SpaceX, compared to 20% at Tesla, where every share has equal voting weight.
Notable
- The SpaceX-Tesla tie-up has its own strong logic, one early SpaceX investor told Bloomberg: âCombined, it would be the only company owning the full physical-AI stack â¦ No competitor has an analog.â

Netflix CEO Ted Sarandos has navigated steep odds before, including the âstreaming correction.â But the question facing the company now is acute: whether a builder culture that prizes homegrown content, and which Wall Street loved, is serving it anymore.
After laying off 6% of employees and bouncing both its content chief and head of feature films last week, Netflix reported its third straight quarter of slowing revenue growth Tuesday and acknowledged its stagnating viewership. Its shares fell more than 5% and are down by nearly 40% since April.
Semafor wrote in February, when Netflix walked away from its pursuit of Warner Bros. Discovery, that the company came out battered from an M&A game it had little experience playing. Hiring new creative leaders like Peter Rice, who has strong roots in film, sports, and television, coupled with a pivot to more theatrical releases for its films, may be enough to dig out of its current jam. But perhaps itâs also time to look to M&A again, especially as NBCUniversal spins out of Comcast next year.

Metaâs Republican policy chief announced his departure just ahead of a projected blue wave in Washington that threatens to rain down scrutiny on big tech companies. Joel Kaplan, who was elevated in the early days of Trumpâs second term, will leave sometime early next year.
When Semafor scooped Kaplanâs ascension in early 2025, we wrote that âMetaâs political operation is now well placed for a Republican-dominated Washington.â Kaplan had replaced the neoliberal UK politico Nick Clegg just as the political pendulum was swinging and companies were rushing to add MAGA credentials to their boardrooms and executive ranks.
Those moves â funding American priorities, hiring MAGA lobbyists, policing their airwaves, and committing to do free work for the government â may age badly as Democrats appear likely to take at least one chamber of Congress next month and take up the hearing gavel.

dc96c2d4cca6.text: The world's most advanced AI models are suddenly capable of blueprinting cyberttacks on critical services like power grids and water systems with alarming success rates, according to new research . Why it matters: Critical infrastructure operators are running out of time. Top-tier frontier models are dangerously adept at mapping out attacks, new research from cybersecurity company Frenos shows, and it's only a matter of time before freely available AI models make such hacks easier to execute. "It's a clock that is moving faster than we've ever seen," Steve Swick, former top security executive at American Electric Power, told reporters during a briefing. Driving the news: Researchers at Frenos tested 10 AI models on their ability to plan attacks against industrial systems, such as the software that monitors water treatment processes. Three out of 10 models tested successfully constructed attack plans in roughly 90% of attempts. Performance varied widely: Three models the researchers considered to be at the frontier of capabilities succeeded in just 17.9% to 31.9% of attempts. The strongest foreign open-weight model succeeded 36.2% of the time, while the strongest U.S. open-weight model succeeded just 5.2%. Frenos did not disclose the names of the models tested. Zoom in : The research included nearly 17,000 tests, including 2,520 attempts to construct complete attack plans. The models received information about potential targets and tasked with piecing together the steps needed to achieve specific objectives. The big picture: Critical services like water systems and manufacturing plants have long been targets for nation-state adversaries and cybercriminals. Many operators face staffing and budget constraints. Testing and upgrading their systems can also risk disruptions to essential services that they can't afford. Unlike traditional corporate networks, industrial systems can be sensitive to unexpected traffic and commands. Even an unsuccessful attack attempt could disrupt essential operations. Threat level: Once attackers gain access to an industrial network, AI could help them quietly map out systems and identify weaknesses without the same time constraints facing human hackers, Frenos co-founder and CTO Harry Thomas said. "AI doesn't have the problem with patience," Thomas said. "It doesn't need to eat. It doesn't need to sleep, and it doesn't need to use the restroom." Paul Shaver, head of operational technology at cybersecurity firm Armadin, added that AI agents can already conduct reconnaissance and analyze large volumes of data without necessarily triggering security alerts. The intrigue : Thomas said the researchers used a relatively simple setup to guide the models through their tasks. More sophisticated tools that provide additional context and feedback could improve their performance. "A more capable harness could have given these AI models more of an edge," he said. What to watch : Several initiatives — including from the White House , frontier AI companies , and cybersecurity organizations — have cropped up in recent weeks to help lower the costs and provide resources for critical infrastructure organizations. Go deeper : Frightening AI advances speed race to secure critical infrastructure

c73de1df24f0.text: OpenAI is bringing its AI models and Codex coding tools to Google Cloud , expanding its reach to customers of all three major U.S. cloud providers — including companies that are also among its fiercest AI rivals. Why it matters: The move underscores a growing recognition that winning the enterprise AI race isn't just about building the smartest models. It's also about making those models available wherever businesses already run their software and store their data. For OpenAI, the agreement offers another way to reach corporate customers without requiring them to establish a separate relationship with the ChatGPT-maker. For Google, it means selling a competitor's AI models alongside its own Gemini offerings, potentially capturing business that might otherwise go to rival cloud providers. Driving the news: Under the agreement announced Wednesday, Google Cloud customers will be able to purchase OpenAI's frontier models through Google's "Model Garden and Marketplace," including by using existing cloud spending commitments. The deal also brings OpenAI models to Google's Antigravity development environment and Gemini Agent. General availability is planned in the coming weeks. The big picture: The agreement follows OpenAI's expansion onto Amazon Web Services earlier this year, after changes to its Microsoft partnership opened the door to broader cloud distribution. AWS CEO Matt Garman said at the time that customers had long wanted to run OpenAI models where their existing applications and data already resided. Amazon has since expanded the OpenAI models and services available through its Bedrock platform, although neither company has publicly quantified the additional business generated by the arrangement. What they're saying: Mike Leone, VP and analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, said the deal is significant for both companies, particularly because many Google Cloud customers want access to OpenAI models without moving their data. "For Google, I read the deal as confidence, because Gemini now has to win those customers with OpenAI sitting right next to it," Leone told Axios. But he doesn't see Google as necessarily hurting Gemini, since customers will still pay Google for its cloud platform, data services and security regardless of which AI models they choose. Yes, but: Distribution is only part of the equation. OpenAI still has to persuade enterprises to choose its models over those from Google, Anthropic and other competitors, many of which are available through the same cloud platforms. That could make the cloud providers' existing enterprise relationships and infrastructure as important as the models they offer. "Once every cloud has the top models, I think the competitive advantage goes to whoever does the best job with a company's data, governance, and costs," Leone said.

The government has approved drilling at the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea.
The decision - which comes after years of debate and legal challenges - will pave the way for gas to be extracted from it and used in Britain's gas network within weeks.
BBC Verify has looked at what this means for energy bills, energy security and the environment.
Where is Jackdaw and how much gas is there?
Jackdaw is a gas field 150 miles (241.4km) east of Aberdeen. It is owned by Adura Energy, which is itself equally owned by the energy companies Shell and Equinor.
The owners of the site, which was first approved four years ago but subject to legal delays until now, estimate Jackdaw has around 10 million cubic metres of recoverable gas., external
Based on official forecasts, external for the amount of gas the UK will need over the next decade, that suggests Jackdaw has the potential to meet around 1.6% of total projected national gas demand between 2026 and 2036.
Operators say it could be connected to the Great British gas network within weeks and could produce gas for the next 11 years.
Where does Britain currently get its gas from?
Around half of the UK's natural gas comes from its existing North Sea gas fields and is pumped ashore via pipelines.
Gas imports, external make up the remainder. Of these, most come from Norway's North Sea gas fields via separate pipelines.
But a higher share of the UK's gas imports now come in the form of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) compared with 20 years ago.
This is natural gas which is extracted, turned into liquid form and then transported by ship to the country which buys it, where it is turned back into gas form to be used as an energy source.
And the UK increasingly relies on shipments of LNG from the US, which accounted for a quarter of all natural gas imports in 2025, external.
Will the approval of Jackdaw mean lower bills?
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh has said the gas from Jackdaw "won't lower energy bills this winter".
And most energy analysts do not expect the additional gas production from Jackdaw to have a significant, direct impact on households' energy bills, either.
This is because of the way natural gas markets work. Great Britain is integrated with wider European gas markets and physically linked to the continent through undersea pipelines.
Gas prices faced by British households and businesses are effectively set at a pan-European level and determined by the price customers across Europe are prepared to pay for the energy.
People across the continent have seen their energy bills rise significantly in recent years, fuelled by the wars in Ukraine and Iran affecting gas and oil supplies.
But the additional gas being pumped into the UK's system from Jackdaw will still be relatively small, and unlikely to significantly move the European price paid by British firms and households.
"Essentially, producing more British energy doesn't necessarily mean cheaper British energy," Karl Matikonis, professor of taxation at University College Dublin, told BBC Verify.
"North Sea oil and gas are sold at market prices rather than reserved for British consumers at a discount."
However, the additional production of gas from Jackdaw could result in more corporation tax revenues for the UK government, because any profits made by the owner would be taxable.
As part of its Jackdaw announcement, external, the government said it was setting up a new energy wealth fund, using tax revenues from North Sea oil and gas to invest in green energy projects. It said this would "help get bills down for good in the long term" by reducing the UK's reliance on gas for electricity production.
The Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has previously said, external the tax revenue from Jackdaw "could be used to bring down energy bills" more directly by taking costs of households' bills directly.
However, both proposals depend on the future profits of the owner of Jackdaw, which cannot be forecast with certainty.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said opening the gas field would "protect hundreds of jobs" and the move has been welcomed by unions.
The owner of Jackdaw has also estimated, external it will help support around 500 jobs, including roles on nearby production hubs, but only 27 direct roles on the Jackdaw gas extraction platform in the North Sea.
What are the arguments for and against Jackdaw?
One of the key arguments put forward in favour of developing Jackdaw is that it would improve the UK's national energy security.
Energy experts take different views on this. Some suggest, external that if, for some reason, foreign LNG shipments were not able to reach the UK, having additional North Sea gas from Jackdaw available and delivered through a pipeline that the UK controls might prove valuable.
They argue that the reliability of the US as a source of energy has been put into question by Donald Trump's recent comments that he was considering banning exports of US diesel , externalto European countries.
However, others are not convinced Jackdaw would make a significant difference to national energy security because the UK would remain heavily reliant on natural gas imports even when the field is up and running.
The enviromental impact of Jackdaw has also been a significant point of contention. Advocates argue the gas field would be beneficial because the carbon emissions arising from production from the the UK's own North Sea field will be lower than those arising from the production of US LNG.
The North Sea Transition Authority (NSTA), which regulates the sector, has estimated the emissions arising from the production, delivery and processing of US LNG are around three times higher than from the production of North Sea natural gas.
That is because the process of liquefying, shipping and then turning LNG back in to natural gas on arrival is extremely energy intensive, compared with pumping it ashore by a pipeline, creating higher carbon emissions.

Primary school children have been left amazed after receiving a personal video message from British astronaut Tim Peake.
Pupils at Thornbury Primary School in Plymouth, Devon, were sent the message after teacher Emily Trevarthen's father met Peake while working on a cruise ship over the summer.
Trevarthen explained that her father and the astronaut got chatting and her father mentioned she was a teacher. "We didn't expect to get what we got really," she said.
Peake told pupils, external: "I hear you've been studying all about space, a subject very close to my heart, something I love, so I'm very pleased that you enjoy it too. Stay curious. Keep looking up at the stars."
Trevarthen said that some children had previously assumed all astronauts were American, but learning about a British astronaut had helped them see that such ambitions were possible.
The video was kept secret until World Space Week, external, when staff revealed it during a celebration assembly.
Trevarthen said the children were "so excited" when they saw the video, with some initially wondered whether the message had been created using artificial intelligence before realising it was genuine.
She said: "The children absolutely loved it. The standout moment was learning that Tim Peake had run a marathon on the International Space Station. They couldn't believe it."
Teacher Joanna Stelmaszczyk said there was "so much excitement" when the video was shown and recalled similar enthusiasm when pupils watched Peake's historic arrival at the International Space Station in 2015.
"I remember it like it was yesterday," she said. "I was teaching Year 1 at the time, and the buzz and excitement in the classroom was something I will never forget."

637e53bca7fe.text:
The News
Global aid groups, including the UN, are facing demands to inform the Congolese government of the whereabouts of more than $700 million that was donated to deal with the Ebola outbreak that has killed more than 4,600 people in the country.
Last week, Jean Kaseya, who heads Africa CDC, the continental body coordinating the response to the spread of the virus, said that Kinshasa had only been told about what had happened to $220 million of the $962 million donated.
In a pointed statement, Africa CDC said it âstrongly deplores the lack of cooperation from organizations,â accusing them of not respecting Congolese sovereignty and threatening to withdraw their permission to work in the country if they fail to comply.
Julien Harneis, the UNâs senior Ebola coordinator, told Semafor that Africa CDC itself has established a joint system with the World Health Organization (WHO) to track disbursements reported by donors. But, he said, the governmentâs request for recipients to report what they had received and spent was new and was taking time to implement, adding that 43 organizations had already submitted the information.
WHO spokesperson Tarik Jasarevic said the UN body supported âclear and transparent processes for tracking financing â¦ including the government establishing a mechanism to account for funds delivered by partnersâ â a message repeated by other UN bodies.
Despite the demands for greater transparency, aid agencies say they still need more money. Jasarevic told Semafor that WHOâs $115 million budget for Ebola was 80% funded, while Fleur Vernat, UNICEFâs partnerships manager in DR Congo, said her agencyâs response faced a 65% funding gap.
Know More
DR Congo is recording fewer daily Ebola cases and deaths than a month ago, but the outbreak is spreading to new provinces in the country, Harneis told Semafor. Nigeria has recorded a case of a woman who had travelled from Uganda, the authorities said and Kenya has now confirmed nine infections.
The Ebola response has drawn funding from several countries, with the US as the largest donor. DR Congoâs health minister, Roger Kamba, had already accused aid organizations in August of withholding information about their spending. âYou cannot tell people that $800 million has been given to Congo when we cannot find out how much you have spent,â he told reporters at a government briefing.
âThey demand traceability and compliance from us as local actors, but they do not do it themselves. It is a double standard,â De-Joseph Kakisingi, who heads a network of Congolese aid organizations, told Semafor. But he acknowledged that DR Congo lacked a law specifying what aid organizations must report to the government about the money they receive and spend.
This latest Ebola outbreak is the second deadliest in history after the 2014-16 epidemic which killed more than 11,300 people, mostly in West Africa. There is no known vaccine for this species of the virus, known as Bundibugyo, but Ervebo, effective against another species, is being tested. So far 9,000 frontline workers have been vaccinated.

The News
Middle East energy executives are more optimistic about their industryâs future than their peers elsewhere, a testament to their ability to keep oil flowing despite the disruption to the Strait of Hormuz, according to research commissioned by the organizers of ADIPEC, the Abu Dhabi energy conference.
Global demand for energy from all sources is forecast to rise over the next decade, driven by electrification and AI adoption. The International Energy Agency estimates energy investment at a record $3.4 trillion this year: $2.2 trillion in clean energy and grids, and $1.2 trillion in oil, gas, and coal. Almost two-thirds of the more than 1,800 decision-makers surveyed expect the pace of capital deployment to increase by more than a fifth over the next five years.
The upbeat assessment isnât surprising from producers who can get their product out of the Gulf amid higher prices from the US-Iran war. Most respondents said the energy system passed its biggest âstress test in 50 yearsâ and proved more resilient than expected, thanks to quick adjustments to shocks, continued supply to customers, and the diversification of sources and routes before the conflict.
But a third of executives from consuming countries in Asia â the most vulnerable to the disruptions â said the global energy system proved less resilient than expected.
Know More
ADIPEC, the worldâs biggest energy exhibition, organized by dmg events, comes at a moment of unprecedented upheaval for a region that supplies a fifth of the worldâs oil and liquefied natural gas. The disruption has pushed dozens of countries to rethink their energy security priorities. While many governments may pursue domestic self-reliance to avert future shocks, those in the industry are betting on a connected system, ranking renewables, source diversification, and infrastructure protection as bigger priorities than self-sufficiency.
The survey showed broad consensus on artificial intelligence, both as a driver of future demand and as a way to unlock efficiencies from the wellhead to distribution. Just 3% of respondents expect electricity demand from AI to be lower than forecast; a majority see the technology as becoming more influential than innovations in renewable energy over the next decade.
AI applications in oil production have moved beyond the pilot phase: One executive said in the report that software âdistributes the power on the drilling rig in the exact amount required and stores the unused energy for later use. It reduces the total power consumption of the rig by 25 to 30%.â
Notable
- The Hormuz closure is the biggest energy security crisis the world has faced, according to IEA chief Fatih Birol, who expects it to reshape investment much as the 1970s oil shocks did.
- Asia is rethinking its reliance on Gulf energy. The region is shifting âfrom just-in-time supply chains to just-in-case supply chains,â one analyst told Fortune.

South Africaâs ambassador to the US says Washington has repeatedly rejected Pretoriaâs trade offers without explaining what it wants instead. His complaint comes a day after President Cyril Ramaphosa told South Africans to brace for losing duty-free access under the African Growth and Opportunity Act.
âItâs not helpful when we hear the answer is, âthatâs not good enough,ââ Roelf Meyer told Semafor. âIt would have been more helpful if we could hear, âwhat is not good enough?ââ
The US Congress extended AGOA to 2028 last month, but the White House reviews country eligibility every year. Removing South Africa from Jan. 1 would require notice to Congress and Pretoria 60 days ahead, so a decision is expected by early November. That scenario has become a distinct possibility after nearly two years of a worsening relationship between Washington and Africaâs largest economy.
Meyer, who took up the post this year after more than a year without a South African ambassador in Washington, describes relations with the Trump administration as a âstalemate.â âIâm not satisfied about where we find ourselves,â he said.
The deeper rift, he suggested, is ideological. Meyer said he read the Heritage Foundationâs Project 2025 early and saw a âdeviationâ from the Republican Party he knew in the 1980s. Asked why Pretoriaâs rebuttals of white genocide claims arenât landing, he said either Washington hasnât heard him clearly, or there is âa fundamental ideological difference.â
Meyer helped lead the apartheid governmentâs side opposite Ramaphosa in the talks that ended white minority rule. He says those negotiations worked because both sides were prepared to talk. âThat is my experience, the difference here,â he said. âItâs hard to find a basis for real dialogue.â
Yet he also signaled flexibility on the policy irritant most cited in Washington. Black EconomicEmpowerment rules in mining and telecoms âstill leave room for further adjustments,â he said, adding that discussions are underway with companies looking to invest.
This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Yinka: President Cyril Ramaphosa warned South Africans to prepare for the possibility that the country could lose its AGOA trade benefits. How confident are you that South Africa will remain eligible?
Roelf Meyer: It is difficult to say because we have not had a clear response on AGOA and the eligibility question. There is a lot of speculation about the final result, and I donât think it serves any purpose to add to that.
From the South African side, we believe we have given clear enough answers. We would like an opportunity to hear where the shortcomings are in the US assessment. It is not helpful when the answer is simply, âThatâs not good enough.â We need to know what is not good enough so we can address it from a negotiating perspective.
I think the president is being realistic, so nobody is completely surprised if things go in the wrong direction. But he is also mindful that it would be better if we could stay in.
What are the main sticking points in the negotiations?
There are difficult issues on which South Africa cannot simply agree with everything the US is asking. We have local interests to consider, particularly in the poultry and pork industries.
These are longstanding, technical issues involving imports and exports. Local producers react when imports affect their production or export potential, and experts from our respective departments have been negotiating with them for an extended period.
But there are also political issues. The US government has raised a number of concerns about South Africa over the past 18 months, and those weigh on the discussions too.
How much of your time is spent on those political disputes, as opposed to trade and investment?
I think it is 50-50. The political relationship has been tense since the executive order on South Africa in February last year, which covered a number of issues and led to the five asks or demands.
My responsibility is both political and commercial. It is about how we keep trade going and expand it.
Do you think the tensions will ease, or have the problems become more entrenched?
It is difficult to say. Some of the geopolitical issues concerning the US were already present under the previous administration, and some concerns coming from Capitol Hill are bipartisan.
Part of the embassyâs job is to address misunderstandings and relay US concerns to our government. We may make assumptions in Pretoria that are wrong, too. It is my responsibility to give the president and government as clear a picture as possible.
Could changes to Black Economic Empowerment policies help attract more investment, particularly in mining and telecommunications?
The BEE framework has evolved from an initial focus on equity toward equity-equivalence measures. Many companies have adjusted to those measures and invested on that basis.
There is still room for further adjustments, particularly in mining and telecommunications. Those sectors have a different character under the current framework, and we discuss possible changes internally and with companies that want to invest.
You have been in Washington for about five months. How would you sum up the state of the relationship?
South Africa had no representation in Washington for some period before I arrived, so there is a lot of catching up to do across the executive and legislative branches. I think we have started to make progress.
But we are still in a stalemate with the executive. I am not satisfied with where we find ourselves. As long as this situation persists, further attention is required, and policy positions may need to change.
My task is to establish exactly what the issues are and report back to Pretoria, while convincing decision-makers here that Pretoriaâs intent is to establish a solid relationship.

Efforts to cap global temperature rises have largely failed and a breach of the Paris Agreementâs limit of 1.5â is now âinevitable,â the UN said.
Overall global warming is now likely to be between 2.6â and 2.8â by the end of the century, the UN Environment Programme predicted.
It warned that the best-case scenario â in which humanity overshoots its target but ultimately reverts to it â would require cuts to global emissions of about 45% by 2035; current national plans, even if fully implemented, would only lead to reductions of up to 15%.
Yet, UNEP argued, âcountries can still limit peak warming, shorten the duration of overshoot, and keep the goals of the Paris Agreement within reach.â

Witkoffâs visit follows what a US official called âconstructiveâ meetings with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and other European leaders.
Kyiv is coming under increased pressure from Washington: US President Donald Trump has pushed Zelenskyy to âmake a deal,â which a senior EU official said could force a âsurrender on Putinâs terms.â

Anthropic reportedly plans to spend $750 billion on adding compute capacity in the coming years, including hundreds of billions in non-cancelable deals, as AI labs race to finance a huge infrastructure buildout. 5a8c5f344dd7.text: White House envoy Steve Witkoff on Wednesday asked Russian President Vladimir Putin to allow the resumption of trilateral peace talks between Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. in order to reach an end to the war. Why it matters: The White House hopes Putin will show more willingness to compromise after President Trump agreed to lift sanctions on Russian diesel sales and took other steps welcomed by Moscow. Driving the news: Witkoff presented Putin with an updated proposal to end the war in Ukraine during a meeting in St. Petersburg. Before the meeting, Russia released U.S. citizen Stephen Hubbard, 74, who had spent more than four years in captivity after being seized by Russian troops in eastern Ukraine in April 2022. Putin announced his release at the top of the meeting with Witkoff. "He is at Pulkovo Airport," Putin told Witkoff in front of the cameras. "Stephen is on his way back home and will soon be with his family. The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return - an unprecedented situation for Russia. There was no 'swap' necessary for this release," Trump wrote on Truth Social. State of play: Witkoff arrived in Russia after a day of talks in Oslo , Norway, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, as well as the leaders of Norway and Finland and representatives from France, the U.K., Germany, Poland, the EU and NATO. Zelensky said Tuesday that the next step should be a trilateral meeting between him, Putin and Trump — a format Russia has so far rejected. The discussions in Oslo focused on developing a unified proposal for a "framework agreement" to end the war. What he is saying: "I believe the talks [in Oslo] were productive, and I would like to say that there is progress, and I will update you on this. I hope that we have truly laid the groundwork for a successful end to hostilities in this Ukrainian-Russian conflict," Witkoff told Putin. Witkoff asked Putin to "consider resuming trilateral talks involving Ukraine, Russia, and the United States, where we could discuss the next steps toward achieving a settlement." Witkoff said the talks could include representatives of technical groups of specialists who could discuss these issues in detail. "We have brought several documents outlining approaches to achieving a peaceful settlement in the Ukrainian-Russian conflict. I would ask you, Mr. President, to review these documents a little later," Witkoff said. The intrigue : Putin also told Witkoff he wants to discuss possible Russian mediation between the U.S. and Iran. "You know that we have a special, trusting relationship with Iran, with our partners in Iran, our friends, built over decades, and if there's anything we can do to resolve this crisis, we'll be happy to do so. You're also well aware of our proposals in this area," Putin said. What's next: Putin told Witkoff he wants to discuss a possible meeting with Trump in China in mid-November.

0d5cfd349347.text:
The minute Gabriela Farfan stepped into a small natural history museum in Madison, Wis., where she grew up, she knew she wanted to work with minerals. Farfan remembers seeing all different shapes and colors and being enthralled. “From that point forward, I knew I wanted to become a geologist someday,” she says.
Farfan is now living her teenage dream as the curator of gems and minerals at the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History in Washington, D.C. Her specialty is biomineralization — how organisms build skeletons, corals, pearls and shells. Farfan hopes to answer questions about how they form and what stories they tell by studying crystal structures and the chemistry of minerals.
These days, she investigates signals trapped within minerals. Corals, for example, build layers of calcium carbonate mineral over time, trapping chemical signatures from the ocean. The data tell all kinds of stories — about stress, disease outbreaks and changes to ocean temperature and sea level. Farfan unlocks those tales using X-ray and Raman spectroscopies, bouncing beams off samples to see what they can tell us.
She hopes museum visitors will remember that the sparkly gemstones, the ones that first enamored her, are just as natural as the plants and bones in other exhibits. “Minerals are actual natural history objects,” Farfan says. “Those are actually formed by Mother Nature and it’s spectacular.”
